Voyager 1's light-day milestone: See the photos behind the discoveries

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1474 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Livescience

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that early Wednesday (Nov.
  • The milestone is largely symbolic, but it comes with practical consequences: While Voyager 1 cruises through interstellar space at roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from our planet, it now takes a full 24 hours for radio signals moving at the speed of light to get from Voyager 1 to Earth, and vice versa.
  • In a recent development, the growing space between Voyager and Earth makes it increasingly hard to troubleshoot problems on the nearly 50-year-old probe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that early Wednesday (Nov. 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit a newly introduced space exploration milestone: The probe, which launched in 1977, became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth.

The milestone is largely symbolic, but it comes with practical consequences: While Voyager 1 cruises through interstellar space at roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from our planet, it now takes a full 24 hours for radio signals moving at the speed of light to get from Voyager 1 to Earth, and vice versa.

In a recent development, the growing space between Voyager and Earth makes it increasingly hard to troubleshoot problems on the nearly 50-year-old probe. But with Voyager 1 still collecting data with two of its science instruments, which are expected to stay powered up into the 2030s, NASA scientists say one thing is certain: The spacecraft isn't done surprising us.

It has been revealed that "What Voyager has taught me is to expect the unexpected," Linda Spilker, who joined the Voyager team in 1977 and is the mission's current project scientist, told Live Science in an interview. "So many times the ideas and theories we had, Voyager was able to prove them wrong.".

Here, we look back at some of Voyager 1's most groundbreaking discoveries, told through its incredible photos.

NASA's Voyager 1 probe releases atop a Titan/Centaur-6 launch vehicle from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

It has been revealed that NASA's Voyager 2 probe released before Voyager 1, on Aug. 20, 1977. Voyager 1 took off a few weeks later, on Sept. 5. (The two spacecraft took slightly different routes through the solar system, allowing Voyager 1 to reach interstellar space first after a gravity boost from Jupiter and Saturn.).

Spilker, who joined NASA right out of college, attended the historic Voyager 2 launch and recalls "that feeling of watching the rocket lift up off the launchpad, feeling the roar of those rocket engines and knowing this was a mission going to visit places I'd always been curious about.".

A few weeks after launching, Voyager 1 took this photo of a crescent Earth and moon from 7.25 million miles (11.66 million km) from Earth.

On its way to the outer solar system, Voyager 1 snapped this image of a crescent Earth and its moon, captured in the same frame for the first time ever.

Voyager 1 photographed Jupiter from January to April 1979, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As the spacecraft zoomed closer to the giant planet, it snapped an image every 96 seconds, creating this incredible time-lapse animation of the planet's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of one Earth month.

The close-up view demonstrated that Jupiter is a far more dynamic world than previously thought. But Voyager also made key discoveries about the planet's many moons.

According to recent reports, while passing by the Jovian moon Io, Voyager 1 witnessed an explosion: the first volcanic eruption ever seen beyond Earth. This proved that there were other geologically active worlds in our solar system, opening up entirely newly introduced avenues of inquiry and exploration.

A blue eruption on Jupiter's moon Io, the first volcanic eruption seen on another world.

"Going in, we thought that the moons would look a lot like our own moon: ancient dead worlds," Spilker noted. "And yet we found out they were very different worlds — like Io with active volcanoes. It was just an incredible change in our thinking.".

By viewing these eruptions, scientists saw parts of Io's surface being changed in real time. "As we got closer [to Io], scientists kept saying the surface is getting younger and younger, because they didn't see any big craters, no medium sized craters, no little craters — until finally parts of its surface are just minutes old," Spilker remarked.

A mosaic view of Callisto taken from Voyager 1 photos at a distance of about 250,000 miles (400,000 km).

In a recent development, some of Voyager's close-up observations also confirmed old theories. For example, Voyager 1's flyby of the moon Callisto in March 1979 revealed vast fields of well-preserved impact craters, proving that Callisto was geologically dead.

Jupiter and its thin ring of dust backlit by the sun in a Voyager 1 image.

Recent findings suggest that A final surprise at Jupiter came when Voyager 1 swooped around the planet's nightside, seeing the gas giant backlit by the sun. This view revealed a thin ring system around the planet, made partly of the dust particles Io spewed into space.

Industry observers note that voyager 1 reached Saturn in November 1980 and made its closest approach to the planet on Nov. 12 of that year. Four days later, the spacecraft took this image of the planet's nightside, showing a broad shadow cast onto the surrounding rings.

"That is one of my favorite pictures: an outbound image, taken by Voyager looking at [Saturn] in a way you could never see from the Earth," Spilker mentioned, noting that we can only ever see Saturn's sunlit side from our planet. "The rings just look so beautiful shining there, and you can actually see the shadow of Saturn on the rings themselves. It's a really, really special picture.".

In addition to discovering a previously unknown ring, Voyager 1 spotted five new moons around Saturn and took close-up photos of several other known satellites.

Voyager 1's closeup view of Titan revealed a dense, hazy atmosphere.

Recent findings suggest that the mission required Voyager to swing by the moon Titan in order to bend the probe's trajectory, sending it away from the solar system's planetary plane and toward a rendezvous with interstellar space. Before that, Voyager 1 revealed Titan's atmosphere to be so hazy that it completely obscured the moon's surface. This demonstrated that Titan's clogged atmosphere was far denser than those of Earth and Mars.

Sources indicate that by 1990, Voyager 1 was so far from the planetary plane that our solar system's planets looked like little more than specks of light. But before turning off its camera for good, Voyager 1 looked back at our cosmic neighborhood and took some of the most iconic space photos of all time.

Industry observers note that in a series of 64 images taken from roughly 40 times Earth's distance from the sun, Voyager snapped its solar system "family portrait," a mosaic of images capturing six planets together for the first time. The portrait included views of Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Frames from Voyager 1's family portrait showing Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.

The image of Earth from this collection is famously known as the "Pale Blue Dot.".

"We took the pictures of the planets in color, and that one is especially one of my favorites," Spilker noted. "There's Earth captured in a sunbeam. A tiny world less than a pixel in size representing all the life that we know in our solar system — just a very special image reminding us just how special and precious our planet is.".

Earth appears as a pale blue dot in this iconic Voyager 1 image.

Voyager 1 turned off its camera immediately after taking these images, concluding its role as the greatest tourist in the history of our solar system. In 2012, Voyager 1 passed beyond the heliopause — the boundary where the sun's radiation gives way to the interstellar medium — becoming the first interstellar spacecraft in history.

Recent findings suggest that voyager 2 crossed the same boundary in 2018 and is expected to reach its own light-day in 2035. In the meantime, several science instruments remain active on both probes, allowing them to measure the strange and mysterious environment between stars.

Even way out there, the probes are still detecting whispers of the sun's power.

"We are still seeing effects from the sun that come out, hit the heliopause, and send shocks and pressure fronts out into the interstellar medium," Spilker said. "I wonder where we will finally reach the point where the sun doesn't influence what we're seeing, and we're in the pristine interstellar medium — and I hope that happens while Voyager 1 is still operating.".

Brandon is the space / physics editor at Live Science. With more than 20 years of editorial experience, his writing has appeared in The Washington Post, Reader's Digest, CBS.com, the Richard Dawkins Foundation website and other outlets. He holds a bachelor's degree in creative writing from the University of Arizona, with minors in journalism and media arts. His interests include black holes, asteroids and comets, and the search for extraterrestrial life.

It has been revealed that A good host is always thinking of others, whether it’s by making guests feel welcome, accommodating everyone’s diets, or setting an Instagram-worthy tablescape to make the night feel extra special. But the holiday season is an opportunity to flip the script and show the host you’re thinking of them, too. Bringing them a gift is the cardinal way to thank the host for all their thoughtful work. The only question remains: what to give?

For those who delight in trotting out their special dinnerware for guests, there’s a world of creative and whimsical gifts out there, even if it seems like they already have the entire CB2 catalog. And if that is the case, this just means you, as the gift-giver, can allow them to indulge in the things they typically would not. Take, for instance, some unique vintage shot glasses, intricately carved chopsticks, and pearl cocktail picks. Not only do these playful takes on essentials inspire joy, but they’re also sure to be conversation starters for future gatherings. And, as the bestower of the new treasured piece, you just might secure yourself the invite for the next one.

You can never have enough serving utensils if you love to host. That moment when you toss your pasta salad, plate everyone’s green beans, or dole out your main dish is an opportunity to flex some of your more decorative yet functional kitchen tools. This ethereal stainless steel set from Leif boasts pewter star-shaped handles with sea glass.

Even Diaspora Spice Co.’s everyday spices come in bold, ready-to-gift packaging, but the equitable spice tech giant’s new holiday spice sampler gift box is an extra colorful treat for the senses. The bundle includes samples of its beloved Nandini coriander, a rare Ceylon cinnamon, a Himalayan foothills-sourced pink garlic powder, and several more spices to inspire your host.

When it comes to gift-giving, we believe in working smarter, not harder. Case in point: Buy a set of nice-looking vintage glasses — these are labeled shot glasses by the seller, but they’re just as nice for sipping cordials — and rather than giving one lovely host a set of eight, split them up into pairs or fours and use them for multiple gifting situations. There’s always a use for little glasses like this (and they’re pretty enough to display, too).

It’s pretty fun to use a posh plaid napkin when you’re digging into some quiche or sipping on mulled wine.

It’s always fun to kick off an evening of cocktails with a caviar bump, which is what makes this Imperia Caviar bundle such a gift for the avid party host. The 30-gram tin of royal ossetra comes with a mother-of-pearl spoon and a caviar tin opener in a velvet bag, and the bundle’s compact size means you can simply slide it into your purse or jacket on the way to the function (unlike a heavy bottle of wine or olive oil, which would likely need their owns bags).

It has been revealed that it really has been the year of the dirty martini. For those who are building a bar cart (or want to start), getting a couple of sets of proper cocktail picks can be a game-changer. Nothing wrong with a traditional wood toothpick, of course, but it really does add a lot of pizzazz to a martini to bite the olives off a pearl-emblazoned skewer.

In a recent development, swooning will abound once people get a look at these beautiful walnut chopsticks featuring inlaid geometric designs. Another great example of “practical, but nicer to look at than what you might get for yourself.” Plus, you can grab a set of five on sale right now for under $20.

When it comes to cocktail cherries, one brand truly reigns supreme: Luxardo, which has been making candied cherries soaked in marasca syrup for 120 years. A classic for a reason!

Jonathan Adler is another designer to keep tabs on when it comes to playful but elevated home decor. This set of Matisse-esque coasters also has a slight lip to keep condensation from spilling, and would be prime for serving up lychee martinis the next time you gather with friends. Snag them while they’re 40% off for Black Friday.

Halen Môn is a salt nerd’s dream. The organic, hand-harvested sea salt hails from the tides of the Isle of Anglesey in Wales (Halen is Welsh for salt; Môn is Welsh for Anglesey), and has earned numerous awards for its subtle crunch and crisp mineral flavor. Any host would be thrilled to receive a bag of the stuff, but this gift set combines the salt with a charming ceramic cellar and spoon.

Matches are always a solid host gift, and a small but useful present that’s made all the better with cool packaging. The lifestyle brand State the Label, for example, has housed its matches in a folk art-inspired cottage (the striker paper is on the bottom of the house).

According to recent reports, those who like to entertain likely appreciate a good placemat. This set of two block-printed placemats from West Elm puts a romantic spin on the dining-table staple with painterly tones and bright hues. Who wouldn’t love to receive these dreamy accents?

Is your host a lover of ice-cold martinis? Perfect gift incoming: Quincy’s fabulous olives, which have superb flavor and are ratioed with drink-perfect brine to make exactly 14 dirty martinis per jar.

Scents are tricky. Unless you really know your host, refrain from gifting them scented candles, and opt for a beeswax pillar candle instead; they can light it sans candelabra (unless you’re sure that they own one and prefer tapers) by simply placing it on a small plate. Above all, beeswax candles make a wonderful dining companion, because they don’t emit the same stuffy, paraffin wax-based smoke as non-beeswax candles.

Sometimes, brevity is wit. Give it to someone who means business, or orders the business women special.

We all love a little Le Creuset in our kitchens, but a Dutch oven isn’t in the price range for what we’d consider an easy host gift. Enter the butter dish, a fabulous little thing to present and say “I brought you something,” presented with a kiss on the cheek and maybe a bouquet of flowers or bottle of wine.

Taking Weight-Loss Drugs? Latest Study Reveals Why Lifting Weights Could Be Essential

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (792 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As weight-loss medications become increasingly common, a clinical trial suggests that three weekly strength-training sessions could help people preserve muscle and maintain physical independence.
  • Losing weight is often the goal for people taking medications such as Ozempic and Mounjaro, but the number on the scale does not tell the whole story.
  • A new study found that adults taking a powerful weight-loss drug shed nearly 50 pounds in 40 weeks, regardless of whether they exercised.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As weight-loss medications become increasingly common, a clinical trial suggests that three weekly strength-training sessions could help people preserve muscle and maintain physical independence.

Losing weight is often the goal for people taking medications such as Ozempic and Mounjaro, but the number on the scale does not tell the whole story.

A new study found that adults taking a powerful weight-loss drug shed nearly 50 pounds in 40 weeks, regardless of whether they exercised. Those who also lifted weights, however, preserved more lean tissue and became stronger, while participants who did not train experienced a decline in strength.

The findings address a growing concern surrounding medications such as semaglutide (Ozempic and Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro). These drugs can produce substantial weight loss and have been found to improve chronic health conditions, reduce the risk of obesity-related cardiovascular disease, and enhance quality of life. However, losing so much weight raises questions about how much muscle people might lose along the way.

“Loss of lean mass, including muscle, is an inevitable part of weight loss by any method – whether through diet and exercise alone, or medical or surgical interventions,” noted Winthrop Professor Danny Green, lead investigator from The University of Western Australia’s School of Human Sciences and HealthSpan Institute.

Lean mass includes everything in the body other than fat, such as muscles, bones, organs, skin, and water. Muscle mass refers specifically to muscle tissue, mostly skeletal muscle. Preserving that tissue is particularly key for people hoping to maintain their strength and physical independence as they lose weight.

“With GLP-1 medicines now widely used and reducing body weight by an average of 20-25 percent, and more than that in many people, it’s crucial that we understand how best to achieve optimal body composition and health in the weight-reduced state.”.

To investigate whether exercise could help, researchers conducted the Tirzepatide and Resistance Exercise (T-REx) study, published in Nature Medicine. It is the first study to examine the combined effects of a GLP-1 medication and resistance training on body composition, muscle mass, strength, and a range of cardiovascular health measures.

It has been revealed that the 40-week trial involved 120 men and postmenopausal women between the ages of 50 and 70. All participants had obesity or were overweight with at least one weight-related health condition. None had type 2 diabetes, and all were prescribed tirzepatide for weight management.

Half the participants completed three resistance-training sessions each week, while the others did not follow a resistance-training program. Everyone received general guidance on hydration, protein consumption, and fiber intake.

Industry observers note that by the end of the study, both groups had experienced substantial weight loss. Participants who exercised lost an average of 22.28 kilograms (49.1 pounds), compared with 22.61 kilograms (49.8 pounds) among those who did not train.

In a recent development, most of that weight loss came from fat. The resistance-training group lost an average of 17.98 kilograms (39.6 pounds) of fat mass, while the group without resistance training lost 17.19 kilograms (37.9 pounds).

The more meaningful difference emerged when researchers examined lean tissue and physical strength. Participants who lifted weights lost 25 percent less lean tissue, including muscle, than those who did not exercise. Their upper- and lower-body strength also increased by 10 percent, compared with a 10 percent decline among participants who did not undertake resistance training.

“We now know that muscle loss can be reduced and strength increased when regular resistance training is used alongside tirzepatide treatment.”.

It has been revealed that for Green, the results suggest that resistance exercise should be part of the prescription for people taking weight-loss medications such as tirzepatide. The goal, he explained, should extend beyond reaching a lower body weight to maintaining the physical abilities that support long-term health.

“This study demonstrates that combining weight loss therapy and resistance exercise improves overall health,” Professor Green remarked.

“In theory, that should translate to a longer healthspan, the number of healthy, independent, and productive years of life that are lived free from debilitating chronic diseases.”.

In a recent development, whether these improvements ultimately translate into more years of healthy, independent living remains to be established. However, the findings suggest that resistance training can help people achieve a more favorable balance between weight loss, lean tissue preservation, and strength during tirzepatide treatment.

Reference: “Resistance exercise to attenuate lean mass loss during tirzepatide therapy for obesity: a randomized controlled trial” by Daniel J. Green, Andrew Haynes, Destiny R. Underwood, Evangeline R. Winterton, Abbey A. Green, Robin M. Daly, Elena S. George, Leanne Lester, Louise H. Naylor, Graham S. Hillis, P. Gerry Fegan and Bu B. Yeap, 9 November 2026, Nature Medicine. DOI: 10.1038/s41591-026-04752-5.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Upcoming England is the ancestral home of moderate Republicans, from the Saltonstalls to the Bushes, whose fiscal conservatism and social moderation defined the national GOP for decades.

Last week, Yankee Republicans suffered a near-total wipeout. Maine’s Susan Collins, Fresh England's last GOP senator, lost her seat to Democrat Troy Jackson, leaving former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, who just won a House seat, as the lone Republican headed to Congress from the region. (The picture was a bit brighter at the state level, where GOP Govs. Phil Scott of Vermont and Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire were both reelected.).

In a recent development, one Republican operative sees a path out of the wilderness in a post-Trump era. In an opinion piece in The Boston Globe, consultant Kristin Tate urged New England Republicans to focus on fiscal discipline and recognize that “independence from national party leadership can be a political asset, not an act of betrayal.”.

After all, as the midterm election results remind us, no political realignment lasts forever.

According to recent reports, three decades ago, there were plenty of moderate Democrats from Southern states serving in Congress, governor’s mansions and even the White House. But in the years since Bill Clinton's exit from the political stage, Democrats have largely written off the South.

Recent findings suggest that which is partly why last week’s Democratic wins in the Carolinas, Georgia and, perhaps most notably, Mississippi were so stunning. All the elements that powered the party to victory nationally – disillusionment with Donald Trump, a rise in economic populism and hunger for change – played a role in the South as well.

But other factors were unique to a region that has seen renewed attempts to dilute Black political power with the redrawing of House districts to favor the GOP.

The Republican redistricting gambit in Southern states did not fully yield the desired results and seems to have helped galvanize Black voters and their allies, powering Democrats to unlikely victories.

It’s too soon to say whether the GOP’s reduced hold on the South represents a temporary blip or an enduring shift.

But Joe Trippi, a longtime Democratic strategist who advised candidates in Alabama and Florida this year, has a message for his party: “We need to invest in the South.”.

It has been revealed that #MSSEN: Democrat Scott Colom defeated GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction and the first in his party to win a Senate seat in the Magnolia State since 1982.

Tar Heel tidal wave: Democrats in North Carolina have picked up at least five House seats, a striking development given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Prior to last week, no House Republican incumbent had lost a general election in the state since Republicans won control of the redistricting process more than a decade ago. And the Democratic gains could grow: In the 5th District, former journalist Chuck Hubbard narrowly leads 11-term Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx, and in the 3rd District, former state Rep. Raymond Smith holds a razor-thin edge over Republican Rep. Greg Murphy. The Associated Press had not called either race at publication time, though Murphy has conceded.

Republicans pick campaign chairs: Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack will be the chairs of Republicans’ respective campaign committees for the 2028 cycle. GOP lawmakers held their leadership elections Tuesday, as our colleagues Savannah Behrmann and John T. Bennett reported. Senate Republicans are sticking with South Dakota’s John Thune to lead them in the next Congress, while House Republicans picked former Freedom Caucus Chair Jim Jordan as their leader.

It has been revealed that redistricting doubts: Maryland could be getting a new congressional map after voters approved a constitutional amendment that would clear the way for new lines in 2028. Our colleague Victor Feldman has more on the result and other election-related ballot measures across the country. But it’s not clear how many other states may look to redistrict next cycle after Republican efforts over the past 18 months largely didn’t pay off in last week’s elections.

Run the table: With Rep. Darren Soto winning a sixth term in Florida, no Democratic incumbent lost reelection to a Republican this year. Soto’s win in a redrawn district also meant that Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had targeted under a new congressional map.

According to recent reports, california contest: Rep. Ken Calvert defeated fellow Republican Rep. Young Kim in a rare member-versus-member contest for a redrawn Southern California seat that turned acrimonious. Republicans are poised to hold just four House seats in the Golden State after Democrats made good on five pickup opportunities under a new congressional map.

Cheesecake Factory caucus: The latest episode of the Political Theater podcast, hosted by Roll Call editor-in-chief Jason Dick, breaks down how candidates in both parties fared in counties where The Cheesecake Factory operates, after the popular chain restaurant became something of a side character in the closing weeks of the midterm campaign.

Back to school: Newly elected members of Congress are on Capitol Hill this week for freshman orientation, an experience Massachusetts Rep.-elect Dan Koh told our colleague Nina Heller is “like high school – but it’s fun high school.” The incoming lawmakers took their class photo Thursday morning and will get to pick their Capitol Hill offices after next week’s famed lottery, Nina writes.

Recent findings suggest that tracking the count: As of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time Thursday, House Democrats had flipped 44 seats, while Republicans had picked up three. Twelve races remain uncalled, including a pair in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. On the Senate side, Democrats have flipped eight seats, with only Alaska’s race still undecided.

It has been revealed that guv update: Democrats flipped at least five governorships last week and will hold a majority of governor’s mansions next year. Two gubernatorial races remain uncalled by the AP: Kansas, where Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher is narrowly ahead of Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson, and Alaska, where Democratic former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is just below the 50 percent threshold to win the election outright. In territorial elections, Republicans flipped the governor’s office in Guam while voters in the Northern Mariana Islands will pick their next governor in a Nov. 20 runoff.

#TNSEN: Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected Tennessee governor last week, is poised to pick her Senate successor. According to the Nashville Banner, the short list includes Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs, a former professional wrestler, Reps. Tim Burchett and Chuck Fleischmann, and Tennessee Deputy Gov. Stuart McWhorter.

2028 on the brain: A handful of House Democrats are already considering 2028 Senate bids, according to Axios, including Kansas’ Sharice Davids, North Carolina’s Don Davis and Pennsylvania’s Chris DeLuzio.

Industry observers note that senator Morrison? Minnesota Rep. Kelly Morrison is earning buzz as a potential appointee to fill the Senate seat that Democrat Amy Klobuchar is vacating to become governor, Semafor reports. House Democrats aren’t likely to be as concerned about open seats as their Republican counterparts were in recent years, given the size of the incoming Democratic majority.

AOC’s future: Progressive activists have rolled out a new organization to encourage New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president in 2028. Meanwhile, Axios reports that Ocasio-Cortez has parted ways with the digital fundraising firm she’s worked with for several years and has brought on the same firm that Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders used during his two presidential campaigns.

In a recent development, women lead: Shirley Emehelu is Newly introduced Jersey’s new lieutenant governor after Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill picked her to succeed Dale Caldwell, who resigned in September amid sexual harassment allegations and other ethical lapses. New Jersey is now one of five states to have women in both the governor’s and lieutenant governor’s offices, along with Massachusetts, Arkansas, Iowa and Virginia. Iowa will come off the list next year after an all-male Democratic ticket swept this year’s gubernatorial race, though five other states elected women to both offices last week.

Congress will once again be filled with losers – i.e, latest members who have lost previous bids for elected office. Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections returns to his biennial tradition as he runs down the latest list of “losers.”.

Industry observers note that ducking the wave: Democrats notched significant wins in unexpected places, but one state grew redder after last week’s elections. The Upcoming York Times checks in with voters in South Dakota, where the GOP won all nine statewide elections.

Here come the MBAs: Democrats with corporate connections were among the winners in last week’s elections, countering the idea that candidates with serious business credentials have struggled within the party, The Wall Street Journal reports. The field of 19 winners with M.B.A. degrees includes Costco board member Helena Buonanno Foulkes, who won the Rhode Island governor’s race, and Paige Cognetti, a Goldman Sachs alum who flipped a House seat in Pennsylvania.

Recent findings suggest that how Ricketts did it: Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts’ election night success was one of the few bright spots for the GOP. Ricketts fended off a challenge from independent Dan Osborn by painting him as a Democrat, questioning his authenticity and highlighting leaked audio of his comments denigrating Trump voters, writes the Nebraska Examiner.

According to recent reports, was it necessary? California redrew its congressional map to favor Democrats in response to Texas taking a similar step to boost the GOP. But some are questioning whether the state needed to cast aside its independent redistricting commission to rejigger the lines, given the scale of Democrats’ wins. “What they were literally saying is, ‘Let’s undo democracy to protect democracy,’” Lincoln Project co-founder Mike Madrid told CalMatters. “There’s something very Orwellian about it.”.

Song of the cycle: The New York Times reviews “Talafreako,” an unlikely viral anthem celebrating the newly elected Democratic senator from Texas.

History does rhyme: An opinion piece in The (Charleston) Post & Courier argues that the win by Democratic Sen.-elect Annie Andrews is the latest in a long line of cases in which South Carolina voters bucked the idea of party bosses picking their leaders.

The man behind the grill: The Latest York Times profiles Russ Hudson, the Mississippi man in Colom’s now-legendary “Pick another protein” ad.

That was the last time Democrats won 11 House seats in North Carolina.

As of Thursday afternoon, they appear on track to match that number. They’ve already won nine seats – a mark they last cleared in the 1982 midterms – and they’re narrowly ahead in two more races.

Sources indicate that if those leads hold, Democrats' 11-member delegation would look much different than the one sworn in some 66 years ago in 1961. Tar Heel Democrats taking office in January would include four women, six Black members and one Hispanic member.

Their 11 representatives (out of 12) in the 87th Congress were all white men who consistently voted to uphold racial segregation and oppose major federal civil rights legislation.

Vote counting in Alaska is expected to conclude by Wednesday, Nov. 18, the targeted date for ranked choice tabulations in races in which no candidate took more than 50 percent of the vote. As of Thursday, Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in the Senate race, though she’s below the 50 percent threshold.

Meanwhile, Democrats are gathering in Denver beginning Thursday to celebrate their historic wins and plot their next steps.

Millions Turn to Turmeric for Joint Pain. Does It Really Work?

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (637 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A closer examination of clinical trial reliability raises newly introduced questions about earlier research suggesting turmeric could help people with knee osteoarthritis.
  • Turmeric supplements are widely promoted as a natural way to ease joint pain, but a major newly introduced scientific review has cast doubt on their effectiveness for knee osteoarthritis.
  • According to recent reports, the findings come from a latest Cochrane review that examined both the results of clinical trials and the reliability of the research behind them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A closer examination of clinical trial reliability raises newly introduced questions about earlier research suggesting turmeric could help people with knee osteoarthritis.

Turmeric supplements are widely promoted as a natural way to ease joint pain, but a major newly introduced scientific review has cast doubt on their effectiveness for knee osteoarthritis. Researchers found little convincing evidence that the popular supplements provide clinically meaningful pain relief, challenging earlier studies that suggested they could help.

According to recent reports, the findings come from a latest Cochrane review that examined both the results of clinical trials and the reliability of the research behind them. Although the evidence remains uncertain, the analysis found no clear advantage for turmeric over placebo or commonly used anti-inflammatory medications.

Sources indicate that the international research team analyzed nine studies involving 1,245 people with knee osteoarthritis. The trials compared turmeric supplements with placebo, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen and diclofenac, and paracetamol. Participants received different turmeric extracts and curcuminoid formulations, with treatment periods ranging from four weeks to three months.

Turmeric contains curcuminoids, including curcumin, which have anti-inflammatory properties. These compounds have attracted interest as potential treatments for osteoarthritis, a disease involving damage and changes throughout the joint. Inflammation can contribute to pain and other symptoms, but the condition has multiple underlying causes. Exercise and medications can help manage symptoms, although no cure presently exists.

In a recent development, previous systematic reviews generally reported improvements in pain and physical function among people taking turmeric supplements. However, the latest Cochrane analysis applied more rigorous screening procedures to assess whether individual clinical trials were trustworthy enough to support reliable conclusions.

Ten trials raised concerns during this screening process and were excluded from the analysis while researchers sought clarification from their authors. Earlier reviews had also included broader categories of studies, such as those involving osteoarthritis diagnosed solely through imaging, non-oral turmeric treatments, or curcumin combined with other active ingredients. These methodological differences may partly explain the conflicting conclusions.

“This review highlights the importance of assessing the trustworthiness of clinical trials,” adds Dr Shirinsky. “Such assessments help identify studies that require further clarification before their findings can be used to inform conclusions about treatment effects.”.

The researchers used a screening method developed by the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth group. Other approaches, including INSPECT-SR, have since been developed to identify potentially problematic studies before their findings influence scientific reviews.

Industry observers note that dr. Ivan Shirinsky, the review’s lead author and a practicing rheumatologist, remarked the results reflect the broader challenges of treating a disease with complex biological mechanisms.

“As a clinician and researcher, I am not surprised by these findings. Osteoarthritis is a complex and still incompletely understood disease. Despite intensive research, effective pharmacological treatment options remain limited, and many promising approaches have yielded limited or inconclusive evidence of clinical benefit. A better understanding of the mechanisms underlying osteoarthritis may help us develop more effective treatments in the future.”.

The review does not establish that turmeric supplements are ineffective in every circumstance. Rather, the available research does not provide sufficiently reliable evidence of a clinically notable benefit. Shirinsky said this uncertainty would shape how he advises patients considering turmeric for knee pain.

It has been revealed that “I would not routinely recommend turmeric supplements to my patients with knee osteoarthritis. However, if a patient asked me about them, I would explain what we know and what remains uncertain about their benefits and potential harms, and help them make an informed decision.”.

Reference: “Curcuma longa (turmeric) or its active ingredients for osteoarthritis” by Ivan Shirinsky, Valery Shirinsky, Katerina Filatova, Ze Yu Yu, Fredh Netterström Wedin, Yuan Chi and Chris Bleakley, 19 November 2026, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. DOI: 10.1002/14651858.CD014683.pub2.

ESA's Hera Probe Uses "Superhuman" Vision to Inspect NASA's Asteroid Crash Site

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (972 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Around four years ago, humanity intentionally hit an asteroid.
  • Industry observers note that the lack of accurate measurement isnât for lack of trying.
  • Industry observers note that to help clear up any ambiguity about the math underlying this planetary defense mission, Hera is equipped with three main imaging tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Around four years ago, humanity intentionally hit an asteroid. The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) was by pretty much all measures a resounding success when it struck the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos going more than 22,000 kilometers per hour. However, we still donât know just how much of a success it actually was - DART was a one-way mission with no real way to track the results of the impact close up. Enter Hera, the European Space Agency (ESA) mission that recently arrived in the binary asteroid system. Now, in a press release, ESA has provided some of the best pictures of the binary system since that fateful day four years ago.

Industry observers note that the lack of accurate measurement isnât for lack of trying. Ground-based observatories have been watching 151m wide Dimorphos and its parent asteroid, 780m wide Didymos very closely over the last four years. They could tell that Dimorphos slowed its orbit around its larger companion by about 33 minutes. But some scientists were surprised by the magnitude of the change in orbit, based on the theoretical math done before the mission.

Industry observers note that to help clear up any ambiguity about the math underlying this planetary defense mission, Hera is equipped with three main imaging tools. Its standard âeyesâ are the Asteroid Framing cameras, which handle both black-and-white photography and navigation. The press release showcases an image from this system showing Didymos from roughly 28.5km away, with features down to roughly 2.7m per pixel.

Fraser talks about Hera's final insertion into the binary asteroid system.

It has been revealed that in the image, you can clearly see the âspinning topâ shape of the larger asteroid in the pair. Didymos spins at a relatively rapid speed for its size, completing a rotation every 2.2 hours. That energy is strong enough to pull boulders and gravel towards the middle of the asteroid, causing a build-up of material that makes it look fatter in the middle than at its poles.

However, seeing an asteroid in black in white isnât as scientifically useful as seeing it in âcolorâ. That is what Heraâs second imaging system, the HyperScout H instrument, is designed to do. It monitors the asteroid over 25 different color bands. With that information, HyperScout H can absorb and reflect light with different unique patterns - essentially it can spectroscopy. Comparing the results to lab experiments on meteorite samples on Earth will help determine what Didymos and its smaller companion are actually made up of.

But why stop at simple hyperspectral imaging when you can also have heat vision? The Thermal Infrared Imager (TIRI), supplied to ESA by Japanâs Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) gives Hera âSuperman-likeâ heat vision according to the press release. TIRI maps the temperature of the surface of the asteroids, and since solid rock dissipates heat much more slowly than porous or fragmented rock, it will also give a good indication of how solid Didymos really is.

Fraser talks about some of the results of the DART test.

Crucially, Dimorphos itself, the actual subject of the original DART test, is surprisingly absent from many of the pictures in this first round of releases. In the visible light images, Dimorphos is tucked almost entirely into the shadow of Didymos, appearing as a tiny sunlit spec beneath Didymos in one of the images. But with TIRIâs âSupermanâ view, the entire 151m wide asteroid is clearly in focus, glowing a shade of cool purple in the infrared. Cameras arenât the only thing Hera is carrying either. It will eventually launch two CubeSats, Juventus and Milan, to study the asteroid binary very closely. They will use ground-penetrating radar and even touch down on the surface of Dimorphos in an effort to understand what itstruly made of.

Industry observers note that but ultimately the overarching purpose of the mission is to get a better idea of how effectively we can move an asteroid out of the way if we need to. DART appeared to be a success on the surface. Understanding what really happened to Dimorphos is what Hera, with all its cameras and companion spacecraft, was literally designed for. And weâre just at the earliest phases of that process. The next step is a major release of even sharper images planned for a live event at the Berlin Museum of Natural History on November 25th. Asteroid watchers, and space enthusiasts more generally, should mark their calendars for our first high-resolution view of one of the biggest impacts weâve had on another body in the solar system to date.

A few Novembers ago, I had a mild crash out over puff pastry. I was planning to meet my partner’s extended family for the first time over Thanksgiving, and volunteered to bring a holiday staple a few weeks prior (in what was one of the most helpful, albeit intimidating Excel sign-up sheets I’ve ever seen). What could be easier than apple pie? The ingredients for the recipe I found weren’t fussy, and it hardly called for fancy technical skills. Plus, I could make it ahead of time knowing that it would travel well.

Then I remembered the puff pastry. For some reason, I attached a moral imperative to the idea of making the whole pie from scratch, and spent the next two weeks poring over puff pastry recipes that felt like casual guides to wizard-tier alchemy. I loved to cook, but I simply wasn’t a big baker. (I also didn’t own a food processor, unless you counted my Magic Bullet.) My mother eventually brought me down to Earth. “Just buy it,” she told me over the phone, undoubtedly rolling her eyes. “Everyone knows it’s a pain in the butt.” Even the Barefoot Contessa herself, she reminded me, famously avoids the time-consuming task (“Nobody wants to make puff pastry!”).

According to recent reports, those words set me free. Once I realized that I could outsource my puff pastry, and the source of my Thanksgiving stress, I was finally able to relax and enjoy the holiday. Folks take pride in their Turkey Day dishes, as they should, but there’s nothing wrong with accepting a little help.

In the hopes of encouraging you to lighten your load, my colleague Bettina Makalintal and I asked some of the coolest people we know in the food industry what they prefer to outsource for Thanksgiving, from smoked hams to appetizers, in order to keep their holiday stress-free.

“There is a single premade item that I purchase for Thanksgiving: a smallish in-house smoked ham from The Meat Hook. It’s a sort of whatever part of the Thursday meal — I make a banging turkey, which commands most of the attention. But! The ham has become a key player during what my family calls Leftover Sandwich Weekend. Having an extra piece of protein mitigates any concerns about not having enough turkey left over. More importantly, a thin slice or two adds a salty, fatty, sweet, and smoky layer to the sandwich architecture. Much needed, very appreciated. Ham: I can’t imagine a turkey sandwich without it.” — Carla Lalli, cookbook author of books including Food is a Feeling.

“I outsource pies because I don’t especially enjoy making them… or eating them!”— Laila Gohar, food-based conceptual designer, artist, and co-founder of Gohar World.

“I almost always outsource appetizers and/or a cheese plate. If I’m making the big stuff (turkey, stuffing, sides, desserts… okay, I’m also a control freak with more time to cook than most), I feel absolutely overwhelmed if I am also making small things. So while I have a couple really simple apps I’ll put out if there are no volunteers, I much prefer having a friend or family member bring their favorite wedge of cheese and crackers, or [crossing fingers] bacon-wrapped dates. Here is one of my simple go-tos (it’s also in my Smitten Kitchen Every Day cookbook): herb-and-garlic baked Camembert. I’d still prefer if someone else can prep it; I don’t mind heating it up.” — Deb Perelman, cookbook author and recipe developer behind Smitten Kitchen.

In a recent development, “We outsource lumpia from Chuck’s mom. We love having them for the holiday but don’t like frying at home when we have everything else cooking that day. She always has a couple hundred in her freezer ready and waiting to be fried for special occasions.” — Hailee Catalano and Chuck Cruz, cookbook authors and recipe developers behind @2peoplecooking.

“I usually get a roast duck from Hay Hay Roasted in Chinatown, because they’ve got it down. It’s consistently delicious and not everyone eats turkey in our family.” — Camari Mick, chef and founder of Calabash.

It has been revealed that “I always outsource the pre-dinner snacks to the grocery store. I have so much respect for people who can construct elaborate cheese boards or spend the morning filling puff pastries, but that’s just not me. I like to set out a few bowls with tamari almonds, Castelvetrano olives, and — this is the most important one — Nacho Cheese Doritos. They’re the perfect mix of salty, crunchy little snacks to have with a drink before dinner is ready. The Doritos always get cleaned out first, so keep a backup bowl waiting in the kitchen.” — Casey Elsass, columnist at Cup of Jo and author of What Can I Bring?

Recent findings suggest that “Last year for Friendsgiving, we collectively decided to skip the hassle of making the turkey and instead ordered Popeyes’ Cajun-Style Turkey. It’s rubbed with a blend of Louisiana-style Cajun spices and comes fully cooked, so all you have to do is thaw, heat, and serve it. It really set the tone for a very unserious dinner, which I think is what you want at a Friendsgiving. We’ll be ordering it again this year.” — Anna Archibald and Kevin Serai, content creators and recipe developers behind Cabagges.World.

“We’re fairly relaxed about Thanksgiving, but if we do end up making food on that day, I usually outsource pie dough! I’m happy to buy organic frozen pie dough because usually it tastes fine and it saves me a little bit of time. I realized I prefer to spend my energy on the other parts of the meal, and I prefer not to add on to my own mental load by also making pie dough. I know it’s quick and easy; I’d just rather not! But I do make my own fillings.” — Ifrah F. Ahmed, author of Soomaaliya.

Industry News: Scientists Discover a Gut Bacteria Molecule That Reverses Severe Intestinal Damage in Mice

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (820 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The bacteria already living in our gut produce a molecule our own cells don’t appear to make, and animal studies suggest it could help damaged intestines heal.
  • It has been revealed that severe intestinal inflammation can leave the gut lining so badly damaged that recovery becomes a matter of survival.
  • In mice with inflamed and damaged colons, untreated animals lost 20% of their body weight and died.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The bacteria already living in our gut produce a molecule our own cells don’t appear to make, and animal studies suggest it could help damaged intestines heal.

It has been revealed that severe intestinal inflammation can leave the gut lining so badly damaged that recovery becomes a matter of survival. Researchers at Rutgers Health have discovered a molecule produced by beneficial gut bacteria that helped mice recover from intestinal damage that proved fatal to untreated animals. The findings raise hope for a fresh way to treat inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), although the compound has not yet been tested as a treatment in humans.

In mice with inflamed and damaged colons, untreated animals lost 20% of their body weight and died. Those injected with the molecule, called (amide-)N-methylnicotinamide (N-MNA), lost just 5% and recovered. In fruit flies with damaged intestines, treatment increased seven-day survival from 43% to 78%.

Sources indicate that the study, published in Science Advances, found that N-MNA helped repair the intestinal lining by stimulating stem cell regeneration. It did so by increasing levels of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD), a coenzyme essential for cellular function that declines with age. Scientists suspect this decline plays an vital role in aging.

Recent findings suggest that NAD cannot enter cells directly, so researchers have been searching for precursor molecules that cells can absorb and convert into NAD. Some gut bacteria naturally produce these compounds, including species available in dietary supplements.

“Humans do not appear to make this exact precursor molecule N-MNA, but some of the bacteria living in our gut do,” remarked senior study author Nan Gao, a professor of pharmacology, physiology and neuroscience at Rutgers New Jersey Medical School.

N-MNA closely resembles a molecule human cells produce when disposing of excess NAD building blocks. However, a small chemical difference allows the bacterial version to be converted back into NAD.

“The molecules animal cells and bacteria make are almost identical, but a tiny difference allows the creation of the bacterial compound back into NAD itself,” mentioned senior study author Xiaoyang Su, an associate professor of medicine at Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School. Su also co-directs the Metabolomics Shared Resource at Rutgers Cancer Institute, New Jersey’s only National Cancer Institute-designated Comprehensive Cancer Center, together with RWJBarnabas Health.

It has been revealed that first author Jiangmeng Han, a doctoral student in biological sciences at Rutgers University-Newark, tracked N-MNA inside human colon cells and found that it supplied approximately 22% of their NAD within 24 hours. The compound was also converted into NAD in human neurons, liver cells, and kidney cells, as well as in the bodies and heads of fruit flies given the molecule.

Recent findings suggest that researchers also examined stool samples from 54 patients with IBD and 20 healthy volunteers. Patients with lower N-MNA levels had significantly higher markers of intestinal inflammation.

“Patients with low levels of this metabolite demonstrated a higher inflammatory activity,” Gao mentioned.

According to recent reports, although the findings suggest a connection between N-MNA and intestinal health, the researchers have not tested the compound as a treatment in people. They also have not determined whether consuming N-MNA-producing bacteria, including Lactobacilli found in yogurt and oral supplements, increases NAD levels in humans.

Gao suggested that stool tests might eventually identify patients who could benefit from certain probiotics, although that possibility remains years away.

“This compound itself may be sufficient, but we cannot rule out the possibility that there are other, better compounds,” remarked Ching-On Wong, an assistant professor of biological sciences at Rutgers-Newark and a senior study author who contributed expertise in fly genetics.

The research brought together doctoral students and postdoctoral fellows from multiple Rutgers campuses and departments.

“Right now, we’re still trying to understand the fundamentals, and this requires a multidisciplinary team of a biochemist, fly geneticist, and intestinal biologist,” Gao noted.

In a recent development, supported by a five-year, $3.6 million National Institutes of Health grant, the team is working to identify the still-unknown human enzymes that process N-MNA. Wong’s laboratory is investigating whether the molecule supports brain-cell health and longevity, while Gao’s laboratory is mapping the bacterial genes responsible for producing it.

Antonio, Jagannatham Naidu Bhupana, Garam Choi, Jiaxing Yang, Eric Chiles, Yan Tong, Mohamed Asik Rajmohamed, Hung-Ting Wu, Dahui Wang, Vik Meadows, Nicolas Lapaque, Jean-Pierre Etchegaray, Rafal Filip, Ta-Chiang Liu, Pawel R. Kiela, Nicholas Bessman, Ronaldo P. Ferraris, Ching-On Wong, Xiaoyang Su and Nan Gao, 6 November 2026, Science Advances. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aef2882.

This research was funded by the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, National Institutes of Health, grant number R01AT013333.

Disclosure: Rutgers has filed a provisional patent application on uses of N-MNA, with Han, Ferraris, Su and Gao named as inventors.

Breaking: Earth's Atmosphere Took Three Deep Breaths of Oxygen Before the Oceans Caught Up

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1444 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, along with the rest of the planets.
  • Industry observers note that earth is one major system.
  • In a recent development, cyanobacteria used sunlight to split water molecules apart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, along with the rest of the planets. Life appeared somewhere between about 4.28 and 3.8 billion years ago; it's difficult to determine clearly. An oxygen atmosphere is a more recent development for Earth, in geological timescales, and understanding how that happened is a substantial part of understanding the present-day Earth.

Industry observers note that earth is one major system. The atmosphere, the oceans, and life itself are all parts of the system. In some respects, they can be studied in isolation. But when trying to understand Earth and its long history, they need to be understood together. The system changed significantly when life changed. Somewhere around 2.4 billion years ago, cyanobacteria appeared, and they brought a newly introduced trick with them: photosynthesis.

In a recent development, cyanobacteria used sunlight to split water molecules apart. That did two things: it generated their chemical energy, and it released free oxygen into water, which eventually found its way into the atmosphere. That was a monumental stage of Earth's development that eventually led to an ozone layer, letting life flourish on the surface. The oxygenation of the atmosphere also led to complex life like us.

Industry observers note that but this all happened a long time ago. At first, the oxygen didn't accumulate in the atmosphere, and figuring out how it all played out isn't simple. Scientists know that the oxygenation history of the ocean and the atmosphere are coupled, but there are many questions. Some researchers argue that the atmosphere's oxygenation took place in different stages, one of which was the Great Oxygenation Event (GOE), while others have argued that the process was smoother. The debate continues.

Sources indicate that newly introduced research in The Innovation shows how Earth's atmosphere was oxygenated in three distinct steps, and that the deep ocean lagged behind in each case. In the last of the steps, deep ocean oxygenation lagged behind by 600 million years.

The research is titled "Stagewise oxygenation of the Earthâs atmosphere and oceans," and the authors are Haiyang Wang and Chao Li, geochemists at the Chengdu University of Technology.

Industry observers note that "Earthâs surface oxygenation was a protracted, multi-step process," the authors write. "It is widely accepted that atmospheric O2 rose through three major steps, each closely linked to key evolutionary innovations.".

The oceans and the atmosphere are linked, and during the quest to understand Earth's oxygenated atmosphere, researchers used the geological rock record to understand ocean chemistry. The well-known banded iron formations are a part of this. They record the ocean's oxygen levels. The atmosphere doesn't hold an ancient record, so the ocean's geological record was used as a proxy for the atmosphere's evolution and oxygenation, too.

So scientists largely think that three stages of rising oxygen created the modern atmosphere: the GOE about 2.4 billion years ago, the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event about 800 to 540 million years ago, and the Paleozoic Oxygenation Event about 400 million years ago.

According to recent reports, the researchers reiterate the understanding that ocean and atmospheric oxygenation are coupled. Research indicates that on billion year timescales, episodes of rising atmospheric oxygen precede the same episodic rise in ocean oxygenation, "whereas on shorter, million-year timescales, their redox states could diverge, exhibiting negative coupling," they write.

"Here, we synthesize geochemical, sedimentological, and palaeobiological evidence to reconstruct this coupled and dynamic atmosphere-ocean oxygenation history and to reassess its timing, mechanisms, and ecological consequences," the authors explain.

This work hinges on fresh geochemical proxies that give researchers a clearer picture of what happened so long ago.

"Recent advances in geochemical proxies, most notably sulfate triple-oxygen isotopes (Îâ²17O), provide new constraints on atmospheric oxygenation, complementing and in some cases revising interpretations from traditional ocean redox proxies," the authors explain.

The researchers say that this sulfate (SO4)offers a cleaner way to understand the oxygenation of the atmosphere. That's because of the isotopic composition of atmospheric oxygen, which is recorded when sulfate forms. It has a deficit of the isotope oxygen-17. So the sulfate can be used to track the rise of atmospheric O2, putting dates on each rise in atmospheric oxygen.

Sources indicate that they found that the GOE is unchanged, sitting between 2.4â2.1 billion years ago. But this work changes the dates of the second and third oxygen rises.

Sources indicate that the second, the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event was 1.3â1.0 billion years ago instead of 800 to 540 million years ago. The Paleozoic Oxygenation Event was 0.42â0.36 billion years instead of 0.44â0.41 billion.

The researchers found something else, too. The previous dates for the Neoproterozoic and Paleozoic events still record something. But instead of dating atmospheric oxygen, they date the delayed oxygenation of the deep ocean. They lagged behind the oxygenation of the atmosphere by about 200 and 30 million years, respectively.

In a recent development, this graphic illustrates the results from new research into the oxygenation of Earth's atmosphere that highlights how Earth's O2 rose unevenly: shallow seas first, then the atmosphere, and much later the deep ocean. During a 2-billion-year transition, atmosphere and ocean O2 sometimes diverged despite long-term rise. Ocean oxygenation was highly variable, with extreme spatial heterogeneity over time. Image Credit: Stagewise oxygenation of the Earth's atmosphere and oceans. Wang and Li 2026, The Innovation.

On shorter timescales, the link between ocean and atmospheric oxygen is still the defining feature in this work. But it shows that a change in one could've pushed the other in the opposite direction. The researchers think that what seems like a signal of rising oxygen levels is actually a drop. When a pulse of oxygen enters the ocean, it oxidized organic carbon and sulfide in the oceans. The organic carbon becomes CO2, and the sulfide becomes sulfate. The more organic carbon and sulfide there was in the ocean, the more it depleted atmospheric oxygen.

Over longer, billion year timescales, the atmophere is oxygenated as photosynthesis continues. But on shorter timescales, it can't keep up.

"Earthâs surface oxygenation history reflects a dynamic and nonlinear interplay among atmospheric O2 evolution, land and ocean redox buffering, and ecological innovation," the authors write. "Overall, the trajectory from localized Archean oxygen oases to the globally well-oxygenated surface environments of today underscores how atmosphere-ocean oxygenation both governsâand is reciprocally shaped byâthe evolution of life.".

This figure reveals the evolution of Earth's atmosphere-ocean redox states through time and space. (A) Before 2.4 Ga: atmosphere and oceans were largely anoxic, with oxygen restricted to localized, shallow-water oxygen oases. (B) From 2.4 to 1.0 Ga: atmospheric O2 remained low; oxygenated waters were confined to the ocean surface, and oxygen oases developed primarily along continental shelves. (C) Between 1.0 and 0.41 Ga: atmospheric O2 increased but fluctuated, while oxygenated waters progressively penetrated to greater depths, with shelf environments continuing to host oxygen oases. (D) Since â¼0.41 Ga: atmospheric O2 approached near-modern levels; deep oceans became pervasively oxygenated, whereas mid-depth waters developed oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) that waxed and waned (solid curves) in response to high organic matter export and oxygen consumption. DOC, dissolved organic carbon. Image Credit: Wang and Li 2026, The Innovation.

Sources indicate that it all happened in stages, as the different elements fed back on one another. This work shows that during Earth's long path to an oxygenated atmosphere, the ocean and atmosphere didn't change in lockstep on shorter timescales. "Throughout the 2-billion-year oxygenation transition, atmospheric and oceanic oxygen levels were episodically decoupled on shorter timescales, superimposed on a long-term trajectory toward global oxidation," they write.

It has been revealed that the pair of researchers acknowledge some of the weakness in the evidence that paints this picture. The record of oxygen isotopes in sulfate is coarse, not exquisitely detailed. Beyond one billion years ago, the levels aren't well-constrained. So it's still more open to interpretation. There may be other steps in the path to oxygenation that aren't clear yet.

Understanding how life and the planet co-evolved together is a monumental task. Scientists know it happened, but all of the details are difficult to detect. But if it happened here, it almost certainly happened on any other habitable worlds.

"These deep-time perspectives illuminate the co-evolution of life and Earthâs surface environments and provide a conceptual framework for evaluating planetary habitability," the authors write.

Psychedelics May Leave a Lasting Mark on the Brain, Upcoming Research Reveals

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (683 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What remains in the brain after a psychedelic wears off could matter for future medicines, as rat scans revealed distinct activity patterns a week after three different drugs were given.
  • Psychedelic drugs are attracting growing interest as possible treatments for depression, anxiety, and addiction.
  • Sources indicate that researchers at the University of Southern Denmark compared three psychedelic drugs, LSD, psilocybin, and the synthetic compound 2C-B, using brain scans in rats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What remains in the brain after a psychedelic wears off could matter for future medicines, as rat scans revealed distinct activity patterns a week after three different drugs were given.

Psychedelic drugs are attracting growing interest as possible treatments for depression, anxiety, and addiction. Yet upcoming research suggests that drugs often grouped together under the same label may affect the brain in very different ways, potentially influencing how scientists investigate their medical uses.

Sources indicate that researchers at the University of Southern Denmark compared three psychedelic drugs, LSD, psilocybin, and the synthetic compound 2C-B, using brain scans in rats. They examined changes in brain activity while the drugs were active and again one week later, after their immediate effects had worn off.

Unlike earlier studies that largely examined one psychedelic at a time, the direct comparison revealed distinct patterns for each drug. Only a few changes were shared across all three.

Recent findings suggest that “Psychedelic drugs are often discussed as if they work in the same way. But when we look at the brain, the differences are clear. Each drug appears to affect its own networks, and that is new knowledge,” says Mikael Palner, Associate Professor at the Department of Clinical Research at the University of Southern Denmark and senior author of the study.

While the drugs were active, LSD and 2C-B produced the greatest number of changes in brain activity. The researchers also identified different patterns one week later, suggesting that the effects of these substances may extend beyond their immediate action in the brain.

“What is interesting is that the differences do not only appear while the drugs are active. We can also see different traces in the brain afterwards. 2C-B mainly affected areas linked to reward, LSD affected areas linked to habits and motivation, while psilocybin stood out by primarily affecting areas involved in emotions,” states Frederik Gudmundsen, first author of the study.

Gudmundsen completed his PhD at the University of Southern Denmark and is now a postdoc at the Department of Clinical Medicine, Translational Neuropsychiatry Unit, Aarhus University.

In a recent development, these differences could help researchers investigate whether certain psychedelics are better suited to treating particular conditions. However, the brain activity patterns alone cannot establish which drug, if any, would be more effective for a specific disorder.

According to recent reports, “If the drugs affect the brain differently, it is also possible that they may eventually prove better suited to different disorders. We do not know that yet, but our study provides a biological starting point for investigating it,” explains Palner.

Recent findings suggest that several psychedelic drugs are already being investigated in clinical trials for conditions including depression, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and addiction. Understanding how individual substances affect different brain networks could eventually help scientists develop more targeted approaches to treatment.

For now, the findings remain limited to experiments in rats and do not show whether the drugs are effective in patients. Further research in humans will be needed to determine whether the same differences occur in the human brain and whether they can help guide future psychedelic treatments.

It has been revealed that reference: “Serotonergic psychedelics induce distinct patterns of metabolic activity and covariance within biologically informed rat brain networks” by Frederik Gudmundsen, Julia Czurylo, Daniel R. Industry News: Tiny Grains of Sand Act as Cosmic Speedometers for Alien Winds

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1006 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that weâve managed to take high-resolution orbital images of many worlds across our solar system, and many of them with an atmosphere have one feature in common - sand dunes.
  • It has been revealed that earth and Mars, the two most commonly thought of planets with sand dunes, arenât the only ones.
  • Understanding why this is notable requires looking at how wind actually moves sand in the first place.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that weâve managed to take high-resolution orbital images of many worlds across our solar system, and many of them with an atmosphere have one feature in common - sand dunes. Scientists have been using the size and orientation of these dunes for decades to act like a weather vane, figuring out which way the wind blows on these other worlds. Unfortunately, weather vanes arenât good at telling the full windy story - they canât tell you how fast the wind is going. However, according to a new paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences by researchers at Stanford, sand dunes can.

It has been revealed that earth and Mars, the two most commonly thought of planets with sand dunes, arenât the only ones. Weâve also seen them on Venus, Titan, and, surprisingly, Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko. Each is made up of different materials, but all share a crucial characteristic - their âsandâ consists of small grains of similar particles, which could be blown around by wind.

Understanding why this is notable requires looking at how wind actually moves sand in the first place. When air is moving across a dune, individual grains stay stationary until the wind itself reaches a critical speed known as the transport threshold. Once it rises above that, the grains begin bouncing across the ground in a movement known as saltation. Each time a grain crashes back to the surface, it kicks up other surrounding grains into the air, creating a self-sustaining cascade of moving sand.

Fraser talks about whether Martian dust storms are dangerous.

It has been revealed that what was unclear to scientists was whether these motions were primarily driven by violent dust storms that were relatively rare, or moderate winds which are much more common on the other worlds where dunes have been seen. It might seem counter-intuitive that a comet would have âwindâ, but a 2017 study highlighted that the âripplesâ ESAâs Rosetta probe found on the comet's surface were created by localized vapor flows caused by extreme day-night temperature cycling.

Recent findings suggest that solving the mystery of what type of wind causes these shifting sands was the focus of the paper. Lead author M. Colin Marvin, a PhD student in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at Stanford, collected wind speed data and detailed grain-size measurements from twenty-four different dune fields spread all over the world. From the Coral Pink Sand Dunes State Park in Utah to the ancient, hundred-meter-tall dunes in the Namib Sand Sea in Namibia, the researchers found a remarkable similarity.

Across every terrestrial site, the most sand was moved when the wind was slightly above the speed required to start moving it. And, crucially, the same relationship also held on a Maritan sand dune. The process didnât require the odd violent gale to get sand moving, just every day wind speeds common throughout the globe. For example, a dune made of sand 0.2 mm across (about the width of two pieces of paper) is mostly moved by winds blowing at only 26 kilometers per hour 10 meters above the ground.

Fraser talks about the Dragonfly mission, which will land next to dunes on Titan.

In a recent development, with that data set in hand, the researchers then turned to simulations. Using a tool called ReSCAL, they grew virtual dunes from flat sand beds using different wind speeds. As part of that process, the team confirmed that, as long as a world has plenty of loosely bound grains of sand and winds that grow rarer as they grow stronger, dunes will largely be formed by the wind speeds that correspond directly to the grain sizes that compose them.

Despite the challenges of finding individual sand grain size from orbit, this technique is useful on more than just Earth. Curiosity has already drilled into the Stimson formation, a layer of sandstone that used to be a windblown dune billions of years ago. Another upcoming interplanetary mission â Dragonfly â is expected to touch down on the surface of Titan, where there are dunes of hydrocarbons, sometime in the 2030s.

Combining the grain size measurements from these missions with the math laid out in the fresh paper will provide scientists with a rough indication of the history of wind speed in the area. There will also undoubtedly be other missions to other dune-ridden planets - Venus comes to mind as a potential target. And from now on, scientists will be able to read a major part of a worldâs geological history directly written into its sand.

Stanford - Scientists discover sand dunes can reveal wind speeds on Earth and beyond.

  • Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Thursday he is working on legislative language ending the war that he wants attached to the next continuing resolution that is needed by Dec.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., talks with reporters in the Capitol on Sept. 30. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

A group of prominent Senate Democrats is pushing to use a must-pass spending bill to cut off funding for the Iran war, complicating the path toward a bipartisan deal for averting a partial government shutdown next month.

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Thursday he is working on legislative language ending the war that he wants attached to the next continuing resolution that is needed by Dec. 11, when current funding runs out.

“I know it’s going to be my main push,” he remarked. “I have to work with colleagues to try to find some language that works. And I’m not there yet, but I’ve told everybody that’s an opportunity.”.

It has been revealed that democratic Sens. Michael Bennet of Colorado, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, Tammy Duckworth of Illinois and independent Bernie Sanders of Vermont released a statement Thursday that they would oppose any deal that does not include “language that restricts the Trump Administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran.”.

“When we vote on appropriations, we intend to fund the government and stop funds for this war,” the senators said. “It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve.”.

It is unlikely that Republicans, who are in control of both chambers of Congress until January, not to mention the Oval Office beyond that, would agree to such a deal.

House Appropriations Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., stated earlier this week that “a Republican Congress is not going to send bills to a Republican president that he's going to veto.”.

Recent findings suggest that while ending the war is a top priority of Democrats as they take back power in the fresh Congress, insisting on doing so this year could lead to a Christmas-time partial government shutdown. If a shutdown starts after Dec. 11, it’s possible it would still be ongoing when Democrats take control of both chambers in January.

But some Democrats appeared to still be weighing how promptly to push for a cutoff of war funding.

Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash, noted that whether or not Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth remains in his job, “we’re still going to have language stopping this war.”.

She was coy on whether that fight would take place on the anticipated continuing resolution in December or wait until next year when Democrats take back power, saying that lawmakers are “looking at all options.”.

It has been revealed that democrats are committed to ending the "reckless and costly war of choice in Iran," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., stated Thursday. He deferred to House Appropriations ranking member Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., "to see what’s possible in advance of Dec. 11" in talks with the other top appropriators.

"I don’t want to get out ahead of Congresswoman DeLauro, but House Democrats have uniformly opposed providing any additional money to Donald Trump’s war machine. to Pete Hegseth’s war machine, over in the Middle East," Jeffries remarked.

It’s not clear how long a potential continuing resolution would last, and DeLauro mentioned earlier this week that she wants it to be as short as possible.

The Office of Management and Budget has not yet submitted “anomalies” — changes to the current spending levels to be included in the continuing resolution — to Congress.

It has been revealed that the administration is considering options including a stopgap bill that would run through March, sources familiar with the talks noted. But no decision on the timing covered by the anomalies has been made.

Aris Folley, Jacob Fulton and Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1867 w)
