📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

A refrigerator is intended to do only three things: preserve food, store it properly, and supply enough lighting to see all contents. We also want our fridge to be reliable and last a long time so we don’t have to go through this exhaustive shopping exercise again until it’s absolutely necessary.

Sources indicate that when shopping for a refrigerator, we're not just looking for something that keeps our food cold. We require aesthetic appeal from our primary kitchen appliance. We also crave convenience in the form of spacious and adjustable shelves and bins, temperature or humidity-controlled spaces, an ice maker so we can ditch the refillable trays, and whatever other clever additions fridge makers come up with to lure us into spending more cash.

If you haven’t shopped for a refrigerator in a while, we’ve got some good news and some bad news. The bad news is that refrigerators may be more expensive due to ongoing tariffs on both foreign steel and aluminum used to manufacture models in the U.S. and on wholly imported fridges. The good news, though, is that there is a wider variety of designs and sizes to match your family’s specific needs, plus features like exterior or interior water and ice dispensing options, separate food-specific cooling spaces, and an abundance of smart tech.

To help you find the perfect fridge for your kitchen, we researched a variety of options based on specific criteria and found the best of the best. We also made sure our picks all varied in terms of style, so below, you'll find our top recommendations for French door refrigerators, side-by-side fridges, and a number of other types, as well.

Recent findings suggest that as with any other appliance, our consideration for best models was primarily based on value—capacity and features for the money. Value also incorporates the reputation of the manufacturer and opinions from both retailers and consumers (from online reviews). We also compared capacities and feature sets of various models and took into account our own hands-on experiences at appliance stores and trade demonstrates over the years.

According to recent reports, when faced with seemingly equal choices, especially on price, we always leaned toward higher-capacity models since we know there’s no such thing as too much refrigerator space. However, we also recognize that higher-capacity refrigerators are usually full or standard depth models that may be too big for many kitchens, so we’ve tried to add less pricey, smaller alternatives where we found them.

Industry observers note that stewart Wolpin wrote the initial version of this article—he's covered consumer technology, including home entertainment and appliances, since the early 1980s. Amber Joglar, a technology and home appliance editor with PM, handled the latest upgrade to this roundup.

While there is a plethora of premium refrigerators priced $5,000 and up—and some priced $15,000 and more—we decided to keep our “Best” choices under $5,000.

If ensuring your food stays cool is at the top of your list when shopping for a refrigerator, then your best bet is investing in this four-door Samsung model. It's equipped with AI hybrid cooling, which essentially means using just electricity, sans refrigerant, via a semiconductor-based component.

This fridge automatically cools down to compensate for when you leave the door open too long. As a result, Samsung claims that meat and seafood are preserved a smidge longer, and your fridge’s overall power usage can be lowered by up to 10 percent.

Industry observers note that beyond this cooling technology, the Samsung offers plenty of convenient features. The beverage center inside the left top door provides a tall water dispenser, a 48-ounce autofill water pitcher with infuser, and a removable nozzle for cleaning. The dual ice maker behind the bottom left door makes both ice cubes and ice spheres.

The fridge’s doors open via gentle touch rather than forcing you to tug on handles, which is useful for when your arms are filled with groceries. You can also set the multi-pantry drawer for the correct cooling conditions to properly preserve fruit and veggies, beverages, or meat and fish.

This Samsung counter-depth four-door has a generous 22.5 cubic feet of capacity and 13.8 percent more cooling capability than previous comparable Samsung models.

Recent findings suggest that this GE fridge is about as basic and uncomplicated as it gets, which explains why it only costs around $800 after discount. What makes this fridge a bargain is its substantial 21.9 cubic feet of storage space, which is more than a majority of other entry-level top-freezer fridges we considered.

One of its door shelves accommodates gallon jugs, and the included bins are modular to adjust to different jar, bottle, and container heights. Temperature controls are straightforward and easy to access on the roof of the fridge. It also includes a Sabbath mode to eliminate all the fridge’s electrical responses when the door is opened. Plus, it’s garage-ready.

This model is available in five finishes, but any colors other than white add to the overall cost. It also lacks both a freezer light and an ice maker, which means you’re going to have to fill and empty trays somewhat regularly.

But if you want to avoid an ice-making mess, you can buy an optional ice maker designed for this model, although it will occupy more than a third of your freezer space. (Or you could buy one of our favorite countertop nugget ice makers instead.).

In a recent development, this is one robust fridge for just $1,200. You get an impressive 27.4 cubic feet of total storage space in this full-depth Samsung stainless steel side-by-side, plus the interior ice maker is located in the door to create even more freezer shelf space.

According to recent reports, aside from being roomy, this fridge includes a raft of both cooling and convenience features normally found on more expensive models. For instance, it instantly lowers the temperature of your fridge and freezer section to quickly bring recently purchased goods to their appropriate storage levels.

The in-door water dispenser also dispenses both cubed and crushed ice, but it lacks a light, which makes it difficult to accurately fill a glass in a dark kitchen. There's an LCD panel on the inside of the fridge for monitoring refrigerator and freezer temperatures, ice maker filter status, and managing lock controls.

According to recent reports, multi-vent cooling lowers the temp in every corner of the fridge, which prevents ice-infused liquids. While it lacks some of the fancier frills of some of our other, more expensive choices, this Samsung provides a lot of storage space, especially in its freezer, for a relatively low price tag.

If it's even possible for a refrigerator to be entertaining, this French door LG does it and thankfully it doesn't skimp on functionality in the process. Right off the bat, you’ll notice a shaded window on the right door—just gently knock twice and it turns clear so you can take a peek inside. Then, grab the door just right, and a door within the main door opens with easy, quick access to snacks and drinks without letting all the cool air out from the main fridge compartment.

If you’re tired of old-fashioned ice cubes, freshen drinks with Craft Ice, an interior ice maker that fashions slow-melting spheric ice modules. The exterior water dispenser also makes both crushed and cubed ice, and the dispenser/ice maker mechanism inside the left door is thin enough to accommodate three door bins.

In a recent development, unfortunately, the freezer is organized with deep, basket-style compartments, which makes it difficult to promptly find what you need in a pinch. But if you’re a frequent party host, the freezer really steps up the ice production, so you’re less likely to ever run out, even during a lively party.

There are side-by-side fridges with fancier features, but you'd be hard-pressed to find a better deal than this Whirlpool model, considering its combination of capacity, extras, aesthetic appeal, and overall cooling excellence.

This fridge has a spacious 28.7-cubic-foot capacity and is equipped with both an extra tall exterior water and ice dispenser to accommodate all sizes of glasses, bottles, and pitchers. The interior ice bin is installed on the door to free up freezer storage space. There's a good variety of glass shelves inside, and they extend wall-to-wall to truly maximize all fridge and freezer space available.

There is also a temperature management system that senses and adapts to keep food fresh. Special pantry and deli drawers maintain organization, too. If any foods have defrosted in between the grocery store and home, the freezer has a Fast Freeze option that quickly drops the temperature 10 degrees lower than the normal setting, so your foods can get back to fully frozen in a jiffy.

Unfortunately, if you’re looking to match this fridge with your kitchen decor, it's available only in a “stainless” finish.

It has been revealed that this full-depth GE bottom freezer, which has been available since 2022, is still well-respected in its category, and it costs around $1,000 less than it was at first launch. Its enduring popularity can likely be attributed to its 24.9-cubic-foot capacity that’s generous for this class of fridge, although the water filter is unusually bulky and takes up a little more cooling space than we would have liked.

Recent findings suggest that fortunately, it includes an ice maker along with a larger-than-average storage bin—perfect for party preparation. A turbo cool setting automatically drops the internal temperature if the door’s been open too long. We also love the unique, horizontally-sliding snack drawer that easily moves across the fridge to make room for taller items below.

Other nice features include touch temperature controls, an open door alarm, and a fingerprint-resistant stainless finish. And, as found on most top- or bottom-freezer models, the top door is reversible, so you can install it to swing open left or right.

This model is also Energy Star-certified, meaning it meets strict standards set by the EPA and uses between 9 and 15 percent less energy than models that have not been rated.

Sources indicate that samsung makes arguably the smartest fridges around, particularly with its Family Hub models that integrate seamlessly into smart home ecosystems. The right door of this appliance boasts a 32-inch vertical touch screen that provides access to recipes, shopping lists, ordering, and other food-related tasks. In addition to these functions, it acts a streaming interface and display for your kids’ school drawings or home videos.

Inside, this fridge has a camera that recognizes and automatically labels 37 unobscured fresh food items such as fruits and vegetables, or you can do this manually. On the left side, there’s a double quick-access door. Behind that lives a beverage center designed with both a regular water dispenser and an auto-refill water pitcher with an infuser.

Sources indicate that open its doors either manually or automatically by touching a sensor. To better preserve different types of food, one of the freezer drawers lets you set one of five different temperatures depending on what you’re storing. A dual ice maker makes both standard cubes and smaller “ice bits,” but not crushed ice. An internal camera lets you see what’s inside your fridge—or not—when shopping via the smartphone app, which also lets you monitor the fridge’s power usage.

GE Profile appliances are considered high-end within the GE family, sitting above standard GE appliances but below its relatively expensive Monogram line. To put it simply, you get luxury features without a large price tag by investing in this model.

According to recent reports, inside the left of the four-door refrigerator is an auto-refillable water pitcher that doubles as a dispenser, and the bottom left freezer compartment contains roomy storage that holds a whopping 12.5 pounds of filtered ice. The bottom right can also function as a freezer, chiller, or fridge if you run out of space up top.

In a recent development, this fridge doesn't have an exterior water dispenser, but it does have a built-in pitcher with advanced filtration inside the left door. The door-in-door with rotating bin is a standout feature for us, too.

From a design POV, you get a smooth stainless steel exterior door finish with sleek handles, and the interior is highlighted by silver shelf and drawer trim handles, and an LED light wall. If you want to take advantage of smart features, the fridge has built-in WiFi and compatibility with the SmartHQ app for a fully customizable experience.

According to recent reports, each fridge form offers varying cubic-foot capacity, usually expressed as total space. Until recently, inside capacity was somewhat restricted by the need for refrigerant circulation and insulation inside a fridge’s thick walls. But many newer models with updated cooling and insulation technologies have slimmed these inside walls to create so-called “max,” “mega,” or “XL” capacity models, creating more inside capacity without increasing exterior dimensions.

Recent findings suggest that bear in mind, some vendors fudge on capacity, often rounding up to the nearest whole number in the name of the fridge. For instance, a “23” cubic foot model may actually only contain 22.5 cubic feet of storage.

So how do you decide how significant your latest fridge needs to be? Obviously, how much capacity you can buy depends on how much space you have in your kitchen for a refrigerator.

Recent findings suggest that figure 4- to 6 cubic feet per family member, leaning toward the higher end for a lot of shared items. Alternatively, you can start with ten cubic feet for the household, then add 1.5 cubic feet per household member to get a minimum capacity.

Sources indicate that in terms of fridge-freezer split, most models assign 65 to 70 percent of space to cooling and the remaining 30 to 35 percent to freezing. If you’re a bulk buyer or frequent meal preparer, we recommend you find a model with more freezer space.

Recent findings suggest that you want shelves and inside door bins to offer varying height adjustments to accommodate the tallest types of containers such as opened wine bottles. Some fridges offer shelves that slide out and door bins that can accommodate bulky gallon jugs or tilt out for easier access.

All refrigerators include storage drawers, but the best are those models that offer drawers with some sort of temperature and/or humidity control. When shopping, check the drawers to make sure they slide in and out smoothly, come out easily for cleaning, and don’t feel cheap.

Sources indicate that refrigerators with twin doors—side-by-side and French—are the only models in which you’ll find exterior in-door water and ice dispensers. Most in-door water dispensers also dispense ice—often both cubed and crushed—but some don’t offer ice, so double-check this before you buy. If a twin-door model doesn’t include an exterior water dispenser, there’s likely one inside the fridge.

It has been revealed that if you’re replacing a fridge without an in-door water dispensing with one that does, you (or, more likely, a plumber) will likely first have to install a separate water line that connects from your under-sink pipes to your newly introduced refrigerator. You’ll also occasionally have to change the refrigerator’s water filter—usually around twice a year—but ask first to make sure of the timing. Our advice: order in a supply of filters so you’re sure you’re always dispensing the freshest filtered water.

A growing number of “smart” refrigerators include interior cameras to let you view your fridge’s contents to confirm if you need something while grocery shopping. A camera-equipped smart model with a smart screen on the door can also scan your remaining ingredients and create an edible recipe, assemble a shopping list and create an order from a grocery delivery service, and even identify what food items have reached their expiration date.

Recent findings suggest that yes, refrigerators still come in basic white, but you also can choose from a growing variety of subtleties such as gray and black tones in shiny or matte finishes (with smudge- or finger-resistant coatings). But a few fridge makers also offer custom-made colors, including finishes to match your kitchen cabinets or decor.

Industry observers note that do note that a model listed as having a “stainless” finish does not necessarily mean you’re getting an actual stainless steel door. In most instances, just the word “stainless” likely means the door is some other material, not stainless steel. To make sure you’re getting a true stainless steel door, first feel it, as stainless steel is cooler to the touch than other materials. Also, take along a refrigerator magnet—most stainless steel doors are not magnetic.

Sources indicate that there are, essentially, only five forms of fridges, all defined by how the doors and drawers are arranged. In order of price, features available, and capacity (low to high), the five fridge forms are:.

Industry observers note that this is the most familiar no-frills fridge format with two doors: a top freezer compartment and a larger fresh food compartment below. Top freezer fridges are usually the least expensive fridge option, landing somewhere between $500-$900. They also range between 10 to 24 cubic feet of space, and are best suited for single folks or couples on a budget, or as a second fridge for a recreational basement or garage.

No frills means you’re unlikely to find any top freezer models with in-door water dispensers or an ice maker. Most models come with reversible doors that open left-to-right or right-to-left, however.

Sources indicate that A.k.a. “bottom freezer” models, these refrigerators are equipped with a single door up top and a freezer drawer usually encompassing two shelving tiers below. Bottom freezer models are presumably more attractive to those with fewer freezer needs since you have to kneel or bend over to rummage through it.

Bottom freezer models generally provide a bit more freezer space than a top freezer— around 18 to 22 cubic feet of total capacity—and typically cost more than a top freezer model. Like a top freezer model, you’re unlikely to find bottom freezer models with in-door water dispensers, but some pricier versions do include ice makers.

Recent findings suggest that rather than a horizontal freezer, side-by-side models offer vertical freezing and cooling compartments. Side-by-side interior horizontal space, however, is narrower than a top- or bottom-freezer model, so wide platter trays or frozen pizzas may not fit. Side-by-sides are more likely to offer in-door water or ice dispensing, which can further reduce freezer space.

Essentially a side-by-side with a bottom freezer, except the two top French doors open out to reveal a single large and wide cooling compartment. Since there’s no wall dividing the top section, French door models offer the highest capacity—up to around 30 cubic feet worth of fresh food room—which makes these the best option for a large and active family.

It has been revealed that french door models usually include either in-door or interior water and ice dispensers. Higher capacity, of course, means higher prices—French door models start at around $1,400 depending on interior space and features, such as more convenient separate dual freezer drawers.

According to recent reports, four-door French-door fridges replace the bottom freezer drawer(s) with freezer doors that open into separate compartments. However, you’ll see models with French doors with dual drawer freezers referred to as “four-door,” which they are not since a drawer is decidedly not a door. More expensive four-door models allow you to convert one of the freezer sections into an extra refrigerator compartment if you need extra cooling space.

Most refrigerators last around seven years. Spending a bit more now on a better model means you can go a lot longer without having to buy a replacement. Models with long warranties usually signal a longer expected lifespan.

Our general refrigerator shopping advice: you already know your current refrigerator’s shortcomings (that’s presumably why you’re looking to buy a fresh one). Match your known needs with the features outlined above that you find attractive before you go to a store and are confronted by a pushy salesperson.

It's not recommended to turn your fridge on and off for short periods of time because it can actually increase wear on the compressor, but powering down during longer absences helps save energy and prevents problems like mold.

Before heading out for vacation or an extended trip, you should remove all food, clean and dry the interior, unplug the appliance, and keep the doors propped open for air circulation.

A 360-Year-Old Manuscript Reveals Galileo May Have Built a Telescope Far Ahead of Its Time

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1037 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Galileo left no technical analyses of his telescopes, but a centuries-old manuscript may offer the clearest look yet at a more sophisticated instrument he could have built.
  • In a recent development, in 1666, a Spanish friar hoping to secure his passage home was given an unusual test of his scientific abilities.
  • Industry observers note that the account was discovered by Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Galileo left no technical analyses of his telescopes, but a centuries-old manuscript may offer the clearest look yet at a more sophisticated instrument he could have built.

In a recent development, in 1666, a Spanish friar hoping to secure his passage home was given an unusual test of his scientific abilities. A powerful colonial official handed him a telescope and demanded a detailed explanation of how it worked. Nearly 360 years later, the account he produced has resurfaced with a remarkable claim: the instrument was made by Galileo Galilei, and its design may be far more advanced than historians previously believed possible for his time.

Industry observers note that the account was discovered by Dr. José María Moreno Madrid, a researcher at the University of Limerick’s School of History and Geography in Ireland, while examining a manuscript written by Dominican friar Ignacio Muñoz. Dated 1666 and titled De Tellescopiis Stellarum, the document describes a four-lens telescope that Muñoz identified with the Latin phrase “fabricatum a Galilaeo,” meaning “manufactured by Galileo.”.

According to recent reports, the description is unusually precise. Muñoz documented the telescope’s individual components, including its reverse-tapered body and an arrangement of four lenses that allowed distant objects to appear upright. His account describes an erecting eyepiece and convex lenses separated by twice their focal lengths, accompanied by detailed diagrams and drawings that show how the instrument was constructed.

It has been revealed that these technical details matter because historical records have generally placed the earliest four-lens telescopes around 1643 to 1645, with their production becoming widespread across Europe beginning in the 1640s. If the instrument really came from Galileo’s workshop, the timeline of telescope development would need to be reconsidered.

In research published in Annals of Science, Moreno Madrid explains what the attribution could mean.

“If, as the text claims, the telescope analyzed was indeed manufactured by Galileo, then the earliest known experimentation with four-lens telescopes would have to be pushed back to 1630 at the latest and credited to him. Moreover, Muñoz’s De Tellescopiis Stellarum would become the most detailed technical analysis of a telescope provenly made by Galileo – and, somewhat paradoxically, it would concern a four-lens telescope rather than the Galilean design that ultimately came to bear his name,” said Dr. Moreno Madrid.

According to recent reports, the circumstances surrounding Muñoz’s examination provide another intriguing piece of the story. After traveling from Spain to the Philippines, he became involved in an illicit attempt to establish a fresh Dominican religious order and was subsequently exiled to Portuguese India. Hoping to return to Spain, he contacted King Philip IV with a proposal that promised to improve the performance of Spanish fleets operating around the world.

Muñoz offered his nautical innovation in exchange for royal sponsorship of his journey home aboard the Manila Galleon, which traditionally stopped in Latest Spain, a Spanish colonial territory. His proposal, however, attracted suspicion from Antonio Sebastián de Toledo Molina y Salazar, the viceroy of New Spain and Marquis of Mancera.

The viceroy questioned whether Muñoz possessed the scientific knowledge he claimed and worried that the friar was simply trying to persuade the king to pay for his travels. To test his abilities, Mancera presented him with the telescope and ordered him to examine it thoroughly. That assignment produced the technical description Moreno Madrid has now brought to light.

Industry observers note that determining whether Galileo actually manufactured the instrument is more complicated. Although the astronomer famously maintained that he had never sold a telescope and never intended to, very few instruments from his lifetime survive with reliable records of their origins. Of the eight surviving telescopes manufactured during the first half of the seventeenth century, none can be attributed to Galileo beyond dispute. Two preserved in the Museum of Florence have traditionally been credited to him, although that identification is not universally accepted. Galileo also left no technical analyses of his own telescopes.

There is, however, a possible connection between Galileo and the Spanish official who possessed Muñoz’s instrument.

It has been revealed that historical accounts indicate that Galileo presented three telescopes, one large and two smaller instruments, to Philip IV and his wife. He hoped to gain favor with the Spanish court and improve his chances of receiving a substantial reward offered for solving the “problem of longitude,” the longstanding difficulty of determining a ship’s east-west position while navigating at sea.

Sources indicate that the optical designs of those three telescopes remain unknown, leaving open the possibility that one was the four-lens instrument described by Muñoz. Moreno Madrid suggests that the Spanish royal family may have later given it to Mancera in recognition of his diplomatic and political achievements.

“I believe that the unambiguous attribution of the telescope in the manuscript, together with the documentary evidence that three telescopes made by Galileo – whose optical configuration remain unspecified – may have been accessible to Mancera through his connections at the Spanish court, at the very least invites consideration of this possibility.”.

No further reference to the telescope appears in Mancera’s surviving correspondence with the Spanish court, making Muñoz’s manuscript the only known document connecting this particular instrument to Galileo.

Sources indicate that moreno Madrid also points to Muñoz’s background in mathematics and astronomy as an key reason to take his technical account seriously. The manuscript describes an optical arrangement absent from existing documentation produced by or associated with Galileo and his contemporaries. Regardless of whether the attribution can ultimately be confirmed, it offers historians a rare opportunity to examine seventeenth-century telescope construction in detail. It also illustrates how these instruments served as prestigious possessions among Europe’s political and scientific elites.

For now, the identity of the telescope’s maker remains an open question, one that Moreno Madrid hopes further discoveries will help resolve.

“It is to be hoped that newly introduced documentary or material evidence will soon emerge to confirm the telescope’s attribution and further enhance our understanding of it.”.

In a recent development, reference: “De Tellescopiis Stellarum (1666). Was Galileo experimenting with four-lens terrestrial telescopes by 1630?” by José María Moreno Madrid, 12 May 2026, Annals of Science. DOI: 10.1080/00033790.2026.2661195.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It was a hot, dry day in the Kalahari Desert, and Mathilde Martin was running after a meerkat.

The animal wore a GPS tracker around its neck and bolted between shelters, like an action hero running for cover, says Martin, a biologist at the University of Zurich. She and her colleagues had captured the meerkat earlier that morning, driven it 1.5 kilometers from its pack and then released it into the desert. They were trying to find out how well individual meerkats could find their way back home.

The answer was quite well, the researchers reported November 19 in the Journal of Experimental Biology. The results suggest that meerkats can navigate expertly on their own, perhaps relying on mental maps charted early in life. “They all seem to be very, very good,” Martin says. It’s a surprise finding for a species known for its group cooperation.

Industry observers note that meerkats (Suricata suricatta), which live in southern Africa, form tight-knit family groups of up to 50 members. These social animals cooperate in many aspects of life, including by babysitting each other’s pups and watching for predators while traveling along foraging paths. Martin and her colleagues thought meerkats might also rely on one another for navigating. Some pack members, perhaps those who’ve had more opportunity to explore solo, might have spatial knowledge of their territory and lead the rest, she indicates. But that’s not what the team discovered.

In a recent development, in separate catch and release experiments with 20 individual meerkats, 18 made a beeline back home, back to their group or back to the site where they were captured. (The other two may have been too stressed to get moving, Martin states.).

It has been revealed that neither age nor individual experience, which researchers had been tracking, seemed to factor into the meerkats’ homing skills. Nearly all of them knew where to go, Martin indicates. She thinks these crackerjack navigators relied on visual cues to orient themselves. They’d pop up on their hind legs and scan the landscape before scampering off in a direct line to their target.

Recent findings suggest that it’s likely that scent played a role, too, though distant scent marks may have faded by the time the meerkats were released. The researchers dropped the animals off in territory they hadn’t visited for at least 30 days. “Otherwise,” she indicates, “it would have been a bit too easy for them to find their way back,” she says.

Making Sense of Chaotic Supernova Ejecta With the JWST

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Finding order in the chaotic aftermath of a supernova explosion isn't easy.
  • According to recent reports, massive stars play an important role in the evolution of the cosmos.
  • Astrophysicists can't see inside stars to learn more about this process, so they have to wait until they turn themselves inside out and then examine the results.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finding order in the chaotic aftermath of a supernova explosion isn't easy. But the JWST has the tools to do it. Its Mid-Infrared Instrument (MIRI) and its Medium-resolution Spectrometer (MRS) were built for situations like this.

According to recent reports, massive stars play an important role in the evolution of the cosmos. They're responsible for synthesizing astronomical metals, the elements heavier than hydrogen and helium that are necessary to form everything from rocky planets to living organisms. Without massive stars, the cosmos would look much different. It would be a simple mixture of hydrogen, with a little helium mixed in, and trace amounts of lithium. Nature can't build planets or create life with that limited palette.

Astrophysicists can't see inside stars to learn more about this process, so they have to wait until they turn themselves inside out and then examine the results.

According to recent reports, massive stars live fast and die young, then explode as supernovae. When that happens, the explosion sends their contents, including their astronomical metals, out into the interstellar medium. Once there, it's available not only for planets and life, but for the next generation of stars.

According to recent reports, when a supernova explodes, it leaves behind a supernova remnant, the matter ejected by the explosion in an expanding shockwave. The shockwave heats up the expanding shell, creating some of Nature's most stunning displays. The shocks can also rebound, creating an inward shock wave. It can create a real mess, but there are still patterns to be discerned. Within the exanding shell, molecules come form that tell astrophysicists what happened inside the star prior to its explosion.

One of the most well-known supernova remnants is Cassiopeia A (Cas A). It's about 11,000 light years away, and it was observed by Earthlings around 1667. Astronomers are interested in it because they can learn a lot about the exploding star that created itâthe progenitorâby analyzing its contents.

The JWST was built for just such an endeavour. In new research in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, a team of researchers used the JWST's MIRI and MRS to determine Cas A's chemical makeup. The research is "JWST Resolves Dust Emission from Individual Ejecta Clumps in Cassiopeia A: Dominant Grain Compositions Point to a Shell Merger in the Progenitor," and the lead author is Tea Temim, a research scientist from Columbia University.

In a recent development, "We present a study of dust emission in the supernova remnant (SNR) Cassiopeia A (Cas A) observed with the MIRI Medium-resolution Spectrometer (MRS) on board JWST," the authors write. "The unprecedented spatial resolution at mid-IR wavelengths allows us to isolate dust emission from individual arcsecond-scale clumps of supernova (SN) ejecta and circumstellar material (CSM) and identify the dominant dust species in each chemically distinct region.".

Massive stars fuse different elements in layers, and that's reflected in the remnants they leave behind when they explode. Increasingly heavier elements are forged in the core, up until iron is reached. Lighter elements are fused together in the surrounding layers. These layers tell the star's history, but it all gets blown into space when the star explodes as a supernovae. To make matters more complicated, these shock waves can bounce back as reverse shocks.

The clumps in the supernova ejecta that the authors refer to are huge, as large as our Solar System. In studying these clumps with the MRS, the researchers were able to identify different dust species region by region, rather than as one mixed up jumble of spectra. They learned that the progenitor star underwent a shell merger.

âMaterial within these shells churns and circulates, which can cause the shells to merge shortly before the supernova explosion,â lead author Temim stated in a press release. âSo, for example, this would be something like the oxygen- and carbon-burning shells in a star merging together and changing the structure of the star significantly. And that would then change the chemical abundances that you would see after a supernova explosion in the ejecta of a supernova remnant.â.

Before they turned to the JWST, they used Spitzer images to identify regions to focus on with the JWST.

Industry observers note that this figure shows Spitzer images on the left and JWST images on the right. The JWST obviously has a much higher resolution, and the researchers used it to map Cas A's dust chemistry all across the remnant. The observations led to a better understanding of the shell mergers the remnant went through right before it exploded, and a better understanding of the progenitor's overall structure. Since astrophysicists can't see inside stars, they have to wait until they turn themselves inside out. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, JPL-Caltech, T. Temim (Columbia University), R. Arendt (UMBC), D. Milisavljevic (Purdue University). Image Processing: A. Pagan (STScI).

The Spitzer identified regions with different dust properties. The researchers focused on three of them with MRS.

"The MRS spectra extracted at positions P1, P2, and P3 ... all exhibit significant emission from warm dust, but with spectral shapes that differ considerably between the three regions," the authors write.

It has been revealed that this image indicates the overall supernova remnant and the locations of three regions with distinctly different dust properties first identified with the Spitzer Space Telescope. The researchers examined these regions more closely with the JWST's MRS, seen as P1, P2 and P3. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, Danny Milisavljevic (Purdue University), Tea Temim (Princeton University), Ilse De Looze (UGhent); Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI).

Recent findings suggest that P1 samples reverse-shocked ejecta that has bright argon emissions dominate by grains of SiO2 (silica). It helps the researchers track the outer layers of the supernova's ejecta. Finding it supports the idea that the progenitor underwent a carbonâoxygen shell merger.

P2 is centered on what astronomers call Cas A's "Green Monster" structure, which is the green structure near the center. It's emissions are attributed to circumstellar matter emissions on Cas A's near side, not material from Cas A's progenitor. It's likely made of mostly Mg2SiO4, which helps astronomers determine that the progenitor's dust and the CSM dust are distinct from one another.

Industry observers note that P3 is another reverse-shocked region. It has very bright neon emissions compared to P1. That favours another shell merger, this time between a carbon shell and an oxygen shell.

It has been revealed that this image of Cas A is from the JWST's MIRI F2100W filter. The P1, P2, and P3 regions are indicated by the white arrows. "The spatial distribution of the P2-like emission associated with Mg2SiO4 CSM dust is shown in green, P1-like emission associated with SiO2 dust is shown in magenta, and P3-like Ne-rich emission associated with carbon dust is shown in blue," the authors write. Image Credit: Tea Temim et al 2026 ApJL 1012 L26.

Industry observers note that "Identifying the different types of dust grains formed in the chemically distinct layers of a supernova brings us one step closer to understanding how much dust supernovae contribute to the interstellar dust reservoir in our galaxy," said co-author Ilse De Looze, associate professor at Ghent University in Belgium. "By revealing the composition of this newly formed supernova dust, JWST also provides crucial insights into how well these grains can survive the powerful reverse shocks that sweep through the supernova debris, ultimately determining how much dust can escape into the interstellar medium.".

This JWST image of Cas A has the synchrotron emissions subtracted. Since synchrotron emissions are non-thermal, and since their emission lines overlap the lines from thermal dust, removing them helps to isolate the signal from the ejecta, which is what the researchers are interested in. So this image basically tracks the thermal emissions from carbon dust. Image Credit: Tea Temim et al 2026 ApJL 1012 L26.

The JWST played a leading role in this effort to piece together what happened to Cas A's progenitor. But it's observations added to an existing observational base from JAXA's XRISM x-ray satellite and NASA's own Chandra X-ray Observatory. Taken together, the more complete picture demonstrates that the progenitor's shell mergers were underway prior to its explosion as a supernova.

After all the imaging, processing, and fitting to models, this is the overall result. This figure shows which parts of the Cas A ejecta are from the existing circumstellar medium (left: Mg2SiO4 grains) and which parts are actually form the progenitor star (right: SiO2 grains.) Image Credit: Tea Temim et al 2026 ApJL 1012 L26.

âWith Webb, the vast improvement in being able to resolve at the individual clump level helps us do more sophisticated dust chemistry,â noted Dan Milisavljevic, associate professor and co-author of the study from Purdue University in the United States. âAs a result, we can tie the explosion back to the makeup of the progenitor star hundreds of years afterward. Itâs telling us about what was happening, we think, in the hours leading up to core collapse. Understanding this process is essential to explaining which elements the supernova explosion will release into the galaxy and how those elements enrich future generations of stars and planets.â.

These results will also help build better model for understanding other supernova remnants.

The authors say this work indicates how important the JWST's high-resolution images are for understanding dust ejecta in supernova remnants and how it was formed. (But smart Universe Today readers already know how important the JWST is.).

"It also demonstrates that spatially resolved dust compositions in young SNRs can serve as a powerful probe of the chemical structure and explosion properties of core-collapse SNe," they conclude.

Legislative Branch bill would hold off on GAO cuts

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A group of visitors walks past the Capitol on Sept.
  • With stopgap funding set to expire in less than a month, Senate Republican appropriators Thursday unveiled a roughly $5.3 billion draft fiscal 2027 Legislative Branch spending bill that would boost security funding and sidestep contentious debates over a key watchdog.
  • The proposal would provide $965 million for Capitol Police, a nearly $83 million hike from fiscal 2026, but still short of the more than $1 billion the department requested as threats against lawmakers rise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A group of visitors walks past the Capitol on Sept. 22. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo).

With stopgap funding set to expire in less than a month, Senate Republican appropriators Thursday unveiled a roughly $5.3 billion draft fiscal 2027 Legislative Branch spending bill that would boost security funding and sidestep contentious debates over a key watchdog.

The proposal would provide $965 million for Capitol Police, a nearly $83 million hike from fiscal 2026, but still short of the more than $1 billion the department requested as threats against lawmakers rise.

And it would bump funding for the Government Accountability Office up to $860 million, an increase of nearly 6 percent from fiscal 2026. That stands in contrast to the version of the bill advanced by the House Appropriations Committee in May, which floated slashing the GAO by 25 percent.

Industry observers note that it joins several other draft spending bills released this week by Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, who is trying to kickstart bicameral negotiations as lawmakers stare down a Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government.

Her committee ran into a stalemate on topline numbers earlier this year that stopped it from marking up any of the 12 annual bills, but lawmakers nipped the threat of a government shutdown in the bud ahead of the midterm elections by pushing through a continuing resolution. With that funding now set to expire next month, appropriators are hoping they can wrap up at least some of the bills while punting the rest into the next Congress with another stopgap.

The Legislative Branch bill is the smallest of the 12 appropriations bills and typically among the least controversial. But debates over the GAO have become a sticking point during the Trump administration as the agency accuses the White House of violating budget laws — a move the Office of Management and Budget has pushed back on, arguing the GAO has no authority over the administration since it is part of the legislative branch.

The GAO has been without a permanent head after its longtime leader Gene L. Dodaro retired last year, although Republicans are now making a last-ditch effort to get one confirmed during the lame-duck session before Democrats take power.

The House version of the spending bill sought to bar the comptroller general from suing under the 1974 budget law restricting presidential impoundments, unless specifically authorized by Congress. But the Senate proposal includes no such language, and overall, it appears designed to avoid drastic or contentious moves.

It would also leave in place a provision that would block cost-of-living adjustments for members of Congress, whose pay has been frozen since 2009.

Senate Democrats, however, criticized the bill text after its release, saying it wouldn’t invest enough in the legislative branch.

“The Legislative Branch bill underfunds key work to support oversight of the Executive Branch, and it underfunds important efforts to keep the Capitol complex safe,” Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., said in a statement.

It has been revealed that the Architect of the Capitol would get $762.5 million, though funding for House office buildings is not included in that total. The agency is requesting $1.6 billion as it seeks to begin large-scale renovations of the Rayburn House Office Building. The architect has repeatedly warned lawmakers that parts of the Capitol complex are in need of critical infrastructure upgrades, arguing that delaying renovations will only make them more expensive as things continue to deteriorate.

The bill’s $5.3 billion proposal represents funding for the Senate and legislative branch agencies, while excluding House-only funds, which are typically added later.

Tech Report: Researchers Just Sent an Unblockable Message Through a Solid Wall Using Gravity

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (714 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers have demonstrated an unusual way to transmit information through solid barriers using gravity rather than electromagnetic signals.
  • Recent findings suggest that physicists at the University of Queensland have transmitted a message through a brick wall using gravity instead of electromagnetic signals.
  • The experiment took place in UQ’s Parnell Building, where researchers moved a 1.8-metric-ton (about 4,000 pounds) elevator counterweight between two positions representing binary 0 and 1.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers have demonstrated an unusual way to transmit information through solid barriers using gravity rather than electromagnetic signals.

Recent findings suggest that physicists at the University of Queensland have transmitted a message through a brick wall using gravity instead of electromagnetic signals. Their unconventional communication system relied on a moving elevator counterweight and an extremely sensitive instrument capable of detecting tiny changes in the gravitational field.

The experiment took place in UQ’s Parnell Building, where researchers moved a 1.8-metric-ton (about 4,000 pounds) elevator counterweight between two positions representing binary 0 and 1. A gravimeter positioned in a nearby bathroom detected the gravitational changes and decoded a single word: “Gravity.”.

According to recent reports, unlike radio waves and other electromagnetic signals, gravitational fields cannot be blocked by ordinary building materials. This means information carried by changes in gravity could potentially reach places where conventional wireless communication struggles.

Dr. Charles Woffinden from UQ’s School of Mathematics and Physics explained the advantage. “Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path,” he noted. “Anyone who has lost phone reception in a tunnel or struggled with Wi-Fi through a solid wall will understand the appeal.”.

“While the present system is far from practical, it demonstrates the possibility of communicating using a method that ordinary physical barriers cannot block.”.

The communication experiment grew out of an unrelated effort to measure vehicle weights without physical contact. Dr. Andrew Groszek and his colleagues were developing a system that could estimate the mass of trucks and other heavy vehicles by detecting their gravitational attraction.

“We were aiming to determine the mass of trucks and other large vehicles by measuring their tiny gravitational pull,” Dr. Groszek noted. “Once we had shown that the idea worked, we realized the same physics could be used to encode and transmit information.”.

The researchers applied that principle to communication by moving a large mass between fixed positions. Each movement altered the gravitational field measured by the detector, allowing the team to encode binary information without transmitting electromagnetic signals.

According to recent reports, although the experiment successfully transmitted information, its data rate was exceptionally low. Professor Andrew White identified the aging elevator as a major constraint.

“Our lift was snail-paced – it’s from the 1950s – so our experiment transmitted just 1 bit per minute, meaning it took an hour to send a single word,” Professor White stated.

“The speed of gravity communication would come down to how big the mass is, how fast you can move it, and the sensitivity of the detector.”.

“It took more than 100 years to go from the first telegraph system to the mobile phone, so while gravity communication is not practical today, it could be in the future.”.

Professor Matthew Davis mentioned the experiment established that information can be deliberately encoded in a gravitational field and recovered by a detector. The achievement demonstrates the underlying physics, although substantial improvements would be needed before the technique could serve as a useful communication system.

According to recent reports, “It’s not often that you get to demonstrate an entirely new way of communicating,” Professor Davis stated. “We have shown experimentally that information can be encoded in the gravitational field and recovered at the other end.”.

In a recent development, the researchers also modeled how more sensitive quantum sensors might improve the technique. Unlike the classical gravimeter used in the experiment, such sensors could potentially detect weaker gravitational changes at greater distances.

“Our experiment used a classical gravity sensor, but our modeling indicates that quantum sensors could, with rather ambitious assumptions, support ranges of up to about 500 meters (about 1,640 feet) and data rates of around 15 bits per minute.”.

Those figures are theoretical projections, not experimentally demonstrated capabilities. Gravity-based communication remains far too slow for practical applications, but more advanced detectors could eventually make it possible to exchange information in environments that radio waves, light, and other conventional signals cannot penetrate.

Reference: “Unblockable communication with gravity” by Andrew J. Groszek, Charles W. Woffinden, Michael D. Harvey, Andrew G. White and Matthew J. Davis, 18 November 2026, Science Advances. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aee0802.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A star's axial tilt as it relates to the circumplanetary disk which surrounds it is known as stellar obliquity.
  • The angle between the spin axis of a star and the orbital axis of its planetsââstellar obliquityââholds clues about how the spin-orbit orientations of stars and planets evolve throughout their lifetime, Lauren Biddle, an astrophysicist at Princeton University, told me via email.
  • In a paper accepted for publication in The Astronomical Journal, Biddle and her co-author, Brendan Bowler, compared stellar inclinations with orbital inclinations for 114 single sunlike stars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A star's axial tilt as it relates to the circumplanetary disk which surrounds it is known as stellar obliquity. Over space and time, there are a myriad of solar type stars with all sorts of obliquities. But the question heretofore has always been what effect a given starâs initial obliquity has on the planetary system that forms around it.

The angle between the spin axis of a star and the orbital axis of its planetsââstellar obliquityââholds clues about how the spin-orbit orientations of stars and planets evolve throughout their lifetime, Lauren Biddle, an astrophysicist at Princeton University, told me via email.

In a paper accepted for publication in The Astronomical Journal, Biddle and her co-author, Brendan Bowler, compared stellar inclinations with orbital inclinations for 114 single sunlike stars.

Recent findings suggest that biddle and Bowler sampled 49 protoplanetary disk systems where planets were just beginning to form around their nascent stars. They also sampled 24 debris disk systems (stars circled by rings of gas, dust, and rocky planetesimals).

Industry observers note that the authors then sampled 21 warm Jupiter systems (where gas giant planets circle their parent stars on orbital periods that range between 10 and 100 days). And finally, they sampled 20 so-called hot Jupiter systems. Hot Jupiters were the first type exoplanets found around sunlike stars and usually orbit their parent stars on insanely short orbits of less than ten days, but at least one has been found to orbit its parent star in only 16 hours.

Yet as Biddle notes, the processes that drive changes in stellar obliquity could differ depending on a combination of how close a planet is from the central star and how old the planetary system actually is.

This work tests for signatures of obliquity evolution across âspaceâ by comparing the spin-orbit angles of planetary systems across a range of orbital distances, and âtimeâ by comparing systems over a range of ages, Biddle told me.

The results show that stellar obliquities are similar across orbital separation and age.

This suggests that after planets form, it is rare for their orbits to undergo large changes, and the changes that do happen are not detectable in the current data, notes Biddle.

Recent findings suggest that some theories predict that orbital inclinations of planets could drastically change over time due to gravitational interactions with other planets or stars; or in the case of hot Jupiters, interactions from tidal forces with the host star, says Biddle. We donât see that in our data; instead, we find that the fraction of misaligned orbits in young planetary systems resembles that of older ones, she says.

According to recent reports, by âstellar misalignment,â Biddle means that the starâs spin axis points in a different direction than the orbital axis of a planet. In contrast, a system is aligned when the starâs equator lies in the same plane as the planetâs orbit, like a spinning top placed at the center of a hula hoop.

Sources indicate that it is misaligned when the starâs spin axis is tipped relative to that plane, says Biddle. But because of observational limitations, we can only measure the lower limit of the angle between a starâs tilt and the orbitâs tilt, she says.

So, the true difference could actually be larger.

According to recent reports, thus far, however, large stellar obliquity changes appear to be uncommon. But Biddle notes that there is a major caveat in their data.

In a recent development, we deliberately chose single stars that are cooler and host giant transiting planets, indicates Biddle. We left out stars with close stellar companions, hot stars, small planets, and non-transiting giant planets on wider orbits, so large tilts could be common in any of those, she says.

Industry observers note that this artist's conception indicates a binary-star, or two-star, system, called HD 113766, where astronomers suspect a rocky Earth-like planet is forming around one of the stars. At approximately 10 to 16 million years old, astronomers suspect this star is at just the right age for forming rocky planets. The system is located approximately 424 light-years away from Earth. Credit: NASA/R. Hurt, JPL-Caltech/C. Lisse, JHUAPL.

In practice, every system we classified as misaligned is tilted by at least 10 degrees, and on average the misaligned ones are tilted roughly 30 to 50 degrees, states Biddle.

A Plethora Of Strangely Mis-Aligned Exoplanets.

It has been revealed that but prior to the discovery of extrasolar planets, our understanding of these alignments was based entirely on the organization of the Solar System, where planets are mostly aligned with the Sun, with the large ones orbiting farther out, says Biddle. So, it came as a surprise when we discovered that giant close-in exoplanets with very misaligned orbits exist, she says.

Our own solar systemâs planetary alignments are pretty much coplanar.

The Sunâs spin axis, however, is tilted by about 6 degrees relative to the average orbital plane of the planets and dwarf planets, indicates Biddle.

Biddle doesnât know for certain if the Sunâs axis was tilted from the start.

According to recent reports, but if we assume it started out aligned, there are several proposed explanations for how the Sun could have become tilted, claims Biddle. They include a past fly-by of another star, tugs from an undiscovered distant planet, torques from stellar winds, and even internal gravity waves, she says.

There isn't evidence that stellar obliquity itself affects planetary habitability, says Biddle. But it does tell us about the history of planets' formation and where they eventually end up around the host star, which matters a lot when it comes to habitability, she says.

This 3D-Printed Robot Runs, Swims, and Climbs Without Any Electronics

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (808 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A robot powered entirely by air could offer a newly introduced way to explore dangerous environments where radiation or strong magnetic fields threaten conventional electronics.
  • A six-legged robot made entirely of soft materials can run at speeds of up to 10.6 miles per hour (4.72 meters per second), making it the fastest soft robot of its kind.
  • It has been revealed that built by engineers at the University of California, San Diego, the machine can race across sand, gravel, and concrete, run down stairs, and even swim.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A robot powered entirely by air could offer a newly introduced way to explore dangerous environments where radiation or strong magnetic fields threaten conventional electronics.

A six-legged robot made entirely of soft materials can run at speeds of up to 10.6 miles per hour (4.72 meters per second), making it the fastest soft robot of its kind.

It has been revealed that built by engineers at the University of California, San Diego, the machine can race across sand, gravel, and concrete, run down stairs, and even swim. Perhaps most remarkably, the entire robot is 3D-printed in one piece using a single material, and it needs no electronics to move.

Recent findings suggest that the breakthrough, described in Science Robotics, takes inspiration from a centuries-old invention, the steam engine. By adapting the way steam engines make efficient use of pressure, researchers found a way to make their soft robot run more than 100 times faster than an earlier version.

The project began with a much slower machine. In 2022, researchers at the UC San Diego Jacobs School of Engineering developed a 3D-printed, air-powered robot that could walk at just 4 centimeters (about 1.6 inches) per second. Described in a 2025 paper in Advanced Intelligent Systems, the original design demonstrated that a robot could move using nothing more than a network of air-filled chambers and valves built directly into its soft body. Its speed, however, was limited by how much air pressure and airflow the internal structures could withstand.

“Our first walking robot demonstrated what was possible, but it was too slow. We hoped to overcome this limitation, and we were fortunate to find a solution to make the upcoming robot 100 times faster,” said Yichen Zhai, a former postdoctoral researcher in Professor Michael T. Tolley’s Bioinspired Robotics and Design Laboratory at UC San Diego.

Zhai and Tolley’s team knew that increasing the air pressure could make the robot move faster. Inside the machine, a connected network of chambers, valves, and tubes directs compressed air to move its legs. Making those structures larger and stronger would allow more air to flow through at higher pressures, but there was a catch. At high speeds, the robot could exhaust pressurized air before using much of its remaining energy, wasting the very power needed to keep it running.

The researchers found their solution in the compound steam engine, which extracts more useful energy by allowing steam to expand through multiple chambers rather than releasing it all at once. They incorporated a similar arrangement into the robot, giving compressed air two jobs as it moves through the body. First, it passes through smaller, high-pressure chambers to operate the valves. It then travels into larger, low-pressure chambers, where it drives the legs.

This two-stage system allows the robot to make better use of its compressed air while achieving speeds far beyond those of its predecessor. It also preserves one of the design’s most appealing features: the entire network of moving parts can be printed together without requiring separate electronic controls.

In a recent development, the researchers described the engineering challenge this way, “The key challenge was to implement a time-tested solution (the compound steam engine) in a soft running robot that can be printed in a single piece out of a single material. We see this as a step towards complex and powerful robots that can be printed on the desktop using inexpensive materials.”.

To see what their creation could handle, the team tested it across concrete, gravel, lawns, mulch, and sand. The robot successfully navigated these different surfaces, ran down stairs, swam in water, and continued functioning underwater. Its ability to move through such varied environments demonstrates what can be accomplished with a relatively simple, flexible design powered entirely by air.

Sources indicate that there is still one major limitation. Although the robot operates without electronics, it remains tethered to an external source of compressed air, such as a conventional air compressor. The researchers hope to reduce its air consumption enough that future versions could carry a portable supply, potentially using a small cartridge of compressed air instead. They also want to develop more sophisticated movements that would allow the robot to steer and manipulate objects.

It has been revealed that eventually, inexpensive robots that can be printed in a single piece and operate without electronics could prove useful in places where conventional machines struggle. The researchers envision applications ranging from disaster response and space exploration to scientific reconnaissance in environments with intense radiation or magnetic fields, where electronic equipment may be unable to function.

Reference: “Printing powerful soft robots on a desktop” by Yichen Zhai and Michael T. Tolley, 18 November 2026, Science Robotics. DOI: 10.1126/scirobotics.aei1264.

The work was funded by the National Science Foundation.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, since the launch of Sputnik, humanity has talked to its spacecraft through radio waves.
  • First, letâs take a second to appreciate the leaps and bounds researchers have made passing data over space laser links recently.
  • Those conditions matter for an optical ground station.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, since the launch of Sputnik, humanity has talked to its spacecraft through radio waves. Radio is great for communication through any weather, but it has hit a limit â traditional radio frequencies are highly regulated by bodies like the International Telecommunications Union, which limits the scalability of radio communications networks to meet the growing demand of bandwidth to and from space. The obvious solution is to switch to infrared lasers, which have an extremely high data transfer rate. However, according to a paper available in pre-print on arXiv from Dr. Slava Turyshev â best known to UT readers for his work on turning the Sunâs gravity into a giant telescope â the raw speed of laser communication isnât the bottleneck, itâs the systemâs reliability.

First, letâs take a second to appreciate the leaps and bounds researchers have made passing data over space laser links recently. Perhaps the most impressive mission was a NASA demonstration called TBIRD, which beamed an astonishing 200 gigabits per second (Gb/s) from orbit, and completed a data transfer of five terabytes in a single five-minute pass over its receiving telescope. That is an astonishing speed for laser communication, but it had the advantage of near-perfect conditions.

Those conditions matter for an optical ground station. One challenge is tracking. A radio communications link spreads its signal over a patch hundreds of kilometers wide, whereas a laser from low Earth orbit might illuminate a patch less than twenty meters across. As a spacecraft hurtles overhead at more than seven kilometers per second, keeping a beam thousands of times narrower locked onto a receiving telescope is far harder than hitting a radio dish.

Fraser takes a question about space-based laser communication.

Another obstacle that radio frequency signals donât have to worry about is airplane interference. Ground stations must automatically shut off their uplink lasers if an airplane passes overhead, so as not to blind the pilots (or the planeâs sensors) with a highly concentrated light beam. While each plane overflight is relatively brief, it can cause consistent disruption which isnât a problem for radio communications frameworks.

Recent findings suggest that the real challenge though is the atmosphere. Anyone that looks up at the sky on a cloudless night can see the stars twinkling. That is caused by swirling pockets of warm and cold air in our atmosphere, and in addition to making the stars seem to dance, it also distorts incoming laser light. To correct for this in optical communication systems, engineers have to use fast-moving deformable mirrors in systems called adaptive optics, or specialized light-sorting microchips. Neither option is cheap.

It has been revealed that but the real difficulty in the atmosphere for optical communications is simple to explain â clouds. No laser in the optical or near-infrared range can punch through thick cloud cover. So when an optical base station is covered by thick cloud cover, it is essentially impossible to communicate with, knocking out both uplinks and downlinks unless another suitable base station happens to be available.

Fraser talks about the power of adaptive optics to make the atmosphere "disappear".

In a recent development, according to the paper, pairing stations together does get some improvement. A single one can be expected to be available a little more than 60% of the time, but pairing two together in the American Southwest, for example, can bump that up to around 85%. According to another paper from the German Aerospace Center, setting up a network of eight separate optical stations around Australia and Newly introduced Zealand drops the chance of an outage to just 0.02%.

However, base stations are expensive. Building eight stations for a single mission is economically infeasible â each station costs roughly two million dollars a year to build, staff, and operate. At that rate, delivering a single terabyte of information to a single mission, if it uses a single station, would cost somewhere between three to four thousand dollars. Scaling that up to eight stations to almost guarantee consistent coverage would mean it would cost $18K to send a single terabyte of data.

According to recent reports, the only way that math works is by multiple satellite companies splitting the same ground network. If they could keep the ground stations busy at least half of the time, it could drop the price per terabyte into a reasonable range. To support those efforts, there is a push for standardization already in place.

Fraser answers a question about adpative optics alternatives.

Industry observers note that the Civil Standard (CCSDS 141.0-B / âO3Kâ) developed by the Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems defines hardware and handshaking specs for high-rate near-Earth links. To support that standard, the US Department of Defense also decided to get involved, introducing the US Space Development Agencyâs Optical Communications Terminal Standard, requiring interoperability across terminals no matter the supplier, which includes requirements for CCSDS communication protocols.

In a recent development, all that being remarked, according to Dr. Turyshevâs paper, there is very little likelihood that purely optical communication will supplant radio for space communication anytime soon. A better approach would be to offer a hybrid partnership between the two protocols. Lasers can serve as the âheavy-liftâ workhorses, downloading massive videos or Earth-observation imagery, and radio waves can maintain unbreakable lifeline support for steering or handling emergencies. That combined approach offers the best way to make sure astronauts and all of our critical space infrastructure stay connected, no matter the weather down here on Earth.

S. G. Turyshev - Optical Ground Stations for Space Communications:Systems Engineering, Availability, and Service Economics Through 2030.

A 72-Year-Old Invention Could Be the Key to Unlocking More Powerful Quantum Computers

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1005 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A technology older than the laser is finding upcoming life inside diamond, offering a potential way to make quantum computers more powerful without overwhelming their sensitive measurement systems.
  • A quantum computer can process information using the strange rules of quantum physics, but getting an accurate answer out of it presents a challenge.
  • Industry observers note that researchers at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) have developed a fresh amplifier that tackles this problem using an unlikely material: diamond.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A technology older than the laser is finding upcoming life inside diamond, offering a potential way to make quantum computers more powerful without overwhelming their sensitive measurement systems.

A quantum computer can process information using the strange rules of quantum physics, but getting an accurate answer out of it presents a challenge. The information is carried by extremely faint microwave signals that must be amplified before they can be measured. Unfortunately, amplifying those signals can introduce unwanted noise, making it harder to tell what the computer is actually saying.

Industry observers note that researchers at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) have developed a fresh amplifier that tackles this problem using an unlikely material: diamond. Their device can strengthen microwave signals more than 1,000 times while adding very little noise. It can also handle stronger signals and operate in magnetic fields, potentially overcoming limitations that make today’s quantum computers difficult to scale up.

The findings were published on November 16, 2026, in Nature Communications.

It has been revealed that in superconducting quantum computers, information is stored in quantum bits, or qubits. To determine a qubit’s state, researchers measure a weak microwave signal associated with it. The difficulty is that these signals are extraordinarily sensitive to interference.

That is one reason superconducting quantum computers operate at temperatures close to absolute zero, the lowest temperature theoretically possible. Keeping the equipment this cold reduces interference caused by heat, but it cannot eliminate the noise introduced by the amplifiers themselves. Once that unwanted noise enters the measurement, subsequent amplification stages strengthen it along with the original signal, increasing the chance of an incorrect reading.

Existing amplifiers can detect these faint signals with remarkably little added noise, although they come with trade-offs. Conventional Josephson parametric amplifiers, for example, can become overwhelmed when several qubits are measured simultaneously. This effect, known as saturation, limits how many signals they can reliably process at once.

Another technology, known as kinetic inductance parametric amplification, can handle stronger signals but generally requires more electrical power and additional wiring. As quantum computers grow, that extra equipment adds cost and complexity. Some systems also use qubits based on electron spin, which require magnetic fields that can disrupt conventional superconducting amplifiers.

The OIST researchers approached these challenges by revisiting a technology that predates the laser.

According to recent reports, masers were first demonstrated in 1954, six years before lasers appeared. Both technologies amplify electromagnetic waves, but while lasers work with light, masers operate with microwaves. They rely on a process called stimulated emission, in which an incoming photon carrying the right amount of energy prompts an excited electron to release another matching photon. Repeating this process strengthens the original signal.

According to recent reports, “Despite being invented before optical lasers, masers — microwave lasers — have been left far behind because they often require cryogenic conditions to function, which made them impractical until very recently,” explains Dr. Yuimaru Kubo, head of the Hybrid Quantum Device Team at OIST. “But now, with quantum computers operating at temperatures very close to absolute zero, we have given them fresh life as very promising candidates for amplifying quantum signals with very little noise.”.

According to recent reports, to put this older technology to work, the team used a specially prepared diamond containing nitrogen impurities known as P1 centers. These impurities contain electrons whose spin, an intrinsic quantum property, makes them behave like tiny magnets.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers apply a relatively weak microwave field to the diamond, supplying energy that pushes most of these electron spins into higher-energy states. When a faint microwave signal enters the amplifier, it stimulates the excited spins to release their stored energy as additional microwaves at the same frequency.

In effect, the diamond transfers energy from its excited electrons into the incoming signal, making that signal stronger without requiring a powerful microwave source.

“We were surprised by how much amplification we could achieve using such a small amount of microwave power,” adds Kubo.

Sources indicate that in testing, the diamond maser amplified microwave signals more than 1,000-fold while introducing just 2.55 quanta of added noise. Quanta are discrete units used to describe energy at the quantum scale. For comparison, the fundamental quantum limit for this type of amplification is 0.5 quantum, meaning that even an ideal amplifier cannot eliminate added noise entirely.

Recent findings suggest that the device also tolerated much stronger incoming signals than conventional Josephson parametric amplifiers. Because the diamond maser operates in a magnetic field, it could be particularly useful for quantum computers that rely on spin-based qubits.

Industry observers note that although the technology is still being developed toward commercialization, its potential uses extend beyond quantum computing. Sensitive microwave amplification is also important in spectroscopy, which scientists use to investigate the properties of materials, and nuclear magnetic resonance, the physical principle behind MRI scanners.

Other possible applications include fundamental physics experiments searching for dark matter, where detecting extremely weak signals could help researchers investigate one of the universe’s most elusive mysteries.

Reference: “A near-quantum-limited diamond maser amplifier operating at millikelvin temperatures” by Morihiro Ohta, Ching-Ping Lee, Vincent P. M. Sietses, I. Kostylev, J. R. Ball, P. Moroshkin, T. Hamamoto, Y. Kobayashi, S. Onoda, T. Ohshima, J. Isoya, Hiroki Takahashi and Yuimaru Kubo, 16 November 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79021-7.

Recent findings suggest that this work was supported by the Proof-of-Concept (PoC) Program by OIST Innovation, the JST Moonshot R&D Program (Grant No. JPMJMS2066), JST-PRESTO (Grant No. JPMJPR15P7), JSPS KAKENHI Grant-in-Aid for Scientific Research (B) (Grant No. 18H01817), Grant-in-Aid for Scientific Research on Innovative Areas (Grant No. 18H04295), the Science Research Promotion Fund from the Promotion and Mutual Aid Corporation for Private Schools of Japan (PMAC), and the Research Encouragement Grant from the AGC Inc. Research Foundation. M.O. and T.H. acknowledge financial support from the JSPS Grant-in-Aid for Fellows (Grant Nos. 23KJ2135 and 24KJ2178), and J.R.B. acknowledges support from OIST Graduate University.

UK-Built X-Ray Telescope Ready For Action at Mercury
