💡 Key Takeaways
  • A first of its kind instrument indicates its stuff prior to arrival at Mercury.
  • The joint ESA/JAXA BepiColombo mission has arrived at Mercury, and among its arsenal of detectors ready to explore the innermost world is an innovative new instrument.
  • Industry observers note that A University of Leicester team recently released an image of an iconic deep-sky object as a proof of concept test for their Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A first of its kind instrument indicates its stuff prior to arrival at Mercury.

The joint ESA/JAXA BepiColombo mission has arrived at Mercury, and among its arsenal of detectors ready to explore the innermost world is an innovative new instrument.

Industry observers note that A University of Leicester team recently released an image of an iconic deep-sky object as a proof of concept test for their Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS). Located on the Mercury Planetary Orbiter segment of the BepiColombo spacecraft stack, UK-built MIXS is the first x-ray instrument on an interplanetary spacecraft, and UK Space Agencyâs instrument contribution to the mission.

According to recent reports, the image shows the Crab Nebula (Messier 1) in x-ray light. Located 6,500 light-years distant, âThe Crabâ is a prominent x-ray source, located 6,500 light-years distant in the constellation of Taurus the Bull. The Crab Nebula made a fine target for calibration and testing. Itâs rare for an interplanetary mission to deliberately image a deep-sky object, though they do occasionally turn up in star-tracker navigation frames.

In a recent development, MIXS image of the Crab Nebula (inset) overlaid on a visible light background. Credit:ESA/University of Leicester/NASA/GSFC.

Fresh Horizons once captured the âWishing Wellâ open cluster NGC 3532 using its LORRI imager.

Industry observers note that âX-rays cannot penetrate Earth's atmosphere to the ground so all X-ray telescopes must be in space,â Adam Fox (MIXS Operations Scientist) told Universe Today. âX-rays can only be reflected to a focus at very shallow angles, which means conventional X-ray telescopes must have very long focal lengths (~10 meters) with nested mirrors, meaning a mass of hundreds of kilograms.â.

âMIXS uses novel X-ray optics called micro-pore optics which have millions of tiny pores (20 microns wide) to allow an X-ray telescope which is 1 meter in length and weighs only 11 kilograms, making it small and light enough to be flown to Mercury.â.

The MIXS instrument had to wait through 8-long years of space travel, until the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) was jettisoned from the stack joined to the Mercury Magnetosphere Orbiter (MMO) and the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) this past September 3rd. This finally exposed MIXS to space, allowing the team an opportunity to calibrate and test the instrument prior to arrival.

The BepiColombo spacecraft stack prior to launch. Credit: ESA.

âUntil early September, the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) which carries MIXS was attached to the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) which provided power and propulsion during BepiColombo's 8 year cruise to Mercury,â states Fox. âDuring this time, MIXS' view was directly blocked by the transfer module, only following this separation has MIXS had a view of deep space for the first time. MIXS has been switched on periodically during cruise for checkouts of instrument health during which only the behavior of the detectors within could be monitored.â.

The image is the result of 55 platform slews over the course of 39 hours on September 11 and 12th shortly after MTM disposal.

MIXS is designed to create a surface map showing the atomic makeup of Mercury at an unprecedented scale. Working in tandem with the Solar Intensity X-ray and particle Spectrometer (SIXS), MIXS will look at fluorescence of surface material created as a result of high energy solar x-rays impacting the surface. MIXS will also document the local environment in x-rays and magnetospheric interaction on the nighttime side of the planet.

The MIXS instrument prior to launch. Credit: University of Leicester.

In a recent development, âThe scientific advantage from having an X-ray telescope at Mercury is that (the) surface emits X-rays when hit by Solar X-rays or particles from the magnetosphere,â Alec McCrea (University of Leicester) told Universe Today. âThese X-rays have characteristic energies corresponding to certain elements which can tell you what the surface is made of. An X-ray telescope can achieve this at a much higher resolution than achieved on previous missions due to both its smaller FOV and imaging capabilities.â.

The arrival for the BepiColombo mission at Mercury occurred late last week on November 21st, when Mercury finally captured the attached MMO and MPO pair into an initial elliptical orbit, after a close 635 kilometer pass above the surface of the planet.

In a recent development, this marked a first a âweak stability captureâ for a planetary mission, as BepiColombo moved inside the gravitational influence of Mercury. The thruster fire was also a first for the spacecraft stack post transfer module separation in September.

According to recent reports, there was a bit of drama last week as Estrack controllers noted the mission briefly entered safe mode and the planned thruster burn ended prematurely. The spacecraft still achieved 77% of the expected velocity change, enough to enter orbit. BepiColombo is now in a 75 hour orbit around Mercury, versus the original planned 58 hour orbit.

This comes after one Earth, two Venus and six flybys past Mercury needed to enter capture and orbit around the innermost world. The arrival was also extended from December 2025 to this month, due to an issue with the thrusters on the MTM. This is JAXAâs and ESAâs first mission to Mercury, and only the second to orbit the innermost world since NASAâs Messenger mission ended operations on April 30, 2015, becoming the first human-made object to impact Mercury.

The first mission to see Mercury closeup was NASAâs Mariner 10 on 1974.

The timeline for BepiColombo's arrival at Mercury. Credit: ESA.

Next comes the release of JAXAâs MMO (Mio) orbiter on December 9-10th, followed by the sun-shield ejection on December 16th. MPO will then settle down into a 480 by 1500 kilometer orbit early next year on March 10th, after which science operations can finally begin on April 6th. BepiColombo is expected to operate around Mercury until the end of the nominal mission in April 2028, with a possible extension until December 2029.

It has been revealed that âDevelopment of such instruments is active. For planetary X-ray fluorescence, a MIXS-like instrument is applicable to many airless bodies in the solar system and would be tailored as such,â notes Fox. âMicropore optic X-ray telescopes though have since been flown on several astrophysics missions, including SMILE, Einstein Probe and the (Space Variable Objects Monitor) SVOM.â.

If youâre up early this week, you can spot Mercury and wave at BepiColombo as well. The planet just passed greatest elongation west of the Sun this past weekend, and sits just below brilliant Venus at dawn.

Itâll be exciting to see what results BepiColombo and MIXS produce as they get down to work in 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • According to recent reports, in the classic Dr.
  • In a recent development, “They say that the Grinch’s small heart grew three sizes that day,” giving him “the strength of 10 Grinches plus two,” claims the narrator of the 1966 movie version.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

According to recent reports, in the classic Dr. Seuss tale, How the Grinch Stole Christmas, the Grinch starts out with a heart “two sizes too small.” He’s a mean one, disguising himself as Santa Claus and stealing all the Whos’ toys, food and decorations. Poised to throw it all off a mountain, the grumpy loner has a change of heart as joyous song rises from Whoville.

In a recent development, “They say that the Grinch’s small heart grew three sizes that day,” giving him “the strength of 10 Grinches plus two,” claims the narrator of the 1966 movie version. With a beatific smile, he pulls the stolen goods back from the brink and returns everything.

Would a too-small heart make you grumpy like the Grinch? And what would happen if your heart went from too small to really substantial in an instant? The answer depends on what causes the heart to shrink or swell, experts say. And whether or not you are a snake.

Heart size is generally pegged to body size, says Michelle Kittleson, a cardiologist at Cedars Sinai Smidt Heart Institute in Los Angeles. Bigger people tend to have bigger hearts. But some people, she says, have hearts that are naturally bigger or smaller than average for their bodies. It’s not clear why. However, she says, “there are negative consequences of having a too-small heart.”.

According to recent reports, in one 2025 study, researchers looked at medical records from more than 360,000 people in Australia. Those with smaller-than-average hearts had a higher risk of dying within five years than people with average or larger hearts, the team reported in JACC: Advances.

Smaller hearts may not pump blood as well as larger ones, making it harder for people to exercise. And if the Grinch didn’t exercise enough, maybe “then that made him really tired, and that made him grumpy,” Kittleson says. “Or maybe he did the research, and he found out that his life expectancy was shortened because of it, and that made him even grumpier.”.

But would rapidly increasing his heart’s size be good for the Grinch?

As the Grinch slides downhill toward Whoville, pulled by a sled piled high with presents he’d stolen and now was returning, he physically undergoes a change. What started as a heart two sizes too small swelled three sizes, both curing his grumpiness and giving him super strength. Or so the classic tale goes. A person going through such a dramatic change may not fare as well.

There are many ways a heart can grow, says Leslie Leinwand, a molecular biologist and geneticist at the University of Colorado Boulder. With vigorous exercise, “your heart gets bigger in good ways,” Leinwand says. That can be true for athletes who do lots of cardio, such as swimmers and marathon runners.

According to recent reports, “Their heart gets bigger and thicker,” Kittleson notes. “But it’s a good thing in them because it helps them pump more blood per minute than someone with a normal-size heart.” Pregnancy also makes the whole organ expand to boost blood to the developing fetus. If people stop exercising, or give birth, their hearts will shrink back to normal size within months.

Recent findings suggest that some diseases, though, can enlarge hearts in deadly ways. “If you’ve got untreated high blood pressure,” Leinwand claims, “you can get a huge heart, and it’s not good for you.”.

Stress, bad heart valves and some genetic diseases can also result in bigger, but weaker, hearts. In those cases, the heart muscle grows in order to pump more blood. At the same time, the inside of the left ventricle — the heart chamber that pumps oxygenated blood to the body — can shrink. That makes it harder for the heart to push blood out. This kind of growth takes time, Kittleson indicates.

There is one rare condition in which the heart can inflate suddenly. Called takotsubo or stress cardiomyopathy — or in some cases, broken-heart syndrome — it is brought on by extreme stress. That can include positive things like winning the lottery or entering a surprise party or negative stress such as break-up or losing a job.

It has been revealed that A surge of epinephrine, or adrenaline, from stress can make the left ventricle bulge into the shape of a pot used to catch octopuses. (Takotsubo is Japanese for “octopus pot.”) That causes immediate heart failure as the heart chamber gets too major to pump blood.

According to recent reports, so instead of becoming super strong, the Grinch “would have keeled over and collapsed,” Kittleson says. (People can survive with prompt medical care and their hearts can return to normal size in a few months.).

Given the Grinch survived his rapid growth, there’s another possible scenario: Maybe his heart is more like a snake’s.

Recent findings suggest that pythons’ hearts can balloon by up to 25 percent in a day after the snakes eat a large meal — sometimes as major as an adult deer. And the bigger a python’s meal, the more its heart grows. Larger hearts pump blood with more force, Leinwand and her colleagues reported in 2024 in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The researchers don’t know if this makes the snakes stronger overall.

Once a meal is digested, the heart shrinks again. Snakes can go through many shrink-and-grow cycles with no ill effect. Leinwand hopes that studying these snakes will lead to treatments that make human hearts healthier.

But becoming kinder, like the Grinch? Maybe not.

Notes Leinwand, “our snakes, when they eat a lot, they get rather aggressive.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept.
  • Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.
  • Sources noted Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who right now serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept. 23. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.

Sources noted Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who right now serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget. The White House submitted ethics paperwork on Ueland — required for nominations — to the GAO, according to a source.

Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., on Thursday posted notice of a committee hearing Nov. 19 to examine more than a dozen presidential nominees for executive and judicial offices, including “a nominee to be Comptroller General.”.

According to recent reports, the post identifies by name all of the nominees except the candidate for comptroller general. The post has been filled by an acting comptroller general, Orice Williams Brown, since Gene L. Dodaro completed his 15-year term at the end of last year.

The move by Paul to short-circuit the convening of a legislative commission to recommend candidates infuriated top Democrats, who excoriated the chairman in a joint statement Wednesday night. A special bipartisan, bicameral legislative commission is supposed to recommend at least three candidates for comptroller general to the president, according to statute.

Homeland Security Committee GOP staff solicited recommendations for a comptroller general from some Democratic congressional offices Wednesday afternoon, imposing a deadline of 8 a.m. Thursday, according to Democratic aides.

The president nominates the head of the GAO, the investigative arm of Congress, with the advice and consent of the Senate.

Paul pushed back on the criticism Thursday, saying, “Democrats have known about this for months and months and months.” He said the last time the special commission made recommendations for the office, when Barack Obama was president, “Democrats submitted their own list, Republicans submitted their own list. So they can complain all they want but they just need to make their list and submit it.”.

In the past, however, the special commission convened, sought applications for the position, interviewed candidates and deliberated before sending recommendations to the president.

A 1980 law states that when there is a vacancy in the comptroller general position, “there is established a commission to recommend individuals to the President for appointment to the vacant office,” and that the commission must submit at least three names.

Under the statute, the commission includes the speaker, Senate majority and minority leaders, House majority and minority leaders, chairs and ranking members of the Senate Homeland Security and House Oversight and Government Reform committees, and the Senate president pro tempore.

According to recent reports, in 1981, for example, after the law took effect, the two congressional leaders, Speaker Thomas P. “Tip” O’Neill Jr., D-Mass., and Senate Majority Leader Howard H. Baker, R-Tenn., sent a letter to President Ronald Reagan saying the special commission had met and voted to recommend eight candidates to succeed Comptroller General Elmer Staats.

“The members of the Commission have taken their statutory responsibility seriously,” they wrote.

Reagan nominated Charles A. Bowsher, who was on the list, and he was confirmed.

After Bowsher’s term ended in 1996, the commission eventually formed, interviewed multiple candidates, and deliberated for several months. Republicans controlled both chambers, and Bill Clinton was president. The members of the commission could not reach agreement, and as a result, the Republicans on the committee submitted their list to Clinton, and the Democrats on the panel submitted theirs.

Clinton also had his own list. Clinton nominated David M. Walker, who was on all three lists, and he was confirmed by the Senate more than two years after Bowsher’s departure. Walker argued Thursday against short-circuiting the commission process.

Industry observers note that “The position is of critical importance and the related statutory Commission process should not be circumvented," Walker said. "Doing so would undercut the credibility of the person and the effectiveness of the GAO.”.

In a recent development, walker resigned in March of 2008, when George W. Bush was still president. He appointed Dodaro as acting comptroller general when he left. The commission got going several months later, creating a website with application instructions and candidate questions.

Over the next two years, the commission interviewed some 20 candidates. Democrats and Republicans on the panel were unable to reach agreement, and Democrats, who had a majority on the commission, submitted their own list to Obama in 2010. Republicans followed up with their list.

“The Commission has been working in earnest on this undertaking for more than one year and has dedicated considerable time and effort to present you with highly qualified candidates for this vital position,” then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., along with other Democratic leaders, wrote to Obama when they submitted the Democrats’ list.

The Democrats’ move drew a rebuke from Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who was ranking member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee at the time.

In a recent development, collins noted in a statement she was “extremely disappointed” that Democrats “abruptly ended the selection process for the next Comptroller General without a bipartisan agreement” on the recommendations. “We have had several exceptionally qualified individuals apply to be the next leader of the GAO, and it should have been possible to come up with a consensus list.”.

Obama nominated and the Senate confirmed Dodaro, who was one of four recommendations from the Democrats.

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1071 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we are consistently launching more and more stuff into space.
  • Industry observers note that to understand why, letâs look at how engineers at the moment grade collision risk.
  • If a tech giant funnels all of its resources into a billion-dollar weather satellite and that satellite is destroyed, that is a financial catastrophe for that one specific company.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we are consistently launching more and more stuff into space. As of now, space agencies track more than 30,000 objects larger than a softball, with an expected one million more bullet-sized pieces of debris orbiting Earth that are too small to spot from the ground.. Government agencies and private commercial entities are planning to have up to 100,000 active spacecraft in orbit by the early 2030s, turning some orbital shells into crowded highways. And according to a latest paper, available in preprint on arXiv by Federico Toson, a researcher at the University of Padova in Italy, the math that regulatory agencies use to determine whether a satellite is âsafeâ in these highly congested spaces is fundamentally flawed.

Industry observers note that to understand why, letâs look at how engineers at the moment grade collision risk. Standards set by NASA and the European Space Agency rely on color-coded charts that sort missions into one of several buckets based on their risk profile. Categories like âLow,â âMedium,â and âHighâ are self-explanatory, but they eliminate important distinctions in risk profiles, and only look at one satellite at a time. And, crucially, they focus solely on the risk to the manufacturer that introduced them.

If a tech giant funnels all of its resources into a billion-dollar weather satellite and that satellite is destroyed, that is a financial catastrophe for that one specific company. But if a mega-constellation operator builds thousands of identical satellites at a cost of a million dollars a pop, losing one barely registers on their financial statements. Consequently, according to the risk profile, all relatively inexpensive, reproducible satellites that make up the mega-constellations end up with a âLowâ risk profile.

Fraser talks about how we make sure satellites don't crash into each other.

The algorithm described in the paper exposes the flaw in that logic by separating the risk into two different scores. First is the âIndividual Riskâ â i.e. the traditional metric of the financial hit a satelliteâs owner takes if the spacecraft is destroyed by collision. The second is the âCollective Riskâ, which ignores the cost of each individual satellite, but captures the physical danger each imposes on every other operational satellite in its altitude band across its entire operational and disposal lifetime.

Mathematically, this is a way of capturing the âtragedy of the commonsâ aspect of orbital space. Economists have long warned that when a âpublic goodâ (such as an orbital path) is free to use, users, whether they are farmers on a field or launch companies trying to build internet satellite constellations, have an incentive to utilize as much of the free resource as they can while not paying any attention to the consequences of that use.

In orbit, those consequences take the form of congestion, dodging maneuvers, and potential destruction of other satellites that are forced on every other company if one decides to ignore their responsibility to properly manage the impact their equipment has on an orbit. As weâve reported before, those consequences are growing, with an average Starlink satellite having to fire its thruster at least once a week to dodge a potential collision.

Fraser talks about how space junk could eventually block our access to orbit.

Industry observers note that starlink itself is a good case in point. A single Starlink V2 Mini, orbiting at 525 km, has a collective risk 317 times higher than the âindividual risk.â In a traditional risk assessment, this would mark it as âLowâ risk, whereas this fresh framework would place it very clearly in the âVery Highâ camp.

There have been some efforts to capture this long-term environmental impact already. ESA uses an index called the Environmental Consequences of Orbital Breakups (ECOB) and researchers at EPFL in Switzerland have put forward the Space Sustainability Rating. However, the simulations underpinning these metrics are computationally expensive and require hours to complete. The tool Toson developed in MATLAB runs in seconds on a standard computer and matches the higher-end benchmarks exceptionally well.

Industry observers note that itâs all good to simply enhancement the categorization of a satellite for its collective risk, but having that information is useless if operators and regulators donât do anything with it. Toson suggests updating the international debris guidelines and licensing rules to take this new metric into account. If a company wants to launch a low-cost satellite that will affect the orbital environment for everyone else, they should be required to either fund active debris cleanup or accept a cap on the total risk posed by their fleet of spacecraft.

Fraser talks about real-life advanced tech that can remove space debris.

Regulators havenât had much time to digest this newly introduced idea, so donât expect to see any such rules anytime soon. But as our orbital highways become more and more congested, satellite operators will need more guidance on how to maintain the commons before we end up in a Kessler Syndrome situation. This new paper may contribute to that standards-setting â and the sooner the better.

F. Toson - A simplified engineering algorithm for collision risk assessment and classification of LEO satellites.

This Common Vitamin Deficiency Could Be Quietly Disrupting Your Sleep

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (666 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A study combining blood tests and wearable sleep monitors suggests that a common vitamin deficiency may play an overlooked role in sleep health as we age.
  • Older adults with higher vitamin D levels slept nearly 20 minutes longer each night and experienced shorter periods of nighttime wakefulness than those with lower levels, according to a study led by researchers at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.
  • Industry observers note that the findings suggest that vitamin D may be an crucial factor in sleep health as people age.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A study combining blood tests and wearable sleep monitors suggests that a common vitamin deficiency may play an overlooked role in sleep health as we age.

Older adults with higher vitamin D levels slept nearly 20 minutes longer each night and experienced shorter periods of nighttime wakefulness than those with lower levels, according to a study led by researchers at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. Vitamin D deficiency was associated with an even greater reduction in sleep duration.

Industry observers note that the findings suggest that vitamin D may be an crucial factor in sleep health as people age. However, the researchers caution that the study cannot establish whether increasing vitamin D levels directly improves sleep.

“These findings suggest that we should investigate more thoroughly whether boosting vitamin D levels can improve sleep health,” claims study senior author Adam Spira, PhD, MA, professor in the Department of Mental Health at the Bloomberg School and a core faculty member of the Johns Hopkins Center on Aging and Health.

The researchers, working in collaboration with scientists at the National Institute on Aging, analyzed data from 460 men and women with an average age of approximately 71. Participants were assessed between 2012 and 2019 as part of the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging. Blood samples provided measurements of vitamin D concentrations, while wrist-worn actigraphs recorded sleep and wake patterns.

After accounting for age, race, sex, and other potentially influential factors, the researchers found significant associations between higher vitamin D concentrations, longer sleep duration, and less prolonged nighttime awakenings.

When participants were classified according to clinical definitions of vitamin D deficiency, insufficiency, and normal levels, those with a deficiency slept approximately 23 minutes less than those with normal levels.

Industry observers note that both vitamin D deficiency and disrupted sleep are widespread among older adults. Poor sleep has been associated with an increased risk of dementia, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and other chronic conditions. Earlier studies have also linked low vitamin D levels to poorer sleep quality, although clinical trials investigating the benefits of supplementation have generally involved small and relatively homogeneous populations.

In the new study, the associations between vitamin D concentrations and sleep appeared strongest among Black participants.

“Black adults in the United States have a higher prevalence of vitamin D deficiency and sleep disturbances compared to white adults, and may benefit more from increasing vitamin D levels,” states study first author Diefei Chen, a PhD candidate in the Bloomberg School’s Department of Epidemiology.

In a recent development, the team also investigated vitamin B12, which previous research has suggested may influence sleep. Women with higher B12 concentrations tended to spend less time awake after initially falling asleep. Among men, higher concentrations appeared to be associated with more nighttime wakefulness. Neither pattern was supported by conclusive statistical evidence.

It has been revealed that the researchers could not determine whether participants obtained their vitamin D primarily through sunlight exposure, food, or supplements. Future investigations could examine whether these different sources influence sleep differently.

The study used a serial cross-sectional design, meaning that researchers analyzed a series of snapshots over time rather than establishing how changes in vitamin D levels affect subsequent sleep patterns.

Further research, particularly larger clinical trials and studies tracking changes in vitamin D and sleep over extended periods, will be needed to determine whether correcting a deficiency can meaningfully improve sleep in older adults.

Industry observers note that reference: “Association of vitamin D and B12 levels with actigraphic sleep in cognitively unimpaired middle-aged and older adults” by Diefei Chen, Jill A Rabinowitz, Fan Wu, Zhikui Wei, Yang An, Jennifer A Schrack, Toshiko Tanaka, Chee W Chia, Mark N Wu, Sarah K Wanigatunga, Luigi Ferrucci, Eleanor M Simonsick and Adam P Spira, 14 October 2026, The Journals of Gerontology: Series A. DOI: 10.1093/gerona/glag212.

Support for the research was provided by the National Institute on Aging (T32AG000247, R01AG050507, HHSN-260-2004-00012C).

A Dark Energy Camera Portrait of the Betta Fish Nebula

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (758 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is the Betta Fish Nebula, a supernova remnant (SNR) around 6,800 light years away in the Centaurus constellation.
  • According to recent reports, astronomers love studying SNRs because they can learn a lot about how heavy elements are spread out into the interstellar medium (ISM).
  • This image is brought to us by a powerful telescope whose main job it is to study dark energy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is the Betta Fish Nebula, a supernova remnant (SNR) around 6,800 light years away in the Centaurus constellation. This display of illuminated gas came into being when a massive star exploded between 7,000 and 10,000 years ago. When it exploded, it expelled its outer layers. Those layers slammed into the interstellar medium, and are lit up by the energy from the shock, and that's what we see today.

According to recent reports, astronomers love studying SNRs because they can learn a lot about how heavy elements are spread out into the interstellar medium (ISM). These explosions shape the dynamics in the ISM, including how stars form there. SNRs also reveal a lot about their progenitor stars. For these and other reasons, they're rich astronomical targets.

This image is brought to us by a powerful telescope whose main job it is to study dark energy. But that telescope also has a side hustle: capturing stunning images for the rest of us that don't necessarily add anything to scientific understanding.

Sources indicate that one of the main efforts to understand dark energy, the puzzling force that drives the expansion of the Universe, is the Dark Energy Survey. It uses a special, purpose-built camera to do its work, called the Dark Energy Camera (DECam.) DECam is a powerful, 570 megapixel, wide-angle camera mounted on the VÃ­ctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory (CTIO) in Chile. It used its power to capture this image of the Betta Fish Nebula.

Like many telescopes, DECam sometimes takes a break from its main job and captures images purely for public interest. It's a way for the professional astronomy community to share some celestial wonder with the rest of us. The latest DECam images of the Betta Fish nebula are in that category.

It has been revealed that only part of the nebula actually looks like a Betta, the popular and colourful aquarium fish. They're also known as Siamese Fighting Fish, but whatever name is used, they're popular for their brilliant colours and flowing fins.

This close-up view demonstrates one portion of the Betta Fish Nebula, the part that most closely resembles its namesake. Image Credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA. Image Processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), D. de Martin & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.

According to recent reports, what's left of the exploded star is a collapsed, ultra-dense stellar core called a neutron star. It's tiny, only about 20 km across, and is invisible in this image. It's actually a pulsar with unusual properties that has been studied extensively. It's radio-quiet and can only be detected in x-rays, and also lacks a pulsar wind nebula. It's so unusual that some researchers think it may be an example of what's called a 'low-mass bare strange star.'.

Industry observers note that this is a less visually interesting, more scientific x-ray image of the central portion of the Betta Fish nebula. It demonstrates what's left of the progenitor star that exploded, labelled in the center. Image Credit: Eppens et al. MNRAS 528, 2095â2111 (2024).

But those scientific details take a back seat to the image's visual interest.

In a recent development, these images have been 'dumbed-down' for internet use. There's a version of the image here that lets you zoom-in and explore it in much greater detail.

It has been revealed that this zoomed-in image highlights the part of the nebula that gave it its name. A cooperative orange/red star even serves as the Betta Fish's eye. Image Credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA. Image Processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), D. de Martin & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab) Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.

Industry observers note that DECam has been observing for more than a decade, and over that time its created a nice catalogue of fantastic images. Here's a few of them.

Recent findings suggest that here are three DECam images the camera has captured over the years purely for public interest. From left to right: the cometary globule CG4, the Rosette Nebula, and the Corona Australis Molecular Cloud. Image Credits: NSF NOIRLab DECam Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.

  • An experimental treatment using tiny particles released by stem cells has delayed the onset of type 1 diabetes in mice, offering a potential way to protect insulin-producing cells from immune attacks.
  • Developed by UCLA researchers, the approach targets the immune response responsible for type 1 diabetes rather than simply controlling blood sugar.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An experimental treatment using tiny particles released by stem cells has delayed the onset of type 1 diabetes in mice, offering a potential way to protect insulin-producing cells from immune attacks. In a 90-day study, 55% of mice receiving the particles through a slow-release gel remained diabetes-free.

Developed by UCLA researchers, the approach targets the immune response responsible for type 1 diabetes rather than simply controlling blood sugar. The findings, published in Nature Nanotechnology, suggest that naturally occurring particles called extracellular vesicles could help preserve pancreatic function. The treatment remains experimental and has not been tested in humans.

The research drew inspiration from pregnancy, when a mother’s immune system typically tolerates a developing embryo despite its genetic differences. Scientists wondered whether stem cells might produce substances capable of preventing harmful immune responses.

Industry observers note that “Nature has designed something amazing,” stated senior author Song Li, a professor of bioengineering at UCLA and member of the UCLA Broad Stem Cell Research Center. “If we can better understand how an embryo avoids rejection by the mother’s immune system, it could be very useful for a lot of immune-related diseases.”.

Sources indicate that li’s team investigated extracellular vesicles, microscopic particles that transport proteins, lipids, and genetic material between cells. They compared vesicles from embryonic stem cells and induced pluripotent stem cells, or iPSCs, with those from mesenchymal stem cells, which are known for their immune-regulating properties.

Experiments involving human and mouse immune cells showed that vesicles from pluripotent stem cells had stronger anti-inflammatory effects than those from mesenchymal stem cells.

The particles also promoted the development of regulatory T cells, specialized immune cells that help prevent attacks against healthy tissue. Further analysis identified distinctive proteins, lipids, and genetic material that may contribute to these effects.

To test whether the vesicles could protect against diabetes, the researchers transferred immune cells capable of attacking insulin-producing pancreatic cells into mice, then treated the animals with iPSC-derived vesicles.

Because extracellular vesicles rapidly disappear from injection sites, the researchers developed an injectable hydrogel that gradually releases them over several days. The treatment was administered beneath the skin near the neck, allowing the particles to interact with immune cells in nearby lymph nodes.

Those immune cells could then circulate throughout the body, potentially reducing attacks on pancreatic tissue.

Two treatments with the vesicles, either alone or in the hydrogel, significantly delayed diabetes onset compared with untreated mice. After 90 days, 55% of mice receiving the hydrogel formulation remained diabetes-free. They also had more regulatory T cells in their lymph nodes and retained more insulin-producing pancreatic tissue.

“One thing that surprised us was that a local injection could provide protection throughout the body,” Li remarked. “That’s the beauty of this approach.”.

Producing enough extracellular vesicles for future therapies presents a major challenge. To address this, researchers grew stem cells in three-dimensional clusters suspended in gently moving liquid instead of on flat laboratory surfaces.

Recent findings suggest that the method increased vesicle production 3.4-fold per million cells while preserving vital particle characteristics. Because iPSCs can multiply extensively in the laboratory, they could provide a more reliable source of therapeutic vesicles than adult stem cells.

Sources indicate that the treatment may be most effective during the early stages of type 1 diabetes, when some insulin-producing cells remain functional. Suppressing the immune attack could help preserve these cells and maintain natural insulin production.

In a recent development, “In the early stages, you still have some pancreatic cells left,” Li remarked. “If you can regulate the immune cells, you may be able to keep the remaining cells functional.”.

Industry observers note that for patients who have already lost most of these cells, immune regulation alone would not restore insulin production. However, the approach might help protect transplanted insulin-producing cells from rejection.

In a recent development, researchers plan to evaluate the treatment in larger animal models, investigate dosing and long-term effectiveness, and determine whether it could weaken defenses against infection. The findings may also inform future treatments for other autoimmune diseases and strategies to protect transplanted cells.

Reference: “Pluripotent stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles for systemic immune modulation in diabetes therapy” by Jana Zarubova, Mohammad Mahdi Hasani-Sadrabadi, Yutong Wu, Graciel Diamante, Jenny Cheng, Soomin Park, Xiao Han, Fatemeh Sadat Majedi, Li Yang, Olivia Wang, In Sook Ahn, Cade M. Matherne, Jia Fan, Jianyi Zhang, Xiaojun Lance Lian, Zhen Gu, Manish J. Butte, Reza Ardehali, Peter C. Butler, Tony Ye Hu, Louis-S. Bouchard, Xia Yang and Song Li, 18 November 2026, Nature Nanotechnology. DOI: 10.1038/s41565-026-02320-z.

The research was supported by the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine, the National Institutes of Health, a UCLA Broad Stem Cell Research Center Innovation Award and Breakthrough T1D.

The therapeutic concept described in this study is covered by a patent application filed by the UCLA Technology Development Group on behalf of the Regents of the University of California, with Jana Zarubova, Mohammad Mahdi Hasani-Sadrabadi and Li listed as co-inventors.

Saul Justin NewmanThe MIT Press | $29.95.

One Tiny Protein Change Could Help Explain Severe Childhood Epilepsy

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists have uncovered a previously unknown molecular mechanism that helps position a protein linked to severe childhood epilepsy within nerve cells.
  • It has been revealed that A single change in a protein associated with severe childhood epilepsy can dramatically alter where it resides inside nerve cells, according to newly introduced research from the University of Liverpool.
  • In a recent development, the study focuses on CDKL5, a protein essential for normal brain development and function.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have uncovered a previously unknown molecular mechanism that helps position a protein linked to severe childhood epilepsy within nerve cells.

It has been revealed that A single change in a protein associated with severe childhood epilepsy can dramatically alter where it resides inside nerve cells, according to newly introduced research from the University of Liverpool. The discovery suggests that some neurological disorders may arise not only from impaired protein activity but also from proteins failing to reach the locations where they are needed.

In a recent development, the study focuses on CDKL5, a protein essential for normal brain development and function. Mutations in the gene that produces this protein cause CDKL5 deficiency disorder (CDD), a rare genetic condition characterized by severe seizures beginning in infancy and significant developmental difficulties. The disorder affects approximately 1 in 40,000 to 60,000 live births worldwide.

Despite years of research into CDKL5, scientists have struggled to understand how the protein is organized within nerve cells and why certain mutations have such devastating neurological consequences.

A research team led by Ben Goult, Professor of Mechanistic Cell Biology at the University of Liverpool, identified a previously unknown molecular docking mechanism that anchors CDKL5 to the structural framework of synapses, the specialized junctions through which nerve cells communicate.

Disrupting this anchoring mechanism altered the organization of nerve cells. The researchers also discovered that even a remarkably small modification to the protein could interfere with its positioning.

It has been revealed that dr. Yasumi Otani, first author of the study and former PhD student in the Institute of Systems, Molecular and Integrative Biology, noted: “What was particularly striking was that changing just a single amino acid at the very end of CDKL5 was enough to dramatically alter its localization in nerve cells. This reveals just how critical the final residues of the protein are for keeping CDKL5 in the right place at synapses.”.

Sources indicate that the researchers also uncovered an unexpected connection between CDKL5 and the mechanical forces generated within cells. CDKL5 binds directly to talin, a protein capable of changing its shape in response to physical forces.

Recent findings suggest that in experiments using cultured cells, interfering with this molecular interaction or reducing the forces produced by the cells changed the distribution of CDKL5. The findings suggest that cellular mechanics may help regulate where CDKL5 carries out its biological functions.

Many genetic mutations associated with CDD produce shortened versions of the CDKL5 protein that lack the newly identified docking sequence. These mutations may therefore disrupt neurological function partly by preventing CDKL5 from reaching its intended location, rather than solely by impairing its enzymatic activity.

It has been revealed that professor Ben Goult stated: “Much of the research into CDKL5 deficiency disorder has focused on the activity of the enzyme itself. Our work highlights another potentially crucial factor: where that activity takes place. By identifying the molecular interactions that position CDKL5, we can begin to understand how the protein is organized within synapses and why disrupting this organization might interfere with communication between nerve cells.”.

The research, conducted in collaboration with scientists at the University of Helsinki in Finland, establishes a molecular framework for investigating how defective protein positioning contributes to CDD. It also opens a potential avenue for therapeutic research, although whether restoring CDKL5 localization could improve neurological function remains unknown.

Recent findings suggest that andreas Borg, founder of CURE5, a parent-led foundation dedicated to finding a cure for CDKL5 deficiency disorder, remarked: “Seeing how profoundly CDKL5 loss affects so many systems in the body also gives us hope that new opportunities for therapeutic intervention remain to be discovered. The new understanding of the protein’s location and function identified in this work opens up one such possibility. As parents, even the smallest improvements in our children’s lives mean the world.”.

Reference: “Cyclin-dependent kinase-like 5 (CDKL5) binds talin and is anchored at the postsynaptic density by direct PDZ interactions” by Yasumi Otani, Emily Goodall, Vignesh Srinivasan, Neil J. Ball, Samuel F. H. Barnett, Youlim Hwang, Dominic P. Byrne, Tobias Zech, Juha Saarikangas and Benjamin T. Goult, 20 November 2026, Science Advances. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aed3338.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the border wall is seen in 2021 stretching along the U.S.-Mexico border near Columbus, N.M. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.

It has been revealed that the Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that held the president could not broadly deny asylum claims under federal law. The case is the latest high-profile fight over one of Trump’s signature domestic policies.

The administration argues in its petition for the justices to take the case that the president has broad authority over asylum claims, which includes shutting down the system entirely because he has decided he will not grant any.

Recent findings suggest that “The proclamation thus lawfully suspends access to asylum, which is a purely discretionary benefit. The court of appeals’ insistence that aliens are entitled to file futile asylum applications elevates empty procedures over substance,” the petition claims.

Sources indicate that trump issued the order on his first day in office, declaring an “invasion” on the southern border and using that as a reason to deny asylum claims by refugees who present themselves there. The order is still in place, preventing asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border while the lawsuit plays out.

In court filings asking the justices to take the case, the administration pointed to “dramatic” reductions in illegal border crossings, which freed up resources to combat human trafficking and other threats.

In Friday’s order, the justices agreed to hear arguments over the legality of Trump’s executive order as well as whether the lower-court judge could grant an order in favor of all asylum seekers rather than just the ones who brought the suit.

Sources indicate that immigration rights groups initially challenged the order and won a successful ruling from a federal judge in Washington. The administration later appealed to the D.C. Circuit, where it lost at a three-judge panel before it brought the case before the justices.

Industry observers note that the D.C. Circuit held that although federal law provides a president discretion in denying asylum claims, he cannot do so categorically.

The ACLU and immigrant rights groups who brought the case defended the ruling in their own filing. The filing argues that Congress mandated the creation of the asylum system and the president “may not invent by fiat a latest removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.”.

Recent findings suggest that last term the justices ruled in favor of a separate policy dating to the first Trump administration that allowed officials to prevent asylum claims by stopping refugees from actually reaching the U.S. border.

A ruling in favor of the refugees could allow the administration to restart that policy and still deny asylum claims.

The case granted Friday is the latest high-profile immigration policy clash on the justices’ docket this term. Earlier this year the justices agreed to hear a challenge to the administration’s policy that most immigrants facing deportation should be detained without bond.

The justices will likely hear oral arguments and decide the case granted Friday before the end of the court’s term next June.

Recent findings suggest that the case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services.

A Metal Foam Designed for Armor Could Make Cars Dramatically Safer

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (818 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Metal foam explored for armor could also make everyday cars safer, with simulations suggesting it could absorb dangerous impacts without adding extra weight.
  • In a head-on collision, a car’s front rails must bend and collapse in a controlled way to help protect the people inside.
  • It has been revealed that A new study suggests that replacing conventional front rails with a lightweight metal foam could significantly improve crash protection, especially at higher speeds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Metal foam explored for armor could also make everyday cars safer, with simulations suggesting it could absorb dangerous impacts without adding extra weight.

In a head-on collision, a car’s front rails must bend and collapse in a controlled way to help protect the people inside. These structures receive impact energy from the bumper and are designed to keep the vehicle from slowing too abruptly. Sudden deceleration can cause severe injuries, including head injuries.

It has been revealed that A new study suggests that replacing conventional front rails with a lightweight metal foam could significantly improve crash protection, especially at higher speeds. Using detailed computer simulations, researchers found that the material absorbed impact energy more effectively than two common designs used in modern vehicles.

According to recent reports, the material, known as composite metal foam (CMF), contains hollow metal spheres embedded in a metallic matrix. The spheres can be made from metals or alloys such as steel, creating a structure that is lightweight and capable of withstanding substantial compression and impact. Researchers have also explored its potential use in aircraft wings, vehicle armor, and body armor.

“CMF is lighter than conventional metals without sacrificing strength, and our work here tells us that its unique structure allows it to better absorb energy during high-velocity impacts,” states Afsaneh Rabiei, corresponding author of the study and a professor of mechanical and aerospace engineering at North Carolina State University. “This is crucial because it slows the rate at which a vehicle decelerates during a crash – and slowing deceleration improves driver and passenger safety.”.

According to recent reports, to evaluate its potential, the researchers compared front rails made from an aluminum tube with a steel CMF core against two conventional designs. One consisted of a long, hollow rectangular steel structure. The other used two hollow aluminum octagons stacked on top of each other, known as a double-octagonal design.

Recent findings suggest that the team built computational models using extensive experimental data on CMF alongside publicly available information about conventional rail materials and designs. They then simulated high-speed frontal collisions to examine how effectively each structure managed the impact.

At 55 mph, CMF rails of the same weight and length reduced maximum deceleration by approximately 38% compared with double-octagonal rails. Overall crash severity fell by about 45%, while the Head Injury Criterion (HIC), a measure of the likelihood of serious head injury, also decreased by roughly 45%.

Industry observers note that the improvements were even greater when compared with rectangular rails. At the same impact speed, CMF reduced maximum deceleration by approximately 84%, overall crash severity by 94%, and HIC by 83%.

Industry observers note that the simulations also indicated that vehicles equipped with CMF rails could withstand substantially higher impact speeds before reaching critical safety limits. Compared with double-octagonal rails, vehicles could travel about 34% faster before reaching the critical crash-severity limit and approximately 40% faster before reaching the head-injury limit. Against rectangular rails, those increases were about 32% and 48%, respectively.

“CMF outperformed the conventional rails across the board,” Rabiei says. “And the higher the speed, the better the CMF performed compared to the conventional front rails. Comparing front rail performance during a 55 mph crash offers a good overview of the difference between designs.”.

Importantly, the simulated safety improvements did not require heavier or longer front rails. The CMF structures matched the conventional designs in both dimensions and weight, suggesting that manufacturers might eventually improve crash protection without compromising fuel economy.

“This also means that you could reduce the length of the front rails, still improve safety, and also make the vehicles more fuel efficient,” Rabiei says.

According to recent reports, the material could also have applications in electric vehicles. Previous research has demonstrated CMF’s resistance to heat and fire, making it a potential candidate for structures designed to protect high-voltage battery packs from damage during collisions.

According to recent reports, the findings are based on computational modeling, and physical testing would be needed to determine how CMF rails perform in actual vehicles. The researchers hope to work with manufacturers to explore these possibilities.

“We are open to working with the automobile industry to conduct testing of rails that make use of CMF in their existing front rail designs – or to develop new rail designs that make use of CMF to improve safety and fuel efficiency,” notes Rabiei.

“We are also interested in working with automakers, suppliers and battery manufacturers to evaluate CMF-based structures for electric vehicles, including battery protection systems. CMF’s combination of lightweight impact-energy absorption and resistance to heat and fire creates opportunities to address multiple vehicle safety challenges with a single material system.”.

Reference: “Enhancing Safety and Crashworthiness of Vehicles Using Composite Metal Foam” by Aman Kaushik and Afsaneh Rabiei, 2 September 2026, Journal of Composites Science. DOI: 10.3390/jcs10090474.

  • Industry observers note that when an intense laser pulse strikes a metal, its electrons absorb energy far more rapidly than its atoms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that powerful laser pulses could transform the crystal structure of a metal without first heating its atoms. Latest research suggests that rapidly exciting electrons can make entirely different atomic arrangements energetically favorable, revealing an alternative way to control the structure and properties of metals.

It has been revealed that in a study published in Physical Review Materials, researchers led by Dr. Sam Azadi modeled 17 elemental metals exposed to extreme electronic temperatures. Nearly all were predicted to undergo one or more solid-to-solid phase transitions driven by electronic excitation, potentially within a fraction of a picosecond (one trillionth of a second).

Industry observers note that when an intense laser pulse strikes a metal, its electrons absorb energy far more rapidly than its atoms. This creates a temporary state in which the electrons reach extremely high temperatures while the atomic lattice remains relatively cold.

Under these conditions, a phenomenon known as electronic entropy can determine which crystal structure is most stable. Electronic entropy describes how electrons are distributed among available energy states. As electronic temperatures rise, changes in this distribution can alter the relative stability of competing crystal structures without requiring conventional heating of the atomic lattice.

It has been revealed that “Our results suggest that electronic entropy should be regarded as a thermodynamic control parameter in its own right. Just as external pressure can transform one crystal structure into another, strong electronic excitation can reshape the free-energy landscape and create entirely fresh phases of matter,” said Dr. Sam Azadi, Research Associate in Theoretical Physics.

Sources indicate that using advanced computer simulations, the researchers calculated how increasing electronic temperatures affect the free energy of metals, a thermodynamic quantity that helps determine which structures are most stable. They identified transitions involving several common crystal arrangements, including hexagonal close-packed (hcp), face-centered cubic (fcc), and body-centered cubic (bcc) structures.

In general, hotter electrons favored crystal structures with lower densities. The researchers attributed this tendency to electronic thermal pressure, which arises as electrons gain energy.

Some metals, however, displayed more complex behavior. Differences in the distribution of electronic states near the Fermi level, an crucial energy reference in metals, can influence which atomic arrangements become favorable under intense excitation.

Recent findings suggest that the predicted transitions occur on femtosecond to picosecond timescales, making them potential targets for experiments using ultrafast X-ray or electron diffraction. These techniques could allow scientists to track changes in atomic arrangements immediately after laser excitation and test the theoretical predictions.

If confirmed experimentally, the findings could enable researchers to use carefully controlled laser pulses to temporarily switch metals between crystal structures, accessing material properties that are difficult to achieve under ordinary conditions. Such capabilities could have applications in ultrafast electronics, high-energy physics, and advanced manufacturing.

Reference: “Electronic-entropy-driven solid-solid phase transitions in elemental metals” by S. Azadi, S. M. Vinko, A. Principi, T. D. Kühne and M. S. Bahramy, 9 April 2026, Physical Review Materials. DOI: 10.1103/nzv9-dskm.

An El Niño amped by climate change has California bracing for the worst

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2201 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • In a recent development, in parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready.
  • What is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

In a recent development, in parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready. The state has strategically stockpiled sandbags, pumps and generators. Debris has been fished out to clear storm drains, seepage blankets shore up aging levees and dams, and wire mesh cages hold back precariously placed boulders.

What is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves. The fury of this year’s El Niño is being unleashed around the globe as well, from inundating Florida with floods to exacerbating drought in the Amazon. And much more is still to come, forecasts show, with the peak of the climate phenomenon expected to arrive between November 2026 and January 2027.

It has been revealed that californians know all too well the threat. El Niño has historically brought relentless rainfall to the state, flooding cities and triggering landslides.

State officials learned a lot about preparedness and emergency water management from previous El Niños — particularly the strong event that spanned the winter of 1997–1998. But this year’s event is likely to be even more challenging, a “Super” El Niño superimposed on the backdrop of global climate change.

Climate change has made water management in California more complicated than it was just 30 years ago — as it has elsewhere around the world, says environmental scientist Letitia Grenier, the director of water policy at the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonprofit, nonpartisan think tank based in San Francisco.

In 1997, California’s overall climate was much drier; El Niño brought a significant, long rainy season that spanned the state, Grenier says. But now, “it’s just so humid. The air is warmer, so it can hold more water.”.

Industry observers note that that waterlogged atmosphere means that even without El Niño, there’s been less of a distinct rainy season in California, and more rapid flip-flop between intense episodes of rain dumped on the ground followed by periods of heat and dryness. “It’s these strange, erratic patterns that we’ve never seen before,” she says. And the state is bracing for how the Super El Niño will clash with this fresh climate normal.

Sources indicate that 1997 was the year that the term “El Niño” shot to global fame. It was the most powerful El Niño in recorded history, and the first to be scientifically monitored in real time, continuously tracked by satellites and breathlessly reported on by news outlets. El Niño’s rise to household name status was even cemented in pop culture by an appearance on Saturday Night Live, in a classic sketch by comedian Chris Farley.

According to recent reports, but the event was no laughing matter. It caused global devastation during its brief reign. El Niño events form as westward-blowing trade winds over the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean weaken, allowing warm water to accumulate at the surface. Those waters can then release massive amounts of heat to the atmosphere, altering the position of the Pacific jet stream and helping to disrupt global weather patterns.

Sources indicate that in 1997–1998, global temperatures spiked by 1.5 degrees Celsius on average. Along with the torrential rains in California, the event brought brutal drought to Southeast Asia and deadly summer floods to central Europe and Peru. Record-breaking floods also hit East Africa, which in turn triggered a surge in mosquito-borne Rift Valley fever. The oceans were so warm that 16 percent of the world’s reefs died.

In all, the El Niño–related weather extremes were linked to more than 22,000 fatalities around the world, including nearly 200 in the United States, and an estimated $5.7 trillion in global economic losses.

Not every El Niño is equally intense, or impacts weather in quite the same way. “There’s a lot of variability event to event,” states Washington, D.C.–based climate scientist Tom Di Liberto, of the nonprofit climate news organization Climate Central.

But there is a general overall pattern to how El Niño tends to affect weather around the planet, Di Liberto indicates. For example, there tend to be more tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean, and fewer in the Atlantic — a pattern also observed in 2026.

Industry observers note that el Niño also tends to flatten and accelerate the Pacific jet stream, shifting its flow southward, notes Mike Anderson, California’s state climatologist for the Department of Water Resources, who is based in Sacramento. And that has historically meant that a conveyor belt of back-to-back moisture-loaded storms is set on a collision course with the U.S. West Coast.

According to recent reports, the El Niño rapidly strengthened during the summer of 2026. As westerly trade winds weakened, warm waters accumulated in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, raising both ocean temperatures and the sea level height (shown in this animation). Red and white colors indicate the highest sea level. Beginning in April and intensifying through November, the El Niño event generated Kelvin waves, massive swells that sweep eastward along the equator toward the Americas.

The 1997–1998 El Niño revealed just how devastating that pattern could be in California.

In a recent development, as much as 30 centimeters inundated parts of the state during the month of February 1998 alone. Storm winds and high surf pounded the coast, while rivers swelled and overtopped their banks. Flooding from the “Groundhog Day Storm” destroyed some 1,700 homes in Bay Area cities Palo Alto and Menlo Park. On February 6 near Rio Nido, about 100 kilometers from San Francisco, a forested hillside suddenly crumbled, sending a wall of mud rushing down the mountain. It destroyed about 30 homes.

Landslides also threatened homes and lives in Southern California.

On February 23, then 25-year-old Jenifer Segraves and her fiancé Glenn Flook were living in an apartment on Laguna Canyon Road, in the city of Laguna Beach. The heavy rains had saturated the neighborhood’s steep hillsides, making the terrain unstable.

According to recent reports, “We lived up against a hill in the canyon, so there were stairs up to our apartment,” Segraves says now. “They became like a waterfall. I remember my fiancé carrying me up the stairs because there was so much water.” Segraves called her father, Gary Segraves, in a panic, asking for help. Then, the slope behind the building failed, the apartment flooded and she and Flook fled into the rushing mud.

Industry observers note that “We were strong enough to get out, but we were waist-high in mud,” Segraves noted. “[My dad] almost drowned getting to us.” All three took shelter at a neighbor’s house, where they showered and hunkered down to wait out the rain.

Around midnight on February 24, the second mudslide arrived.

According to recent reports, the neighbor’s “whole house went down,” Segraves says. She escaped through a second-floor window, but her fiancé fell through the floor and was knocked out. He didn’t make it out.

Gary Segraves, meanwhile, was swept down the hillside and landed in a pile of rubble against a rocky cliff. Battered and missing his glasses, he looked around and saw what looked like a doll.

In a recent development, he reached for the little form — and discovered that it was a baby, very cold but alive. Somehow, the 9-month-old had survived being swept out of her crib from a nearby home. The little girl “wouldn’t have survived if he hadn’t picked her up,” Segraves notes.

It has been revealed that the havoc wreaked across California by the event 30 years ago cast a stark light on the desperate need to expand waterways, maintain infrastructure and coordinate emergency services, Grenier says. “An engineering system can only work as well as its capacity.”.

Much of the state’s infrastructure is deteriorating. An October 13 report by the California state auditor noted that the condition of dams and levees across the state “remains a high-risk issue,” with some 57 dams in the state in poor or unsatisfactory condition. “Poorly maintained dams and levees continue to pose a risk to public safety,” the report stated.

It has been revealed that california’s water management system was also originally designed specifically to simply shunt excess water away from residential areas, rather than try to capture the water or help it infiltrate into aquifers, Grenier indicates. But that system worked for a different climate, one that wasn’t so prone to “weather whiplash” — wild, sudden swings between extremely wet and extremely dry conditions.

Alongside punishing, drenching back-to-back storms called atmospheric rivers, the state has also experienced frequent episodes of drought, including two recent severe events, one lasting from 2012 to 2016 and another from 2021 to 2025.

In a recent development, those years of drought, dwindling snow and pumping too much water from aquifers have dramatically depleted the state’s subsurface water stores. And the heavy rains don’t necessarily help; the torrents of water mostly run off across the surface instead of infiltrating soils to reach the underground aquifer.

Sources indicate that such hydroclimate whiplash isn’t unique to California by any means. It’s a global problem, and it’s becoming more common. A small increase in air temperatures can give a significant boost to the atmosphere’s capacity to hold water vapor, increasing that capacity by about 7 percent for every 1 degree C of temperature increase. All of that water vapor has contributed to an increase in extreme precipitation events around the globe since the mid-20th century.

Industry observers note that precipitation is just half of the problem. Rising air temperatures also make the air “thirstier,” causing it to draw even more moisture out of vegetation, soil and surface bodies of water during drier periods — which makes the land more vulnerable to severe drought and wildfire.

It’s now clear that these hydrodynamic shifts have been increasing the frequency of weather whiplash events around the world over the last 75 years or so, scientists reported in 2025. And that whiplash is likely to increase as the world warms more.

Months before reaching peak intensity, the 2026–2027 Super El Niño has begun making its presence known. The Amazon is suffering under intense heat and drought, priming the region for wildfires and pushing the forest closer to a worrisome possible fate: a transition from tropical forest to savanna grasslands. Fires have also begun blazing across Southeast Asia, while heavy rains began inundating the Horn of Africa in October. Arriving on the heels of severe drought, that one-two punch could devastate the region’s crops and pasturelands.

In California, the first harbingers of the arrival of the Super El Niño appeared in early September. Heavy surf pounded the coastline. Regions from San Francisco to Los Angeles saw record high tides by late October that flooded city streets and battered coastlines and seawalls, even as the skies remained clear.

The waves were amped up by an unfortunate trifecta: higher sea levels due to climate change; a lunar cycle that exerted its maximum pull on the tides; and an El Niño–linked phenomenon called Kelvin waves.

Kelvin waves are massive, slow-moving swells of warm ocean water, part of the complicated interplay between wind and water that produces the El Niño Southern Oscillation, the overall weather pattern that includes El Niño and counterpart La Niña events, says Josh Willis, an oceanographer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif.

As prevailing west-blowing winds weaken over the tropical eastern Pacific, Willis states, water normally pushed west by the winds instead sloshes back eastward. Kelvin waves have historically given a boost to sea levels along the U.S. West Coast of as much as 30 centimeters. This year, that impact could be larger, researchers reported September 30 in a preprint study posted on EarthArXiv.org. Computer model simulations suggest that the risk of the risk of extreme sea levels could be 10 times higher during this El Niño year than during previous events, for coastlines from Alaska all the way to Chile.

Then, by late October, the Santa Ana winds arrived: Hot, dry gusts blowing down the mountains toward the coast, fanning wildfires in Southern California. The fires scarred the landscape, denuding it of vegetation, roots that helped stabilize and fortify the soil. Such loosened soil is more likely to become mobilized into a debris flow during heavy rains.

Those rains are now on the way. By mid-November, researchers began tracking storms headed for California. The peak of El Niño is expected to arrive by late November or early December and persist through February or March.

Recent findings suggest that segraves, after surviving nearly 30 years ago, says she is aware that another El Niño is coming. But she hasn’t been following the news closely. She’s placed herself on a news diet since her ordeal. She refused to speak to media for years, or even read the coverage about her own story.

“Everyone wanted to talk to me and I just wanted to be left alone,” she indicates. Staying away from the news “freed me from all that. It changed my view on life. I take each day as it comes.”.

But, she adds, one lesson has stayed with her. “I swore I would never live on a cliff again.”.

Researchers Have Discovered a Previously Unknown Crystal Form of Silver
