Tiny changes in your pupil size and blinking rate reveal how hard your brain is working

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1024 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An eye tracker in a VR headset can determine how hard people are concentrating by reading how pupil size changes.
  • It has been revealed that A person’s concentration level during a difficult mental task demonstrates up in the eyes.
  • A team in England asked whether a virtual reality headset could use those signals to tell when a person with chronic pain is working too hard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An eye tracker in a VR headset can determine how hard people are concentrating by reading how pupil size changes.

It has been revealed that A person’s concentration level during a difficult mental task demonstrates up in the eyes. Pupils open wider and blinks come faster, and a VR headset with an eye tracker inside can record both.

A team in England asked whether a virtual reality headset could use those signals to tell when a person with chronic pain is working too hard. The answer was mostly yes for healthy volunteers, and not yet for the patients.

Jordan Tsigarides of the University of East Anglia‘s School of Health Sciences led the study, which was part of his Ph.D., with colleagues at UEA and the University of Southampton.

Virtual reality is already used as a drug-free way to ease pain, he said. His goal is a headset that changes what it shows, based on how a patient is coping.

“Imagine putting on a VR headset that can recognize when you’re becoming mentally tired or overwhelmed and automatically adjust the experience to suit you,” Tsigarides mentioned in an interview with Earth.com.

“On a difficult day, it might simplify an activity or guide you through a calming environment.”.

It has been revealed that the study tested only whether the headset could read the effort. It didn’t treat anyone’s pain.

Between March and June 2025, 84 adults put on a consumer VR headset with built-in eye tracking and played a memory game.

Half had lived with musculoskeletal pain for at least three months, most often rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis, osteoarthritis or fibromyalgia.

Recent findings suggest that the other half were healthy university students and staff. They were younger on average, 35 years to the patients’ 58.

According to recent reports, letters appeared one at a time on a gray panel, each for three-quarters of a second. At the easiest level, a player pressed a button when a letter matched the one just before it. At the hardest, the match was four letters back. The whole session lasted under 20 minutes.

Players found it hard, and said so. Their own ratings of effort kept climbing through the top level, even after their scores had stopped getting worse.

Pupils widened as the levels got harder, by about a fiftieth of an inch (half a millimeter) at most, which is less than the thickness of a credit card. Blinks came more often too.

Both changes showed up in people with chronic pain and in people without it, and pain and fatigue scores made no difference to either one.

“What fascinated me was that people’s eyes responded to mental effort in remarkably similar ways, whether or not they lived with chronic pain,” Tsigarides told Earth.com.

According to recent reports, A plain average of pupil size told a computer almost nothing. A simple model that used average pupil size alone to sort the easiest level from the hardest guessed right 56 percent of the time in healthy volunteers.

In a recent development, in patients it managed 51 percent, which is barely better than chance. The pattern was in the way the pupil changed second by second, not in its size.

It has been revealed that machine learning models that read the full, second-by-second trace did much better, at least in healthy volunteers. Tested on people they had never seen, the best models picked the easy level from the hard one with 88 percent accuracy.

In the chronic pain group, the same models managed 58 to 65 percent.

Sources indicate that age didn’t explain the gap. When the team matched volunteers and patients by age, or adjusted for it, the patients’ eyes were still harder to read.

The two groups also differed in education, medication and other illnesses, and the authors said a sample of 84 can’t untangle all of that.

Recent findings suggest that the patients were a varied group. Nearly all had two or more long-term conditions, and 45 percent took opioids. A quarter had dry eyes or another eye problem. None of those factors, on its own, predicted whose eyes the models misread.

“Rather than expecting one algorithm to work for everyone, we may need headsets that learn how each individual responds,” he mentioned.

Sources indicate that one result was encouraging. People with chronic pain rated their motivation above 90 out of 100 at every level of the game, the same as the healthy group. Motion sickness scores were low in both groups, and pain scores didn’t rise during the session.

Recent findings suggest that tsigarides holds an honorary chief medical officer role at Revolve Labs Ltd, a company that helped fund his Ph.D. The paper discloses both.

Virtual reality for pain has so far been a fixed experience, Tsigarides mentioned: everyone gets the same woodland walk or the same puzzle, however they feel that day.

His earlier work tested VR therapy in people with fibromyalgia, and he said this study is a step toward a version that adjusts itself.

Recent findings suggest that everyone was measured once, on one day. The researchers can’t say whether a patient’s eyes behave the same way on a good day and a bad one, and Tsigarides indicates investigating that question comes next.

“Someone’s ability to concentrate might be very different on a good day compared with a day when their pain or fatigue is particularly severe,” he noted.

The team also wants to move from a letter-matching game to the kind of calming scenes a real therapy uses, where changing light levels will complicate the pupil readings.

All of the models in this study were run afterward on a desktop computer rather than live inside the headset. None was tested on an outside group of patients.

Tsigarides told Earth.com he hopes early adaptive systems can be tested within a few years. Whether a headset that reads mental effort and responds to it actually eases anyone’s pain is a trial that hasn’t been run.

The full study was published in the journal Scientific Reports.

One of the world’s rarest fish lives in a single cave in Death Valley National Park, and earthquakes have left it on the verge of extinction

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (911 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Devils Hole pupfish live in just one cavern of Death Valley National Park.
  • It has been revealed that one of the rarest fish on Earth lives in just one place: a water-filled cavern in the Nevada desert called Devils Hole, part of Death Valley National Park.
  • The National Park Service unveiled the new figure in November.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Devils Hole pupfish live in just one cavern of Death Valley National Park. Earthquakes are rapidly pushing this fish towards extinction.

It has been revealed that one of the rarest fish on Earth lives in just one place: a water-filled cavern in the Nevada desert called Devils Hole, part of Death Valley National Park. In the spring of 2025, after two earthquakes shook its tiny home, biologists counted only 38 of them.

The National Park Service unveiled the new figure in November. Divers and surface counters found the 137 Devils Hole pupfish during a survey on October 10, nearly double the 77 seen in the spring of 2026 and about double the 69 recorded in the fall of 2025.

Devils Hole is a cave about 12 feet wide and more than 500 feet deep. The bottom has never been mapped. The water stays at a constant 92 degrees Fahrenheit (33 degrees Celsius).

Pupfish have been found as deep as 66 feet, but they feed and spawn only on a shallow rock shelf near the surface, where algae grows.

The species has been isolated there for 10,000 to 20,000 years, longer than any other pupfish in the Death Valley system. The region’s caves keep other long records too, like a Nevada cave that reveals 580,000 years of climate swings.

Sources indicate that it is the only naturally occurring population of the species, which was listed as endangered in 1967. Biologists from the National Park Service and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service have counted the fish almost every spring and fall since 1972, with scuba divers in the cavern and counters at the surface.

One of the fish’s main threats can come from thousands of miles away. Large earthquakes as far away as Japan, Indonesia and Chile have made the water slosh in Devils Hole like water in a bathtub, according to the park.

Waves can splash as high as two meters (about 6.5 feet) up the walls and sweep the shelf clean. The park calls it a tsunami in the desert, although it is tiny next to the ocean tsunamis that significant earthquakes can unleash.

That is what happened in the winter of 2024 to 2025. Two earthquakes, one in December and one in February, set off waves that moved algae, organic material and fish eggs off the shelf.

Industry observers note that the spring count in 2025 found 38 fish. One year earlier, the official spring count had recorded 191.

It has been revealed that on July 29, 2025, just 21 minutes after a magnitude 8.8 earthquake struck Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula, waves rippled through Devils Hole, nearly 4,000 miles away. Those waves were only about 10 inches high and removed just some material from the shelf.

Sources indicate that then, after an earthquake in Panama on October 9, 2026, nearly 3,000 miles away, biologists at first saw signs of stress in the fish. On a later visit, they found them in healthier condition.

The team had prepared for a crash like this for years. Pupfish eggs from Devils Hole had been collected regularly to build a backup population at the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s Ash Meadows Fish Conservation Facility.

It has been revealed that in 2025, biologists added captive-raised fish to the wild population for the first time. Between March 2025 and February 2026, scientists released 72 of them into Devils Hole. They also gave the fish extra food while the algae grew back.

Sources indicate that the fish live an average of only 10 to 14 months. Because of that, biologists believe most of the 137 fish counted this fall hatched and grew up in Devils Hole itself.

“It’s exciting to see Devils Hole pupfish numbers increase so significantly over the past year,” said Death Valley National Park Superintendent Mike Reynolds.

“These results reflect the dedication of our scientists and conservation partners working to protect this extraordinary species. While challenges remain, we’re encouraged by this progress and committed to its long-term survival.”.

Recent findings suggest that the pupfish has survived human threats before. In the late 1960s, a farming operation drilled large wells in the Ash Meadows area, and the water level in Devils Hole began to drop toward the shelf the fish need.

Biologists even hung a floating, artificially lit shelf in the cave as a substitute. The fish never used it.

In a recent development, A federal court halted further pumping in 1971, and the fight reached the U.S. Supreme Court. Its 1976 decision in Cappaert v. United States recognized the water right of Devils Hole as part of a national monument and limited pumping so the natural shelf would stay underwater.

Industry observers note that until the mid-1990s, spring surveys counted more than 200 fish. In the early 2000s, spring counts averaged about 90, and in 2013 the number fell to 35. The cause of that long decline has not been determined.

The new count is an encouraging step, but the park says the population naturally fluctuates and remains highly vulnerable.

It calls continued monitoring, research and habitat management essential if one of the world’s rarest fish is to keep its foothold in a single desert cave.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service’s fall 2026 count announcement, its spring 2025 update, its report on the Kamchatka earthquake and its Devils Hole page.

#180205. What you just touched can change how the next thing feels

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (843 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

What you just touched can change how the next thing feels

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (843 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A study in rats found that frontal brain activity helped predict how an earlier vibration would bias judgments about the next one.
  • Recent findings suggest that what you feel right now depends partly on what you felt a moment ago.
  • A region of the frontal cortex represented both the current and previous vibrations, and its activity helped predict how the previous vibration biased the rats’ judgments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A study in rats found that frontal brain activity helped predict how an earlier vibration would bias judgments about the next one.

Recent findings suggest that what you feel right now depends partly on what you felt a moment ago. In rats trained to judge vibrations, the primary sensory cortex mainly tracked the current vibration.

A region of the frontal cortex represented both the current and previous vibrations, and its activity helped predict how the previous vibration biased the rats’ judgments.

The study was carried out by neuroscientists at SISSA, the International School for Advanced Studies in Trieste, Italy.

“Perception is often thought of as a direct mapping of the external world,” explained Mathew Diamond, a cognitive neuroscientist at SISSA.

Recent findings suggest that “Yet what we experience depends not only on what is happening now, but also on what happened moments ago. In short, every percept is constructed against a backdrop of recent experience.”.

Scientists call this effect serial dependence, and it’s easy to picture. “Imagine feeling a vibration with your fingertip (for instance, from the cell phone) and then feeling a second vibration shortly afterward,” Diamond noted.

“The second stimulus will not be experienced as an independent event; instead, perception is systematically biased by prior inputs. The brain, in effect, carries traces of the recent past into the present.”.

“Perception is not a photograph of the world. It is more like a film, in which the experience of each frame is influenced by those that came before.”.

Psychologists have known about the effect for a long time. Where the brain does the mixing, and how, has been much harder to work out.

Industry observers note that theories of “predictive processing” propose that the brain constantly combines incoming signals with expectations built from experience. What nobody had clearly shown was the neural machinery that brings the two together.

Recent findings suggest that to find it, Diamond’s team trained rodents on a simple touch task. On each trial the animal felt a stimulus and had to decide whether it was weak or strong.

Meanwhile, the researchers recorded the activity of hundreds of neurons.

The animals’ judgments were consistently pulled by the previous trial. After a strong stimulus, the next one was more likely to be judged weak.

After a weak one, the next was more likely to be judged strong. A medium-strength touch could feel faint or firm depending on what had come right before it.

“The key finding emerged from comparing two cortical regions,” mentioned lead author Iacopo Hachen.

“Activity in the primary sensory cortex mainly reflected the stimulus presently being processed, a direct representation of the ongoing input.”.

According to recent reports, “By contrast, neurons in a frontal cortical area carried information about both the current stimulus and recent sensory history. There, neural representations of the present were embedded within a context established by the past.”.

The first stop for touch signals in the cortex, in other words, stayed true to the present. The frontal region carried the present and the recent past together.

The frontal region also helped predict the animals’ choices.

When its activity rose or fell from one trial to the next, the animals’ judgments shifted in step.

“Variations in this frontal-cortex activity predicted corresponding variations in perceptual judgments from one trial to the next, suggesting that while the sensory cortex faithfully reports the ongoing input, the frontal cortex integrates that input with recent experience to shape perception,” Hachen explained.

One region reports what is happening, and the other decides what it means given what just happened.

The researchers also identified a possible mechanism at the level of individual cells.

It has been revealed that fast-spiking neurons played a prominent role in how the frontal region represented both vibrations. Their firing patterns suggest they may be inhibitory neurons.

There was also an unexpected finding. While a touch was happening, the frontal neurons encoded it as an ongoing sensory event.

Once the animal committed to its answer, the code switched to a different, memory-like format. That stored version lasted and went on to bias the next decision.

Sources indicate that in other words, the brain doesn’t just keep a recording of what happened. It rewrites the experience into a fresh format as it moves from perception into memory.

That rewritten trace then colors the next moment.

It has been revealed that the authors see the work as evidence for a basic principle of how the brain works. Perception comes from a constant back-and-forth between latest sensory evidence and traces of the recent past.

“Our findings suggest that the brain does not treat each moment in isolation. Instead, the recent past becomes part of the neural representation of the present, a unitary construct that mirrors our experience,” Hachen concluded.

Understanding this exchange could help explain how prediction normally supports behavior, and how it might go wrong in neurological and psychiatric disorders.

The study is published in the journal Science Advances.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally released a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

The lame-duck session continues as lawmakers look ahead to Thanksgiving and the funding deadline that arrives in December. The primary legislative business this week is the Senate's bipartisan permitting overhaul, but a late-breaking aviation funding fight and the Senate Democratic leadership contest are also commanding attention.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally launched a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., and both men are accumulating supporters ahead of leadership votes that are at the moment scheduled for early December — though there's been an effort to move that up to this week.

Van Hollen has expressed disagreement with Schumer's participation in primaries.

​"I don't think it's the role of the Senate majority leader to get involved in open, contested Democratic primaries," Van Hollen said Sunday on CNN.

​Van Hollen has also remarked he wants to use all available tools to stop funding for the Iran war immediately, with a government funding deadline in December. That's going to be one of several flash points for December's funding discussions, as President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans try to use what leverage they have before Democrats take the gavels in the House and the Senate in January.

A fresh problem is the state of federal air traffic control after Friday's nationwide ground stop, with the Trump administration now seeking $50 billion to upgrade systems.

Latest Update: Your home may be full of wildlife you’ve never noticed

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1173 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A survey of indoor spaces across the U.S.
  • Homes across the United States and Canada are full of wildlife.
  • A continent-wide survey has found nearly 2,100 species of wild organisms living indoors, mostly insects and spiders, plus centipedes, snails, fungi, and many animals most people have never heard of.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A survey of indoor spaces across the U.S. and Canada recorded nearly 2,100 species, from familiar house spiders to an alligator in a garage.

Homes across the United States and Canada are full of wildlife.

A continent-wide survey has found nearly 2,100 species of wild organisms living indoors, mostly insects and spiders, plus centipedes, snails, fungi, and many animals most people have never heard of.

One record is an alligator that turned up in somebody’s garage.

This is the largest study of indoor wildlife so far. Nearly all of it is built from photos taken by ordinary people.

The study was led by researchers at North Carolina State University and Colorado State University.

Over 60 co-authors contributed, including museum curators, university entomologists, and independent experts from across North America and Europe.

In a recent development, ecologists have spent decades cataloging life in rainforest canopies and on the deep sea floor. The places where most of us spend most of our time have received far less attention.

“While researchers have focused significant attention on a variety of natural ecosystems – from rainforest canopies to the deep sea – we know remarkably little about the ecosystems of manmade, indoor environments,” mentioned lead author Bradley Allf from Colorado State.

“Our goal with this work was to treat the indoors, at the continental scale, as an ecosystem that we wanted to explore as ecologists,” he explained.

Earlier surveys of indoor life either covered much smaller areas or relied on DNA traces, which can’t always pin down exactly which species was present.

This is the first survey of indoor life spanning the United States and Canada.

The team launched a citizen science project called Never Home Alone on iNaturalist, a website where people share photos of the living things they come across.

Participants were asked to photograph wild organisms in their homes, offices, and other indoor spaces. The rule for “wild” was simple: anything that was neither a pet nor a potted plant.

Industry observers note that submissions came from at least five continents. This study focuses on North America.

Sources indicate that about 3,000 people contributed 23,782 observations, from every US state and every Canadian province. Most were taken in homes, but some came from offices, schools, and airports. The records cover almost three decades, from 1996 to 2024.

Industry observers note that every observation was checked by specialists. Dozens of experts identified each organism as precisely as they could.

“This work underscores the value of natural history expertise and the ability to identify species, which is a skillset that is less common among biologists than it once was,” Allf said.

Sources indicate that about 95% of the observations were arthropods, the group of animals with jointed legs and hard outer skeletons. Insects made up 60% of all records, mostly beetles, flies, moths, wasps and ants, and true bugs.

In a recent development, spiders accounted for 30%. Animals with backbones made up only 4%, most of them reptiles and mammals.

The rest included fungi, plants, earthworms, snails, small crustaceans, and even single-celled organisms.

Eight species were recorded more than 200 times each.

In order, they were the Asian lady beetle, the brown marmorated stink bug, the house centipede, the varied carpet beetle, the long-bodied cellar spider, the triangulate combfoot spider, the bathroom moth fly, and the eastern parson spider.

“The organisms we found ranged from Asian lady beetles – which were the most commonly found species – to an alligator that unexpectedly turned up in one person’s garage,” Allf said.

“But one of the things that was striking was how common predator species were – including hundreds of different spider species.”.

Half of the top eight are hunters, and some of them do useful work.

“One study participant noted that they view jumping spiders as working animals, because the spiders play an active role in reducing the population of flies and other pests that they don’t want in their home.”.

Senior author Rob Dunn from NC State pointed out that most people share their homes with these animals every day and have no idea what they are.

“Another thing that is striking about this work is that most people could look over a list of the most commonly found species and wouldn’t know what most of those animals even are – and yet they are around us, all the time,” he mentioned.

“For example, I suspect most people are unfamiliar with comb-footed spiders, but we have more than a thousand observations of this family of spiders.”.

He sees this as a fairly recent loss.

“This is a stark departure from what we would have expected historically, when our ancestors would have been more aware of the living things around them.”.

“That’s something we lost. And this is a first step toward regaining that understanding.”.

Industry observers note that the list has a very long tail. About 52% of the species were recorded indoors just once.

The true total is almost certainly higher than 2,100, because 44% of the observations couldn’t be identified down to species.

The authors also point out the dataset’s limits. Nobody controlled how hard each person looked, so large, eye-catching animals are probably overrepresented.

In a recent development, and not every animal that ends up indoors actually lives there. Some had simply wandered in and become trapped.

The survey also shows how little is known about even the most common indoor animals.

“It could inform future research in many ways,” Dunn said.

“For example, house centipedes were the third most commonly found animals, and yet I’m not aware of anyone who is studying them. That’s worth exploring.”.

Some of these animals might even turn out to be useful.

Sources indicate that “For example, we now know that camel crickets carry a microbe that can break down paper products. That could be useful. What else might be out there, in our own homes?”.

“Once we know what’s there, we can begin asking additional questions,” Dunn noted.

“Why are these organisms there? What are they doing? Are they beneficial?”.

“But knowing what’s there is the first step. And it’s exciting because these are the animals we’re around all the time, but we just overlook.”.

Sources indicate that the scientists want to investigate how the climate outside shapes what turns up inside. They also proposal to figure out which species have actually adapted to life in buildings.

Every record has a date and a location, so the dataset can also serve as a baseline for spotting latest arrivals or disappearances in the future. The data are free for anyone to use.

The project is still running, and anyone with a phone can contribute.

Industry observers note that “People can still submit observations to Never Home Alone. The more data the project collects, the more insight we’ll have on the unique and growing ecosystem of the great indoors,” Allf concluded.

The study is published in the journal Ecology.

In a West Texas rock shelter, archaeologists found a hunting kit that was left behind 6,500 years

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Archaeologists in Texas uncovered a roughly 6,500-year-old hunting kit with darts, an atlatl and a rare preserved pronghorn hide.
  • Deep inside San Esteban Rockshelter, south of Marfa, Texas, archaeologists recovered parts of a hunter’s weapon kit that someone left behind thousands of years ago.
  • According to recent reports, the Center for Substantial Bend Studies at Sul Ross State University presented the find in its spring 2025 newsletter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Archaeologists in Texas uncovered a roughly 6,500-year-old hunting kit with darts, an atlatl and a rare preserved pronghorn hide.

Deep inside San Esteban Rockshelter, south of Marfa, Texas, archaeologists recovered parts of a hunter’s weapon kit that someone left behind thousands of years ago.

According to recent reports, the Center for Substantial Bend Studies at Sul Ross State University presented the find in its spring 2025 newsletter. The center puts the kit’s age at about 6,500 years and calls it “potentially the oldest example of a full weapon system in North America.”.

The kit as a whole has not yet been described in a peer-reviewed study. Only one of its pieces, a spear-thrower known as an atlatl, has been the subject of a journal paper.

The kit includes six stone-tipped dart foreshafts – the front section of a dart – and four self-tipped hardwood dart foreshafts.

There are also four dart nock-ends, the rear tips that fit against the atlatl. A broken hunting boomerang and a partial atlatl complete the weapons.

According to recent reports, the excavators also found a folded pronghorn hide. It had been tanned, and its hair was still intact.

Spaced holes ran around the hide’s perimeter so it could be tied to a frame, as Plains groups often did.

“We just sat there and stared at it in wonder,” noted Bryon Schroeder, then director of the center. Someone had folded the hide and set it on top of a rock, he explained.

“And nobody touched it for 6,000 years,” Schroeder said.

According to recent reports, an atlatl is essentially a wooden stick with a handle on one end and a hook or socket on the other. It acts as an extension of the human arm, increasing leverage against the dart, the National Park Service explains.

The San Esteban atlatl is described in a 2023 atlatl paper by Schroeder and Devin Pettigrew, an assistant professor at the center.

A radiocarbon date indicates that the atlatl is more than 6,000 years old. That made it the oldest directly dated atlatl in North America at the time, the authors reported in the Journal of Massive Bend Studies.

In a paper published in 2026, Pettigrew and other archaeologists at the center measured how fast modern throwers launch darts.

That research shows that heavier darts, paired with strong and skilled throwers, become lethal to very large animals such as mammoths, the center said.

“In most archeological sites in Texas, only things made of stone survive,” notes Texas Beyond History, a project of the University of Texas at Austin. The dry Lower Pecos rock shelters are an exception.

Industry observers note that those shelters have yielded hardwood dart foreshafts and rabbit sticks, as well as bow fragments and arrow foreshafts from the bow-and-arrow era. Complete atlatls are very rare even there.

Unique depositional conditions favored the preservation of the Schöningen wooden spears in Germany. A 2025 dating study placed them at about 200,000 years old.

Industry observers note that A mammoth-ivory boomerang from Poland is one of the oldest known in Europe, an Obłazowa Cave analysis concluded. A statistical model built on dated bones from the same layer places it between 42,290 and 39,280 years ago.

“We can use the wood to reconstruct the environment and learn more about the amount of time they spent working on tools,” Schroeder remarked.

Industry observers note that schroeder’s reading of the scene is that a person came to the back of the cave and sorted through the gear piece by piece. Some parts were judged good and others not, and then the person went on their way.

“But that one small act is going to have profound implications in understanding the environment,” he said.

The shelter sits in Presidio County along Alamito Creek, a tributary of the Rio Grande. A spring-fed rock pool, or tinaja, lies in front of it.

It has been revealed that the center has worked there since 2019 with the Odyssey Archaeological Research Fund at the University of Kansas. The partners were looking for traces of the region’s earliest people.

The Odyssey fund was established in 2003 with an endowment from Joseph and Ruth Cramer. Its director is Rolfe Mandel, a distinguished professor of anthropology at the university.

In 2020, the excavators uncovered a hearth-like feature with burned and unburned bird eggshells dated to about 15,200 years ago.

Sources indicate that “Though this site was pot-hunted in the past, the many large boulders that spalled from the ceiling preserved pockets of shelter deposits,” the Kansas team’s site summary states. Pot-hunting means digging for artifacts to collect.

The atlatl foreshafts and darts came from intact deposits in an area the excavators call the Sandal Shaft. The Kansas team dates them to about 6,200 years ago, a little younger than the center’s figure.

The pronghorn hide lay about 2 inches (5 centimeters) above them, capped with a metate, a grinding stone.

The hide yielded a raw radiocarbon age of 5,621 years, plus or minus 24, not yet converted to calendar years. That makes it about 600 years younger than some of the foreshafts and darts, the Kansas researchers report.

The information was obtained from the Center for Massive Bend Studies.

Flightless kākāpō parrots from New Zealand are genetically healthy despite 10,000 years of inbreeding

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (730 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists sequenced the DNA of Upcoming Zealand's endangered kākāpō and found that 10,000 years of inbreeding actually helped natural selection clear out harmful genetic mutations.
  • Industry observers note that on New Zealand’s Stewart Island, flightless parrots called kākāpō spent about 10,000 years cut off from the rest of their species, breeding with relatives.
  • A 2021 study of their DNA found the opposite: the island kākāpō carried fewer harmful mutations than mainland kākāpō, which have since died out.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists sequenced the DNA of Upcoming Zealand's endangered kākāpō and found that 10,000 years of inbreeding actually helped natural selection clear out harmful genetic mutations.

Industry observers note that on New Zealand’s Stewart Island, flightless parrots called kākāpō spent about 10,000 years cut off from the rest of their species, breeding with relatives. In theory, that should have left the birds with more and more harmful mutations.

A 2021 study of their DNA found the opposite: the island kākāpō carried fewer harmful mutations than mainland kākāpō, which have since died out.

The researchers wrote that the finding is evidence a small population can survive hundreds of generations of isolation. The species is still critically endangered, though, and many of its eggs fail to hatch.

Nicolas Dussex, a researcher at the Centre for Palaeogenetics in Stockholm, led the study. Few birds anywhere are as inbred or as endangered as the kākāpō, Dussex said.

Kākāpō likely numbered in the hundreds of thousands before people reached New Zealand. Overhunting and predators introduced by people reduced them to 51 birds by 1995.

In a recent development, fifty came from Stewart Island. The other was a mainland male named Richard Henry.

When the study came out, 201 kākāpō were alive, all on island sanctuaries.

In a recent development, for 49 kākāpō, Dussex’s team analyzed each bird’s complete set of DNA, called its genome. Thirty-five were Stewart Island birds.

The rest were mainland birds: Richard Henry and 13 museum specimens. Those specimens were collected between 1847 and 1924.

An inbred bird’s DNA has a recognizable pattern. A chick gets one copy of its genome from each parent. When the parents are related, long stretches of the two copies match.

Recent findings suggest that in the Stewart Island birds, matching stretches made up 53% of the genome on average. In the mainland birds, matching stretches made up 15%.

It has been revealed that so the island birds were far more inbred. The team then counted the most damaging kind of mutation, the kind predicted to stop a gene from working.

Mainland birds carried 34.1 of those mutations on average. Island birds carried 17.6 of them, about half as many.

It has been revealed that many of these mutations seem to do harm mainly when a bird inherits the same one from both parents. That happens more often when the parents are related.

Chicks that inherit the mutation from both parents are less likely to survive or breed, the team suggested. Over many generations, the mutation becomes rarer. Geneticists call that process purging.

Industry observers note that the team tested the idea with computer simulations spanning 25,000 years. A simulated population that stayed small, like Stewart Island’s, ended up with fewer harmful mutations than a larger one like the mainland’s.

It has been revealed that but in a simulated population one-tenth as large as the island’s, the harm from mutations grew instead. So purging seems to need enough birds for natural selection to work.

After the kākāpō’s recent decline, the team wrote, the birds may now face the same growing harm as that smallest population.

Conservation managers have favored matings with Richard Henry and his offspring, to help the population keep its ability to adapt.

“We show that the single male survivor from the mainland, Richard Henry, has more harmful mutations than Stewart Island birds,” mentioned Love Dalén of the Swedish Museum of Natural History, who supervised the study.

“Therefore, there could be a risk that these harmful mutations spread in future generations.”.

Richard Henry was also genetically distinct, Dalén added, and may have carried useful genetic diversity. The team recommended weighing that benefit against the risk and, if necessary, limiting breeding between the two family lines.

Dussex’s team counted mutations in DNA and didn’t measure what they do to a living bird. Their effects on survival and breeding weren’t known.

The team called for research into the genetic causes of the kākāpō’s low fertility and hatching success.

In some other shrinking species, harmful mutations increased as numbers fell, the authors wrote. In others, the mutations decreased.

Next, the team planned to examine other highly inbred birds and mammals, to learn whether the kākāpō is a rare exception.

The full study was published in the journal Cell Genomics.

Tech Report: Growing mountain ranges played a major role in sparking life on Earth

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1144 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rocks once buried in mountain belts suggest Earth's ranges grew taller in two steps, each near a rise in oxygen and in complex life.
  • Recent findings suggest that picture the young Earth and you probably see mountains in your mind.
  • Rocks that were once buried deep inside mountain ranges suggest the ranges grew taller in two steps, a new study finds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rocks once buried in mountain belts suggest Earth's ranges grew taller in two steps, each near a rise in oxygen and in complex life.

Recent findings suggest that picture the young Earth and you probably see mountains in your mind. For the planet’s first billion years or more, it may not have had any that would resemble the majestic mountain ranges our planet has today.

Rocks that were once buried deep inside mountain ranges suggest the ranges grew taller in two steps, a new study finds. The first step ended about 2.2 billion years ago and the second about 700 million years ago.

Each step came around the time Earth’s air gained oxygen and life grew more complex.

Matthijs Smit, an associate professor of earth sciences at the University of British Columbia, led the work.

Industry observers note that the link to life is a match in timing, not a demonstrated cause. The authors call it a hypothesis that still has to be tested.

Sources indicate that when two plates collide, rock gets shoved downward as well as up. Minerals that form under that squeeze keep a record of the pressure they felt, and pressure translates into depth.

The deepest-buried rocks that later return to the surface mark roughly how thick a mountain belt’s crust had grown. Smit’s team gathered pressure and age estimates for such rocks from around the world.

It has been revealed that the team relied on garnet, a mineral that forms during the burial itself and can be dated precisely. They also added latest measurements from ancient rocks in Cameroon and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

In an interview with Earth.com, Smit said the debate over the early Earth has run between two pictures.

“Some would argue that it was an almost alien world, with no emerged lands, whereas others would argue that it operated very much in the same way as the modern Earth, with large mountain chains, active tectonics and widespread emerged lands,” he said.

According to recent reports, before about 2.7 billion years ago, the rocks record burial no deeper than roughly 19 to 22 miles (30 to 35 kilometers). In the long middle era that followed, mountain belts buried rock to 34 to 37 miles (55 to 60 kilometers).

It has been revealed that the middle-era depth is roughly double the earlier one. In the current era, rocks have come back from about 56 miles (90 kilometers) down, about half again as deep.

The modern figure matches the crust under the Himalaya and Pamir today.

What surprised Smit was how steady the maximum depth stayed within each era, and how consistently it changed from one era to the next.

“There does seem to be a specific tectonic style for each episode in the tectonic evolution of the lithosphere, which dictates in a broad sense how thick (and tall) mountains could become,” he said.

Thicker crust generally stands higher above sea level. Using the relationship between thickness, density, and elevation seen today, the team converted the depths into rough heights.

Before 3 billion years ago, the highest terrain comes out at sea level, within the error bars. Through the middle era, the highest peaks could have stood about 3.1 miles (5 kilometers) tall, roughly half the height of Everest.

Mountains of that era were real, then, but they were not the giants of today.

It has been revealed that for the modern era, the method gives about 5.5 miles (8.8 kilometers). That is the height of Everest, K2, and Kangchenjunga, to within the uncertainty.

Recent findings suggest that the authors note the sea-level comparison holds for recent geological time and probably for the middle era too. In the earliest era, the oceans were larger and the crust denser, so those early heights are rougher guesses.

Most of the sediment that rivers carry to the sea comes from mountains, and the amount depends on erosion above about 1.9 miles (3 kilometers) of altitude.

Taller mountains mean more rock washed into the oceans, and with it phosphorus, which limits how much marine life can grow.

Both growth periods line up, broadly, with the two great rises in atmospheric oxygen. Each oxygen rise was followed by a Snowball Earth ice age and then by a jump in the amount and variety of life.

Strontium in ancient seawater, which tracks how much material was coming off the continents, also rose during both periods. Phosphorus would have behaved the same way, the authors argue, because it is held in similar minerals.

“It’s likely not a coincidence that life on Earth developed and diversified approximately during the same period that the two growth spurts occurred,” said co-author Ellen Kooijman of the Swedish Museum of Natural History.

Recent findings suggest that the match isn’t perfect, and the authors say so. Some records of oxygen and living matter don’t move in step with the mountains. That could mean the hypothesis is wrong, or that the planet responded to extra nutrients in thresholds and delays.

In a recent development, why would mountains grow taller only at certain times? “We suspect that these increases are ultimately linked to the cooling of our planet,” Smit mentioned. “As a result, the process that makes mountains changed, allowing mountains to grow taller.”.

In the authors’ reading, the first change was the arrival of plate tectonics as we know it, with one plate sliding beneath another and crust piling up.

It has been revealed that the second came as the cooling mantle let continental margins be dragged deeper before snapping free. That is how the thickest mountain belts are built today.

According to recent reports, old, deeply buried rocks rarely survive. Such rocks are the most likely to be altered by later events or lost back into the mantle, so the record is thinnest exactly where the first step happened.

Smit told Earth.com that the first change is pinned down only to a window of several hundred million years, ending around 2 billion years ago.

“We don’t know precisely how this change occurred in time and whether it was even one continuous change or whether there were short bursts by which mountains were able to get higher and higher,” he stated.

Until that window narrows, the timing can’t be checked closely against the changes in the oceans and atmosphere, Smit noted.

Industry observers note that that work starts with more field research in ancient terrains, sampling rocks and measuring their pressures and ages. He also suggested Earth system models that include step-like, tectonically driven increases in phosphorus.

Industry observers note that the full study was published in the journal Science Advances. Co-authors are at Utrecht University, the Swedish Museum of Natural History, and the Geological Survey of Canada, among others.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Dor Minzer remembers sitting in an undergraduate computation class at Tel Aviv University. He was intrigued by his professor and soon found himself pulled into a latest world: the mystifying intersection of math and computation, first laid out by Alan Turing during World War II. Working with the professor, Minzer became deeply interested in the limitations of what computers can and can’t do.

In a recent development, “My part is actually to prove not only do I not know how to do it, but I can prove that it’s impossible,” Minzer states. “You have to really be curious.”.

Minzer’s hard work has paid off. In 2018, he proved a theoretical computer science problem called the 2-to-2 games conjecture. It asks whether computers can efficiently distinguish games where almost all rules can be satisfied from those where almost none can be satisfied, when the rules have a strict structure.

In September, Minzer and his two graduate students at MIT posted a 95-page milestone paper on the unique games conjecture, which builds off the 2-to-2 conjecture. The paper wasn’t quite ready, but they published to get ahead of a press release from OpenAI, describing its proof for the same problem, slated for only days later. It’s a situation that many mathematicians have found themselves in this year as AI companies flood the field with findings at lightning speed.

Minzer says it’s critical to remember that math, and all the research and contemplation behind it, is very human. “It’s a human activity,” he says. “Research is sort of a living organism, a living body.”.

According to recent reports, minzer teaches his own students now. Some days, he talks to his class and gets the sense that nobody is paying attention. But other days, he gets a few students that participate. They have ideas, they’re excited, and they remind him of his own days as a graduate student.

In a recent development, “I feel like now I feel like I’m passing the torch,” he claims. “Before you have a Ph.D. adviser, you’re like a fresh person in a dark room. There are infinite places to go. Your Ph.D. adviser is the person that holds your hand and says, ‘Okay, let’s walk here.’”.

In 1966, Buzz Aldrin took the first spacewalk selfies, and photos from Gemini flights like his helped inspire the revolutionary Landsat satellites

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that sixty years ago, Buzz Aldrin took the first spacewalk selfies on Gemini XII.
  • In a recent development, sixty years ago this month, Buzz Aldrin opened the hatch of his Gemini spacecraft, looked outside and exclaimed, “Man!
  • According to recent reports, near the end of that spacewalk, on November 12, 1966, he mounted a camera on the edge of the hatch, pointed it at himself and took the first selfies ever taken during a spacewalk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that sixty years ago, Buzz Aldrin took the first spacewalk selfies on Gemini XII. NASA says Gemini photos also helped make the case for satellites like Landsat.

In a recent development, sixty years ago this month, Buzz Aldrin opened the hatch of his Gemini spacecraft, looked outside and exclaimed, “Man! Look at that!”.

According to recent reports, near the end of that spacewalk, on November 12, 1966, he mounted a camera on the edge of the hatch, pointed it at himself and took the first selfies ever taken during a spacewalk. NASA notes that it happened decades before the concept even existed.

According to recent reports, that flight, Gemini XII, is better known for something else. It finally demonstrated that astronauts could do useful work outside a spacecraft, a skill NASA needed before it could send anyone to the Moon.

And a NASA image article published on November 13 points to a quieter legacy: photos like the ones Aldrin and his commander took from orbit helped inspire the program that led to the Landsat satellites.

It has been revealed that aldrin and command pilot James A. Lovell introduced on November 11, 1966, on a four-day mission. It was the final flight of NASA’s Gemini program, which had to prove the techniques that Apollo would need to land on the Moon.

Those techniques included rendezvous and docking, spacewalking, and showing that spacecraft and astronauts could function for at least eight days, the minimum for a round trip to the Moon.

Sources indicate that spacewalks were the weak spot. Astronauts on the Gemini IX, X and XI missions had run into significant difficulties outside their spacecraft, and NASA looked for better ways to train.

On September 12, 1966, Aldrin became the first astronaut to train for his spacewalks underwater, using mockups of the Gemini and its target vehicle in a school swimming pool in Owings Mills, Maryland. Neutral buoyancy training, as it is called, is still in use today.

Gemini XII launched about 90 minutes after an uncrewed Agena target vehicle. When the crew’s rendezvous radar proved erratic, Aldrin used backup methods and onboard calculations to guide them in.

In a recent development, he had written his doctoral dissertation on orbital rendezvous. They docked on the third orbit.

Sources indicate that A problem with the Agena’s engine stopped a planned boost to a higher orbit. Instead, Mission Control told the crew that a slight change would put them on the path of a solar eclipse the next morning.

On November 12, as they flew over the Galapagos Islands, the nearly total eclipse came into view, and Aldrin took several photographs and a short film clip.

Recent findings suggest that it was the first time a solar eclipse was photographed from Earth orbit, according to NASA. Gemini XII passed within 3.4 miles of the center of the eclipse’s path.

Sources indicate that later that day, Aldrin made his first spacewalk, a “standup” outing in which he stayed in the open hatch. He installed a handrail on the Agena for the next day, photographed stars in ultraviolet light and took his selfies. He spent two hours and 28 minutes outside.

The next day, tied to the spacecraft by a 30-foot umbilical, he moved along the handrail to the Agena and later worked at the back of the Gemini with his feet in restraints called “golden slippers.”.

He completed 19 tasks in all, reporting no problems with keeping his body in position. At two hours and nine minutes, it was the longest umbilical spacewalk to that time.

Industry observers note that A third standup spacewalk brought his total to a then-record five hours and 48 minutes. Aldrin credited his underwater training and adequate restraint systems for his success.

Spacewalks have come a long way since then: in September 2024, the crew of SpaceX’s Polaris Dawn mission carried out the first civilian spacewalk.

On November 14, 1966, Lovell and Aldrin also photographed the area around the Red Sea and the Nile River valley. NASA featured that image in its November 13 article.

According to the agency, the photos taken by Lovell, Aldrin and other Gemini astronauts demonstrated the value of orbital imagery for studying Earth’s surface, and helped scientists make the case for a dedicated Earth observation satellite program.

One of the strongest advocates for Earth-observing satellites was William T. Pecora, director of the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) from 1965 to 1971.

In a 1969 statement, he mentioned the Earth Resources Observation Satellite program he championed, which later paved the way for Landsat, was “conceived in 1966 largely as a direct result of the demonstrated utility of Mercury and Gemini orbital photography to Earth resource studies.”.

For more than five decades, Landsat and other Earth-observing satellites have been used to monitor crops, wildfires, flooding, vegetation health and land use. In October, Landsat 9 captured autumn’s colors in the forests around Ripton, Vermont.

Lovell and Aldrin splashed down in the Atlantic Ocean on November 15, 1966, only three miles from the planned target. The flight lasted 94 hours and 34 minutes.

Gemini flew 10 crewed missions in 20 months, and all of the program’s major objectives were accomplished. Less than three years later, Aldrin walked on the Moon with Apollo 11. The Gemini XII spacecraft is on display at the Adler Planetarium in Chicago.

The information was obtained from NASA’s history of the Gemini XII mission, its account of eclipses seen from space and its image article on Gemini Earth photography.

The 2026 ozone hole grew to more than twice the size of the U.S., but a 1987 treaty kept it from getting even bigger

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 2026 Antarctic ozone hole was the seventh largest in 48 years.
  • This year’s ozone hole over Antarctica grew to cover an area more than twice the size of the United States.
  • It has been revealed that that sounds like bad news, and in part it is.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 2026 Antarctic ozone hole was the seventh largest in 48 years. But it would have been bigger without the Montreal Protocol.

This year’s ozone hole over Antarctica grew to cover an area more than twice the size of the United States. NASA and NOAA scientists say it was the seventh largest in 48 years of monitoring.

It has been revealed that that sounds like bad news, and in part it is. But the same scientists say the ozone layer is still on track to recover later this century, and that the hole would have been even bigger if the world had not cut back on the chemicals that destroy ozone.

Many of those chemicals came from everyday products like refrigerators, air conditioners and building insulation. Some of them are still around, which is one reason the recovery is taking so long.

During the peak ozone depletion season, from September 7 to October 13, the hole covered an average of about 9.6 million square miles (25 million square kilometers), according to NOAA and NASA, which reported the results on November 4.

Recent findings suggest that it reached its greatest extent for the year on September 18, at 10.5 million square miles (27.1 million square kilometers). That is about 90% as large as the largest ozone hole ever observed, on September 9, 2000.

“The 2026 ozone hole is large but could have been 1 to 2 million square miles (3.5 million square kilometers) larger if ozone-depleting substances were as prevalent in the atmosphere today as they were at their year 2000 peak,” remarked Paul Newman, a senior scientist at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County (UMBC), and longtime leader of NASA’s ozone research team at the Goddard Space Flight Center.

The word “hole” is not literal. No place is empty of ozone. Scientists use it to describe the area where ozone concentrations drop below 220 Dobson units, a level that had never been observed before 1979.

The stratospheric ozone layer works as Earth’s sunscreen. It absorbs ultraviolet light, which damages DNA in plants and animals and leads to sunburns and skin cancer in people.

This is not the same as ground-level ozone, an air pollutant that commonly results from human activities and that reached dangerous levels for billions of people in 2026.

In a recent development, every southern spring, ozone thins over Antarctica. Human-made compounds containing chlorine and bromine rise into the stratosphere, where ultraviolet light breaks them down.

The freed chlorine and bromine atoms then interact with cloud particles in the frigid Antarctic stratosphere and destroy ozone.

It has been revealed that A ring of seasonal winds called the stratospheric polar vortex keeps that cold air in place. In 2026, the vortex was unusually powerful.

“The polar vortex was unusually large this year in part because planetary-scale weather systems that typically well up from the lower atmosphere and break up the vortex were especially weak in August and September,” said Amy Butler, a research scientist at the NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory.

That weak wave action kept the strongest winds several degrees of latitude farther from the South Pole, she said, which created a larger area where ozone could be destroyed.

Size is only part of the picture. The 2026 hole was not as deep as the record-breaking holes of 10 or 20 years ago.

NOAA scientists launch balloons carrying instruments called ozonesondes from the South Pole Baseline Atmospheric Observatory.

They found that ozone directly overhead reached its lowest value of the year, 105 Dobson units, on October 17. The lowest value ever recorded over the South Pole was 92 Dobson units, in October 2006.

One hundred Dobson units of ozone, compressed at sea level, would make a layer 1 millimeter deep, about as thick as a dime.

“The annual ozone hole has been forming later in the season in recent years, which tells us the ozone layer is healing,” Newman remarked.

“But an unusually powerful polar vortex has extended ozone depletion in the Antarctic this season, allowing the hole to grow to proportions we haven’t seen in a decade.”.

The ozone hole was first reported in 1985 by British Antarctic Survey scientists, and NASA satellite instruments revealed its continental scale.

Scientists traced the damage to chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs, which had been used in refrigerators and aerosol sprays since the 1930s.

That led to the Montreal Protocol in 1987, a treaty in which countries committed to phasing out ozone-depleting substances and replacing them with less harmful alternatives.

According to NOAA and NASA, the controls set by the treaty continue to drive the long-term recovery of the ozone layer.

Since their peak, chlorine levels in the Antarctic stratosphere from ozone-depleting substances have declined by about a third relative to the 1980s, said Stephen Montzka, senior scientist at NOAA’s Global Monitoring Laboratory.

Ozone recovery is also having unexpected effects, like the way it is changing life in Antarctica.

The ozone hole forms over Antarctica, far from the United States. But the chemicals behind it came from ordinary products, and they do not go away promptly.

Recent findings suggest that NOAA indicates CFCs and similar compounds can linger in the atmosphere, or leak out of old products and landfills, for many decades. As those older compounds break down, scientists estimate that the ozone hole will recover by the 2070s.

That is why the way old appliances are thrown away still matters. Under the Clean Air Act, the Environmental Protection Agency requires refrigerant to be recovered when refrigeration and air conditioning equipment is disposed of, to keep it out of the air.

Household refrigerators and freezers, window air conditioners and car air conditioners usually reach the end of the line with their refrigerant still inside.

In those cases, the EPA indicates the final person in the disposal chain, such as a scrap metal recycler or a landfill owner, is responsible for making sure the refrigerant is recovered first.

The EPA also notes that reduced ozone means more UVB radiation reaching the ground. In Antarctica, the amount of UVB measured at the surface can double during the annual ozone hole.

The agency says it is always important to protect yourself from UVB, even without ozone depletion, by wearing hats, sunglasses and sunscreen.

Sources indicate that satellites have tracked the ozone layer since 1979. This year, instruments on NASA’s Aura satellite, the NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 satellites and the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership satellite, run jointly by NASA and NOAA, all contributed to the monitoring.

Sources indicate that weather can still make some years worse than others. Year-to-year changes in size and depth are caused by differences in stratospheric temperature and circulation, and colder conditions produce a larger hole, according to NASA’s Earth Observatory.

Without the cuts that began in 1987, this year’s unusually strong vortex would have had more chlorine to work with, and scientists say the hole would have been even larger.

The information was obtained from NOAA, NASA, NASA Earth Observatory and the Environmental Protection Agency’s pages on appliance disposal and the effects of ozone depletion.

Tech Report: Mice start moving indoors when fall nights turn cold, and a 1/4-inch gap in your house is enough to let them in

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (902 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that house mice often enter homes as temperatures drop.
  • In places where house mice live outdoors for most of the year, the animals often enter homes in autumn and winter as the nights grow colder.
  • That pattern is described in a house mouse guide updated in July 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that house mice often enter homes as temperatures drop. Learn how to seal entry points, set traps safely and clean up droppings without risk.

In places where house mice live outdoors for most of the year, the animals often enter homes in autumn and winter as the nights grow colder.

That pattern is described in a house mouse guide updated in July 2025. Its authors are Niamh Quinn of UC Cooperative Extension and Matt Frye of the Cornell IPM Program.

Recent findings suggest that “House mice can squeeze under gaps ¼ inch tall, and through openings 3/8 inch wide,” the two wrote. Those measurements equal about 6 and 10 millimeters.

Sources indicate that the house mouse (Mus musculus) is native to Central Asia. It crossed to North America aboard ships carrying settlers from Europe and elsewhere.

The species lives close to people because they store cereals and grains, the foods it prefers.

According to recent reports, an adult weighs about 0.5 ounce (14 grams) and is 5 to 7 inches (13 to 18 centimeters) long, tail included. It can eat up to 20 percent of its body weight a day, taken in roughly 200 small meals each night.

A house mouse rarely strays more than 30 feet (9 meters) from its nest and its food. It builds that nest in a sheltered spot, using finely shredded paper or other fibrous material.

Where resources stay plentiful and stable, house mice can breed all year. A female may produce five to ten litters in one year, each with about five or six pups.

According to recent reports, the young arrive 18 to 21 days after conception and can breed at five to six weeks of age. The usual life span is nine to 12 months.

“If a pen fits under a door, a mouse can enlarge the gap to enter,” Quinn wrote in November 2025. For rats in cities, Quinn put the smallest usable opening at the size of a quarter.

Mice climb well and can scale any rough vertical surface. They also run along wire cables and ropes, and can leap as high as 12 inches (30 centimeters) from the floor onto a flat surface.

Entry points listed by Quinn and Frye include cracks in building foundations and the openings around water pipes, vents and utility cables.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) advises checking inside and outside the home for gaps and holes.

“Exclusion is the most successful and permanent form of house mouse control,” the guide states.

It calls for metal or concrete to seal those cracks and openings. Doors, windows and screens need a tight fit, and door and window edges may need a metal cover to stop gnawing.

Plastic screening, rubber, vinyl, expanding foam and wood are classed as gnawable, and as ineffective plugs for mouse holes.

According to recent reports, “Steel wool scouring pads make good temporary plugs but may rust over time,” Quinn and Frye cautioned. The CDC advises steel wool ringed with caulk for small holes, and lath screen or metal, cement, hardware cloth or metal sheeting for larger ones.

Quinn’s article adds door sweeps built to exclude pests, rather than weather strips, and metal mesh over vents.

Ultrasonic devices are of very limited use, because the sound is directional and does not pass behind objects. Some cats and dogs catch mice, but pets seldom keep a rodent population under control.

In a recent development, for mice already indoors, the California guide favors setting enough traps to keep the trapping period short. It puts the maximum spacing at about 10 feet (3 meters) in areas with mouse activity.

Setting traps in pairs, 1 to 2 inches (2.5 to 5 centimeters) apart, can raise the catch of mice that jump over obstacles. Good spots are behind objects, in dark corners and wherever there is evidence of mice.

Peanut butter is a popular bait because mice find it very attractive, though it can pose allergy risks to some people.

In a recent development, every rodenticide is toxic to people, pets and wildlife. Poisoned mice often die inside the building being treated, and in that case trapping may be the better approach.

It has been revealed that droppings and gnaw marks can reveal where mice are active. One house mouse leaves approximately 50 to 75 droppings a day, according to University of Nebraska–Lincoln Extension.

House mice can carry leptospirosis, salmonella and lymphocytic choriomeningitis (LCM), a viral disease. Quinn and Frye cite an estimate that five percent of house mice across the United States carry the LCM virus and can transmit it.

People can catch LCM through exposure to fresh urine, droppings, saliva or nesting material from infected rodents. The most common hantavirus that causes lung disease in the United States comes from another species, the deer mouse.

“Don’t vacuum or sweep rodent urine, droppings, or nesting materials,” the agency’s cleanup instructions warn. That can put tiny droplets carrying viruses into the air.

The steps start with rubber or plastic gloves and a household disinfectant or freshly made bleach solution, left to soak for five minutes. The bleach mix is 1.5 cups (355 milliliters) in 1 gallon (3.8 liters) of water.

The information was obtained from the University of California Statewide Integrated Pest Management Program (IPM).

Psoriasis treatment may work better with an over-the-counter supplement

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1085 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pantethine, a vitamin B5 relative sold to lower cholesterol, calmed the immune cells behind psoriasis and improved skin in a small trial.
  • It has been revealed that pantethine is a vitamin B5 derivative sold as a dietary supplement.
  • Putting it back calmed the immune cells that drive the disease and eased psoriasis-like inflammation in mice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pantethine, a vitamin B5 relative sold to lower cholesterol, calmed the immune cells behind psoriasis and improved skin in a small trial.

It has been revealed that pantethine is a vitamin B5 derivative sold as a dietary supplement. In a small blood-sample comparison, researchers found lower levels in people with psoriasis than in healthy volunteers.

Putting it back calmed the immune cells that drive the disease and eased psoriasis-like inflammation in mice.

In a small 12-week trial, psoriasis severity scores improved more among patients who took pantethine alongside a prescription ointment than among those who used the ointment alone.

Wei-Na Zhang of the State Key Laboratory of Biomedical Analysis in Beijing led the work with four colleagues, including Cheng-Xin Li of the Chinese PLA General Hospital.

The first authors, Ai-Ping Cao, Jun-Cheng Li and Rui Wang, work at the Beijing laboratory, Fudan University in Shanghai, and the hospital.

Sources indicate that the trial was small and ran at one hospital. The authors wrote that it indicates the approach is feasible, not that the mechanism they found in mice is what helped the patients.

“Our investigator-initiated clinical trial demonstrated encouraging therapeutic efficacy of pantethine as an adjunctive therapy in psoriasis, but these findings should be interpreted as proof-of-concept for clinical feasibility rather than direct mechanistic validation,” Zhang mentioned.

Psoriasis is an immune disease that happens to show on the skin.

It has been revealed that immune cells called dendritic cells, whose job is to show the rest of the immune system what to attack, get overactive. They set off the inflammation that produces the scaly plaques.

In a recent development, the team went looking for enzymes that were unusually busy in those cells. In blood and skin samples from patients with psoriasis, lupus and other immune diseases, a family of enzymes called Vanins stood out.

In one set of skin biopsies, from 92 psoriasis patients and 82 healthy people, two of the three Vanin genes were among the most strongly switched on.

Vanins break pantethine down, and one of the products is vitamin B5. In blood from 12 psoriasis patients, pantethine was lower than in 17 healthy people, and mice with psoriasis-like inflammation showed the same shortfall.

The team worked in mice given a cream that triggers psoriasis-like skin inflammation over six days.

Mice whose dendritic cells lacked the main mouse Vanin gene, Vnn3, developed much milder disease, with less skin thickening, lower severity scores and fewer immune cells in the affected patches.

Industry observers note that giving ordinary mice a daily injection of pantethine during the six days did the same, and so did a drug called RR6 that blocks Vanin. Both raised pantethine and lowered cholesterol in the blood.

Was it the dendritic cells, or just lower cholesterol in general?

To check, the team removed those cells from mice and replaced them with cells that had been treated with pantethine beforehand. The mice with pre-treated cells still got less disease.

It has been revealed that why would a vitamin relative quiet an immune cell? Zhang’s team traced it to cholesterol.

When Vanin is busy and pantethine runs low, dendritic cells make more cholesterol and pack it into their outer membranes.

According to recent reports, cholesterol-rich patches of membrane are where the cells’ alarm receptors cluster. A cell with more of those patches responds harder to the signals that switch it on.

Recent findings suggest that pantethine reversed that. Cells treated with it carried less cholesterol in their membranes and fewer clustered receptors, and they sent weaker signals through the inflammatory pathways that drive the disease.

Dendritic cells taken from psoriasis and lupus patients and treated in the dish behaved the same way.

High blood cholesterol is already known to make psoriasis worse and its treatments less effective, the authors wrote, which is what made a cholesterol-lowering supplement worth trying in people.

Industry observers note that the team enrolled 27 people with mild plaque psoriasis at the Chinese PLA General Hospital and randomly assigned them to two treatment groups. The 12-week analysis included 24 participants.

Everyone used a standard prescription ointment that combines a vitamin D relative with a steroid. Half also took a 300-milligram pantethine capsule twice a day, from a brand sold over the counter.

It has been revealed that two dermatologists scored each patient’s skin from photographs at the start, at eight weeks and at 12 weeks, using the two scales psoriasis trials usually rely on. The trial is registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry.

Recent findings suggest that over 12 weeks, the group taking pantethine improved more on both scales than the group using ointment alone. The dermatologists didn’t record any side effects tied to the treatment.

The difference was concentrated in people who started the trial with abnormal blood fats.

Among them, the pantethine group’s lipid profiles improved and their skin scores at 12 weeks were clearly better than those of similar patients on ointment alone.

Among patients whose blood fats were normal to begin with, the two groups ended up about the same, so the capsule didn’t add much.

The split fits the mechanism, the authors wrote, but it also narrows the finding.

“We found that pantethine administration effectively alleviated psoriasis in mice, suggesting that insufficient pantethine levels may be the crucial contributor to hyperactivation of dendritic cells and autoimmune inflammation following the up-regulation of Vanins,” Zhang said.

Twelve people took the supplement, at one hospital, for three months, and the comparison group took no placebo capsule. Whether the gain holds up in a larger, blinded trial over a longer period is the first open question.

It has been revealed that the mechanism was worked out in mice and in cells. Other immune cells may have helped the patients improve, the authors wrote. And what switches Vanin on in the first place is still unknown.

Vanin demonstrates up in many kinds of cells, not only dendritic cells, and the team wrote that the pathway may matter in other inflammatory diseases.

Beyond psoriasis, though, the evidence so far is a pattern in patient data, not a test in a disease model.

The next step the authors described is to test the pathway in those other diseases.

Whether people with normal blood fat levels can get anything from the supplement is a question this trial could not answer.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Experimental Medicine.
