💡 Key Takeaways
  • By measuring gene activity in 5.4 million immune cells, researchers uncovered genetic clues to disease that whole-blood studies had missed.
  • A blood sample is usually read as one mixture, and for years the studies linking genes to disease have read it that way too.
  • Yet a gene’s tie to a disease can be found in one kind of immune cell and nowhere else, so a whole-blood reading misses it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By measuring gene activity in 5.4 million immune cells, researchers uncovered genetic clues to disease that whole-blood studies had missed.

A blood sample is usually read as one mixture, and for years the studies linking genes to disease have read it that way too.

Yet a gene’s tie to a disease can be found in one kind of immune cell and nowhere else, so a whole-blood reading misses it.

Researchers sequenced each participant’s genome and measured gene activity in more than 5 million immune cells, one cell at a time.

About half of the effects linked to common genetic variants showed up in only one or a few cell types.

That is the main result of the first phase of a project called TenK10K, which aims to build the same map for 10,000 people.

The study’s senior authors included Joseph Powell of the Garvan Institute of Medical Research and UNSW Sydney and Daniel MacArthur of the Centre for Population Genomics.

The center is a joint initiative of Garvan and the Murdoch Children’s Research Institute.

Industry observers note that the work is a map of associations rather than a test of any treatment. Every participant was of European ancestry.

“Most of the biological mechanisms we uncovered were invisible to prior studies,” Powell said.

The team took blood from 1,925 Australian adults who had joined two earlier studies, one of eye health in Tasmania and one of heart disease in Sydney.

They sequenced each person’s whole genome. Then they measured which genes were switched on in each of 5.4 million immune cells and sorted the cells into 28 types.

Comparing people’s DNA with gene activity in each cell type revealed which genetic variants turn a gene up or down, and in which cells.

They found common variants affecting 83% of the 21,404 genes they tested.

Whole-genome sequencing also let them see rare variants, which the DNA chips used in most earlier studies read poorly. Rare variants left signals on 47% of the genes, more than 30,000 effects in all.

About half of the common-variant effects appeared in only one or a few of the 28 cell types.

Almost none appeared in all of them. A whole-blood study averages signals across cell types, so it can miss effects that appear in only one or a few.

The team compared their map with the largest whole-blood study of this kind.

Industry observers note that that study drew on more than 30,000 people and found roughly 17,000 genes whose activity was associated with genetic variants. The single-cell map found about the same number using data from 1,925 people.

About a quarter of the genes in the single-cell map (4,572) were absent from the whole-blood study’s list.

“This is the most detailed map to date of how genetic variation shapes the immune system,” MacArthur said.

The team then matched their map against known genetic risk regions for 16 diseases, among them asthma, autoimmune conditions, cancers and infections, and for 44 blood traits from UK Biobank.

Where a risk variant and a gene-activity variant turned out to be the same one, that gene became a candidate cause.

Nearly 1,500 genes were tied to the diseases this way. Of all the genes tied to a disease or a blood trait, 893 had no reported genetic effect on their activity in the big whole-blood study.

Sources indicate that A gene called OSM is the example the team keeps coming back to. It is switched on in 20 of the 28 cell types.

Its link to inflammatory bowel disease, though, appears only in natural killer cells, where the OSM gene was more active in people carrying the risk variant.

The same matching tied a gene called IGHG4 to Alzheimer’s disease in one cell type only, memory B cells.

Sources indicate that in an email interview with Earth.com, the Garvan team was asked which finding surprised them most. They pointed to “how often the link to disease sits in just one type of immune cell.”.

Sources indicate that A gene can be active across the immune system yet connect to disease in a single cell type, they wrote. “Earlier whole-blood studies simply couldn’t see that.”.

Recent findings suggest that A map like this names candidate genes and the cells they act in. It does not show that changing a gene changes the disease, and no drug was tested.

The authors also wrote that their cutoff for calling an effect cell-specific is conservative, with no second dataset of the same size to check it against.

“This first phase focused on people of European ancestry, and we want our findings to apply to everyone,” the team told Earth.com.

As the project grows, they wrote, more people will let them detect rarer genetic variants and study rarer cells.

“In the next few years, the biggest impact will be on drug discovery rather than in the clinic,” they wrote.

Drugs backed by human genetic evidence are more likely to succeed in trials, they added, and over time the map could help match patients to treatments.

Which of the nearly 1,500 candidate genes actually drive disease is the open question, and this map can’t answer it on its own.

The summary data are free for other researchers to use, and two companion papers add layers on repeated DNA and on which stretches of DNA are open in each cell.

Someone still has to run the experiments that switch a candidate gene off in the right cell type.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

#180190. Could intermittent fasting help reverse diabetes? A new study offers a clue

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1363 w)

Could intermittent fasting help reverse diabetes? A new study offers a clue

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1363 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Intermittent fasting helped diabetic mice restore normal blood sugar by improving insulin production without requiring extra calorie cuts.
  • In a upcoming study of mice with diet-induced diabetes, two feeding regimens produced different results even though the mice consumed about the same number of calories.
  • The difference was seen in beta cells, the pancreas cells that make insulin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Intermittent fasting helped diabetic mice restore normal blood sugar by improving insulin production without requiring extra calorie cuts.

In a upcoming study of mice with diet-induced diabetes, two feeding regimens produced different results even though the mice consumed about the same number of calories.

The difference was seen in beta cells, the pancreas cells that make insulin.

One group had unlimited access to regular chow, which contained fewer calories per gram.

A second group was given fatty food on alternate days. Both groups consumed about the same number of calories and ended at the same weight.

Yet blood sugar returned to normal only in the every-other-day group.

The difference emerged even though the two groups consumed about the same number of calories.

Recent findings suggest that the mice fed every other day stored more insulin in their beta cells. The researchers think fasting days gave those cells a break.

The research was conducted at Michigan Medicine, the University of Michigan’s academic medical center.

Peter Arvan, a professor of internal medicine, led the study.

Sources indicate that arvan is also a member of the Caswell Diabetes Institute. Research investigator Maroof Alam was the first author.

According to recent reports, all of the mice were male. Each carried a gene change that makes it prone to diabetes on a fatty diet.

Industry observers note that insulin is first made as a longer molecule that is not yet finished. It has to fold into the right shape before it can work. Biologists call it proinsulin.

Mice carry four copies of the genes that make it. In these mice, one copy had been altered. As a result, some of their proinsulin was prone to folding wrong.

In a recent development, on regular food, the mice don’t need treatment. Young males that gain weight on a high-fat diet, however, develop diabetes swiftly. Females are resistant, so only males were studied.

From 5 to 11 weeks of age, the males were fed chow with 60% of its calories from fat. By the end, every mouse had diabetes. Their blood sugar was above 250 mg/dL at a random check.

People with a change at the same spot in the insulin molecule also develop diabetes. In those patients, diet plays an key part in when it starts and how it progresses.

After those six weeks, the diabetic mice were moved onto upcoming diets for five weeks. Littermates were alternated between the two main groups.

Fifteen mice switched to regular lab chow, which gets about 14% of its calories from fat. These mice could eat as much as they liked every day.

Fifteen more stayed on the high-fat food but could eat only every other day. This pattern is a form of intermittent fasting. At noon, each mouse was moved to a fresh cage. The cage held either plenty of food or none.

Five more mice kept eating the high-fat diet every day. Those mice gained more weight, and their diabetes got worse.

Industry observers note that both diet groups ate fewer calories than before, and both stopped gaining weight. Neither group actually lost any. By the end, their body weights matched, and so did the energy they burned.

It has been revealed that insulin sensitivity also improved equally in both groups. This measure shows how well the body’s cells respond to insulin.

According to recent reports, ten days in, both groups handled a dose of sugar the same way. By five weeks, however, the every-other-day mice cleared sugar from their blood better.

These mice also reached normal levels on both standard blood sugar checks. One check was taken at a random time, and the other after a fast. The mice on daily chow did not reach normal levels.

According to recent reports, “In the end, both groups of diabetic mice consumed and burned the same number of calories,” Alam remarked. “However, mice that were fed on alternate days had more insulin in their beta cells.”.

Insulin sensitivity couldn’t explain the gap, because the two groups matched on it. Insulin supply could. More insulin was found in the blood of the every-other-day mice. Their ratio of insulin to blood sugar was four times that of the chow group.

In a recent development, beta cells sit in small clusters called islets. Islets from the every-other-day mice held more than 85% more insulin than those from the chow group. When high sugar was added, more insulin was released from these islets as well.

In a recent development, the islets weren’t any bigger. Under an electron microscope, though, more insulin packets were seen in beta cells from the every-other-day mice. These tiny packets are where finished insulin is stored.

The researchers also compared insulin and blood sugar at the end of a feeding day and at the end of a fasting day.

The every-other-day mice were also checked at the end of a day without food.

By then, their average blood sugar had dropped by at least 45%. Insulin in the blood fell too. This drop suggests the beta cells were sending out less insulin.

Sources indicate that yet the insulin stored in their islets was about the same after fasting and feeding days. The cells released plenty after meals without running low. So they must have been replacing what they sent out.

“We wanted to see whether rest periods between meals allow the pancreas to recover from the stress of previous meals,” Arvan said.

Inside the cells, more proinsulin was being made in the every-other-day mice. A chemical signal known to slow proinsulin production was found at lower levels in their islets.

In a recent development, cells usually make more of a certain protein when misfolded proteins accumulate. In these mice, levels of that protein did not increase. The extra proinsulin, it seems, was produced without added stress on the cells.

Sources indicate that in both diet groups, proinsulin was found in the same share of islet cells. The two groups probably had similar numbers of beta cells, then.

What changed with fasting, it appears, was the maturity of the existing beta cells and not their number.

The two foods were not identical apart from fat. Regular chow and high-fat chow also contain different amounts of protein. They may differ in vitamins and other compounds too. The authors themselves flagged these differences in the paper.

In a recent development, every animal in the study was a male mouse carrying the same insulin gene change. The results have not been tested in females or in other forms of diabetes.

It has been revealed that the authors also cited earlier work in people that found related results. In one human study, insulin fell further with modified alternate-day fasting than with similar calorie cutting on no set schedule.

In a separate trial of adults with metabolic syndrome, fasting blood sugar fell more with modified alternate-day fasting than with daily calorie restriction.

The National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases says scientists are still studying fasting in diabetes.

Its advice for doctors is that patients with type 2 diabetes who fast should have their medications watched closely.

The mice in this study started their new diets after six weeks of high-fat eating. A separate set of mice stayed on the fatty diet for 11 weeks. By that point, far less insulin was left in their islets.

Animals this sick, the authors wrote, might already be beyond the point where every-other-day feeding can restore their islets.

“You need to have restoration of functional beta cells, but when diabetes is advanced, there might not be enough remaining beta cells to restore,” Arvan noted.

In the paper, the authors also suggested that more than five weeks of fasting days might raise beta-cell maturity further.

“On the other hand, even though it might take longer to fix more severe stages of diabetes, we need to test if intermittent fasting can help,” he said.

For now, the result has only been shown in young male mice whose diabetes was treated early.

The full study was published in the journal Molecular Metabolism.

Petunias reveal an unexpected link between flower color and scent

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1310 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists studying petunias discovered that the same biological machinery responsible for flower color also shapes their scent.
  • Petunias use the same raw ingredient, an amino acid called phenylalanine, to make pigments and many of their scent compounds.
  • Researchers at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem found that a protein called EOBV works with two proteins involved in pigmentation to regulate the flower’s scent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists studying petunias discovered that the same biological machinery responsible for flower color also shapes their scent.

Petunias use the same raw ingredient, an amino acid called phenylalanine, to make pigments and many of their scent compounds.

Researchers at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem found that a protein called EOBV works with two proteins involved in pigmentation to regulate the flower’s scent.

When the researchers removed this protein, the flowers released more compounds associated with the smell of cloves and vanilla.

However, they released less methyl benzoate, normally the most abundant scent compound in these petunias.

Oded Skaliter and Alexander Vainstein ran all of it in petunias. The chemistry moved. Nobody has checked whether a nose, human or moth, can tell the difference.

In a recent development, wild petunias have different ways of attracting pollinators. One species releases its fragrance at night to attract moths, another attracts bees with purple flowers, and a third uses red flowers to attract hummingbirds.

Petunia pigment is run by a committee of three, known to biologists as the MBW complex.

Two of these proteins, AN1 and AN11, remain the same. The third can be any one of several proteins belonging to a family called MYB, and its identity determines which genes the group controls.

Skaliter and his colleagues examined when AN1 and AN11 were most active.

Activity peaked as the flowers opened and remained high for another two days, around the same time that scent production reached its peak.

Recent findings suggest that then they knocked each gene down, one at a time, with a plant virus. Air from around the petals went into the analyzer.

Recent findings suggest that both treatments increased the release of eugenol and vanillin. The amount of methyl benzoate roughly doubled.

Rather than helping the flowers produce more fragrance, the pigment proteins appeared to hold scent production back.

The researchers suspected that the missing piece of the puzzle was the third protein in the group.

Six MYB proteins were already in the frame here, all of them previously linked to petunia fragrance.

Each went up against AN1 and AN11 in yeast cells that change color when two proteins bind. EOBV was the only hit.

The team repeated the experiment in living plant tissue. This time, they used a system that produces betalain, the red pigment found in beets, when proteins interact.

It has been revealed that leaves of a tobacco relative turned red when they received both AN1 and EOBV. Leaves that received AN1 alone produced a weaker color signal.

Recent findings suggest that the strongest red color appeared when all three proteins were present. Removing any one of them greatly reduced pigment production in the test.

It has been revealed that AN11 and EOBV would not bind each other. AN1 had to stand between them.

In a recent development, the researchers also found very little EOBV gene activity outside the petals. Within the petals, activity was about 1.8 times higher in the upper surface layer, through which fragrance escapes.

Previous work from the same laboratory found that a gene responsible for giving petals their identity also activates scent production.

Sources indicate that the next step was to remove EOBV completely. A virus carried CRISPR gene-editing tools into petunia tissue, and the team recovered three groups of edited plants.

According to recent reports, in one group, the instructions for starting the protein were gone, along with the first 42 amino acids. Production in the other two stopped after 58 and 91 amino acids.

The edited plants still looked and flowered like the originals.

Two-day-old flowers then went into sealed jars, two flowers to a jar, and whatever they gave off over the next 24 hours was trapped and measured.

According to recent reports, without a working version of EOBV, the flowers released more eugenol, both forms of isoeugenol and vanillin. These compounds give cloves and vanilla their familiar aromas.

However, the flowers released less of almost every other scent compound, including methyl benzoate. The total amount of fragrance released also fell.

The team then ground up petals to measure how much of each compound remained inside. The clove and vanilla compounds had increased there, too.

The petals contained similar amounts of methyl benzoate and several other scent compounds even though the edited flowers released less of them.

According to recent reports, A repressor has to act on something, so the next question was which genes EOBV holds down. Gene activity was compared between edited and unedited flowers.

Sources indicate that most showed little difference. However, two genes, known as C4H2 and ADT3, became more active after the researchers removed EOBV.

C4H2 controls the carbon supply to the branch that produces eugenol, isoeugenol and vanillin.

The rise in C4H2 gene activity may help explain why the edited flowers made more eugenol, isoeugenol, and vanillin.

It has been revealed that the team then tested that link directly. They connected the region of DNA that controls C4H2 activity to a system that produces red pigment.

Petals that received EOBV showed no visible red color. Petals without the additional EOBV produced more than twice as much pigment.

Two other fragrance genes, PAAS and BSMT, became less active in the edited flowers. Since EOBV does not appear to bind directly to the regions controlling these genes, the changes were probably indirect.

According to recent reports, researchers found a similar pattern in 2011 when they reduced the activity of another petunia gene called PhMYB4. PhMYB4 and EOBV are about 80% identical. Genetic testing confirmed that PhMYB4 itself had not been edited.

In a recent development, EOBV becomes more active when petunias grow in warmer conditions. The researchers wanted to see whether removing it could protect flowers from heat.

They grew the plants in a greenhouse for a month before moving them into two rooms. The cooler room had temperatures of 72°F (22°C) during the day and 61°F (16°C) at night. The warmer room reached 82°F (28°C) and 72°F (22°C), respectively.

Industry observers note that after measuring 38 flowers, the team found that unedited flowers became 12% narrower in warmer conditions. Edited flowers shrank by only 6%.

Heat also reduced the amount of scent released by unedited flowers, mainly due to lower emissions of benzaldehyde and methyl benzoate. Edited flowers maintained their overall scent output.

Meanwhile, PhEXP1, a gene that helps petal cells expand, became less active in both groups by similar amounts.

Heat-shrunk petunia flowers were traced to slower cell division in a 2021 study, a step this team did not measure.

More vanilla and clove compounds might sound appealing, but would these petunias actually smell better?

Nobody has asked people to smell the edited flowers. The researchers haven’t tested pollinators either.

It has been revealed that removing EOBV also has limits. In purple varieties, reducing EOBV activity left pigment levels unchanged.

EOBV belongs to the color machinery without fixing the shade of purple itself.

It has been revealed that the team also crossed the edited plants with petunias lacking EVER, another scent regulator. Those flowers did not outperform either parent. The authors suggest limited carbon, or a limited capacity to release scent.

The authors also disclosed a commercial interest. Skaliter and Vainstein are chief technology officer and chief scientific officer at CapsiBreed, which uses gene editing in hot and sweet peppers. Peppers and petunias are relatives.

One obvious next experiment is to switch EOBV off in plants that are already missing AN1 or AN11.

In a recent development, the team also wants to know whether other flowering plants are wired this way. And growers will want an answer to a blunter question: does a reshuffled scent give them flowers that anyone wants to buy?

The full study was published in the journal Plant Physiology.

#180188. Do You Trust Your Own Intuition? Here’s How You Sharpen It—And Win at Life, Researchers Say

Do You Trust Your Own Intuition? Here’s How You Sharpen It—And Win at Life, Researchers Say

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1049 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.
  • Think about the phrase “it’s just like riding a bicycle.” At first, it’s hard, and you have to pay attention to what you’re doing, but after you’ve practiced for many hours, bike riding becomes so natural you don’t even have to think about it; you just hop on and go.
  • Intuition is about finding the solution automatically and without deep thought, claims Wim De Neys, a cognitive psychologist and CNRS research professor at the University of Paris.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

Think about the phrase “it’s just like riding a bicycle.” At first, it’s hard, and you have to pay attention to what you’re doing, but after you’ve practiced for many hours, bike riding becomes so natural you don’t even have to think about it; you just hop on and go. In fact, you can hardly explain how you learned in the first place or exactly how you’re keeping your balance as you pedal on. You just trust your body to do it. The same applies to cognitive activities: As a child, you had to really think about how to arrive at the answer of 2+2, but now, you just know it’s four, without thinking.

Intuition is about finding the solution automatically and without deep thought, claims Wim De Neys, a cognitive psychologist and CNRS research professor at the University of Paris. At its core, your intuition is a behavior your brain develops based on patterns and experiences over time, a kind of automation for something you’ve done countless times. That’s why intuition is often linked to expertise. Trusting your gut may sound ill-advised, so why wouldn’t you want to think things through? But it turns out that generating your instincts for decision-making can both help you make the right choice in times of confusion and stress, and also free up mental resources for other tasks.

So, can you train your intuition to sense better choices?

Well, it’s not that simple, according to De Neys, whose research focuses on how intuitive and deliberate thinking develops over our lifetimes. You can’t sidestep the deep reflection needed to build the foundation of your intuitions. But you can tap into them in a more meaningful way, especially over time.

“Having gut feelings and intuition and even valid intuitions, there’s science to back it up,” De Neys indicates. “It exists, but it’s always tied to expertise, and expertise means it’s something that you’ve done a lot.”.

Intuition isn’t some overall sense; instead it’s tied to one area of expertise, like an interviewer being able to pick up on the candidate who’ll be the right fit for the job, or an experienced doctor delivering a diagnosis. While you won’t have expert intuition about everything under the sun, there are a few ways you can boost your own decision-making.

In a recent development, first, you need to get better at pattern matching, and that means practice. Intuition is tied to pattern-matching, Jeff Larsen, PhD, a professor of psychology at the University of Tennessee, explains. For example, chess masters earn their distinction by practicing so much that when they see the board, they don’t have to stop and think about what the two or three best moves will be. Others with less expertise may watch a game and think, “that was a silly move,” but they don’t realize the master player has spent years building up pattern recognition, or an accurate gut feeling, Larsen explains.

In a recent development, second, stop second-guessing your intuition. You can do this by asking yourself, “How might I be wrong?” One approach is to ask a friend who may disagree with you or might have an outside perspective. This can also help you understand that, often, an instinctual choice you made in the heat of the moment is correct. Even if the choice isn’t exactly right, it’s probably good enough to keep you safe. For example, when you’re driving down the interstate, you have some intuition about whether you can make a lane change or not, and whether you need to slow down or speed up to avoid an accident. Thinking about the consequences of your decision-making can also help give you more confidence in your intuition.

It has been revealed that sometimes you have to trust your gut on a truly life-changing decision. When it comes to marriage, the information overload can sometimes feel overwhelming. However, when it comes to close relationships, you’ve presumably experienced many behavioral exchanges with your partner, and this allows for substantial information-gathering to “feed your gut,” Michael Olson, PhD, a professor of psychology at the University of Tennessee, explains.

It has been revealed that since you can’t possibly keep this massive load of information in your conscious memory at all times, it translates into a neat summary of all those behavioral exchanges. Now you have a gut feeling that this person is right for you—or not.

Industry observers note that and the research agrees. A study Olson coauthored, published in Science, found that the “explicit,” or “conscious” evaluations couples in the study made of their partners while in the so-called initial “honeymoon stage” didn’t mean as much when stretched over four years. Instead, those who reported positive gut feelings over this time period had a more accurate idea of their happiness in their relationship.

Your gut doesn’t just extend to your love life. Trusting it can also help you to be successful in business. Elizabeth Rea, an evidentiary clairvoyant psychic medium, now teaches established founders and CEOs to tap into their own intuitions, through her firm, Insightful. As a medium, Rea has also assisted U.S. federal special agents investigating cold murder cases.

In a recent development, when working with clients, she asks them to relax what they consciously believe. Sometimes so-called gut feelings may come to us in the form of chills down our spine or another physical sensation. But since we’re living in a left-brained culture that prizes making decisions using logic and analysis, those instincts often get passed off as coincidences and ignored, Rea notes. Sometimes, gut feelings may also be ignored because of self-doubt. Your intuition often whispers to you, she tells clients. Honing these signals will help you improve your self-trust—thereby improving your intuition.

Overall, training yourself to trust your intuition will help you become a better decision-maker. You’ll make the right choices without the agonizing process of picking through pros and cons and running scenarios in your brain for days on end.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s a lot more cost-efficient if we can offload [decision-making] to our intuition,” De Neys states. “Often that’s going to be helpful because then it frees up resources for something else that might be more crucial at that point in time.”.

Biden: ‘Hard to take’ as Pelosi, Schumer turned on him in 2024

💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Joe Biden, Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., arrive for The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 bill signing at the White House, on Aug.
  • Sources indicate that in conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir.
  • Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Joe Biden, Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., arrive for The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 bill signing at the White House, on Aug. 9, 2022. In his upcoming memoir, Biden remarked he was disappointed when Pelosi and Schumer urged him to drop out of the presidential race in 2024. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Sources indicate that in conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir. The consensus view, even among some who’d worked for the former president, was that if he did anything other than accept some responsibility for his role in Donald Trump’s return to the White House, they didn’t have much appetite to hear what he had to say about anything else.

Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.

But while his perspective on the climactic moment of his political career will be the most scrutinized portion of Biden’s upcoming book, “Promise Me, America” seems primarily intended to offer the former president a platform he has otherwise not had since leaving office: to catalog what he sees as his historic achievements and offer his perspective on how he wrestled with the major concerns of our time.

Sources indicate that it’s often said that the only thing better than being president is being a former president. That has hardly been the case for Biden in the nearly 22 months since he left the White House, especially as he’s endured what his son Hunter has described as “debilitating” physical pain following a cancer diagnosis last March.

But where “Thanks, Obama” became a popular mantra nearly a decade ago for Democrats seeking to defend and celebrate the 44th president’s record in contrast with the first Trump administration, no such widespread nostalgia has emerged around Biden, as the party is loath to revisit the trauma of the summer of 2024.

According to recent reports, the sheer length of his latest book — more than 400 pages — seems an implicit acknowledgment that presenting a positive portrait of Biden’s single term in office is largely to be a solitary effort. Over 15 chapters, Biden offers sometimes mechanical descriptions of specific policies and their impact, but also new details of the sausage-making required to pass major initiatives like the Inflation Reduction Act. That legislation, he writes, was revived thanks in part to an Italian dinner hosted by Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo to make peace between West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin III and White House Chief of Staff Ron Klain.

Biden writes in sweeping terms about other accomplishments like responding to the COVID-19 crisis he inherited, calling his administration’s work “one of the most monumental achievements in public health history.” He repeatedly defends his frequent efforts to warn Americans about the need to safeguard our democracy even as critics in the press and his own party suggested he focus more on economic concerns.

Recent findings suggest that supporting Ukraine in its war against Russia gets the most extensive treatment of any single issue in the book, including a detailed account of Biden’s clandestine trip to Kyiv in February 2023. And the former Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman takes great effort to delve into the complexity of the U.S.-China relationship and his relationship with President Xi Jinping, while asserting that Taiwan “will likely be the most important foreign policy challenge in the world over the next generation.”.

Sources indicate that recurring throughout the book are expressions of optimism that under his administration, Washington was beginning to work again like it was supposed to, that America’s global leadership was being restored through its alliances, and that he was tackling problems that previous presidents had sidestepped. And in offering this comprehensive presentation of his record, Biden also offers his primary rationale for running again.

Industry observers note that “We had accomplished so much —  I wanted to finish the job. And yes: I believed I was the best person to do it,” he says. “I was the only person who had ever beaten Donald Trump. And I felt I was the best person to do it again.”.

One of Biden’s top advisers put it to me a different way in the months leading up to his decision to seek another term. “He has been running for president for 50 years. And the idea that he would actually be president and stop running for president is almost laughably preposterous.”.

The biggest question, of course, was his age, something Biden, who was 81 when he dropped out of the race, asserts he gave serious consideration.

It has been revealed that “I knew better than anyone how old I was. I knew what I was —  and wasn’t —  capable of doing. I carefully monitored how I was meeting the demands of the job. And there is not a single example of me failing to handle my responsibilities,” he writes.

The June 27 debate, of course, created a very different perception, as Biden acknowledges that his flubbed comment that “we finally beat Medicare” was to become “Exhibit A that I was too old to do the job.” But he tries to argue it was no different than the poor showings of previous incumbent presidents, including President Barack Obama, in their first debates.

“The difference was that every other president was given the chance to redeem themselves in a second debate. As it turned out, that chance would not be available to me,” Biden writes.

He argues the response he was seeing from voters at his public events after the debate didn’t justify the panicked response of elected Democrats in Washington, and that public polling revealed only minor slippage after the debate, until a steady drumbeat of elected Democrats publicly began calling for him to step aside.

Describing separate visits from former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., personally urging him to step aside, he indicates there was a “yawning gap between what I was seeing with Democratic voters and what I was hearing from the Democratic leadership in Washington.”.

“I have to admit it was personally hard to take so many old friends turning on me,” Biden says. “I told Schumer he had a lot of gumption (I may have said it differently at the time), coming to my home and telling me to get out of the race. Loyalty matters to me. If I give you my word, I stick with you. If I say I’m with you, I’m with you to the end.”.

At one point, Biden seems to reflect some resentment that some of the Democrats who would ultimately call on him to drop out of the race had themselves been too afraid to challenge him in the first place, saying: “Anyone who was scared off from running has no business being president.” While there was a constant narrative about the weakness of his candidacy, Biden acknowledges, the lack of a serious challenger was in fact a sign of his strength.

In a recent development, “I had it on good authority that several substantial names in Democratic politics had looked at running. They held meetings and took polls and talked to donors and to potential staff. If they thought I was weak or vulnerable, they would have taken their shot. But they didn’t,” he writes.

Biden’s defiant tone, and his insistence that the lack of party unity was a greater threat to his continued candidacy than his own performance, may be dismissed by Democrats who don’t want to revisit this difficult chapter. But as Schumer and other Democratic leaders are now facing their own internal challenges, “Promise Me, America” may also serve as a cautionary note for an ambitious crop of potential candidates hoping to reclaim the presidency in 2028.

#180186. Tech Report: Helping sick students stay home could matter for an entire campus

Tech Report: Helping sick students stay home could matter for an entire campus

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1298 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Encouraging sick college students to stay home for three days may help reduce the spread of flu-like illnesses.
  • According to recent reports, staying home when sick is advice that most people have heard many times over.
  • A campus trial now suggests that a polite request to stay in may help limit the spread of illness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Encouraging sick college students to stay home for three days may help reduce the spread of flu-like illnesses.

According to recent reports, staying home when sick is advice that most people have heard many times over. College students are known to attend class while ill anyway, according to earlier research on campus health.

A campus trial now suggests that a polite request to stay in may help limit the spread of illness.

Students with flu-like symptoms in that trial were encouraged to remain in their dorm rooms for three days.

It has been revealed that nobody was forced to comply with the request. Snacks and drinks were delivered by trial staff so that staying in would be easier for sick students.

The analysis was led by Brian Richardson, a statistician at Wake Forest University.

In a recent development, richardson worked with Allison Aiello of the Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health. Michael Hudgens of the UNC Gillings School of Global Public Health was also involved.

According to recent reports, the authors describe the evidence as moderate. The data also come from a single campus.

“It seems like almost every day in class, at least one person is sick,” stated Richardson.

In a recent development, the data were gathered in eX-FLU, a trial led by Aiello during the 2013 flu season. The trial was carried out at a large public university.

It has been revealed that college campuses can be particularly vulnerable to outbreaks of flu-like illness. Crowded housing and large social gatherings are the main reasons given by the authors.

In a recent development, A total of 579 students from six residence halls were enrolled in the trial. Many of them were recruited through friends who had already joined.

In a recent development, the six halls were split into 112 residential clusters for the purposes of the trial. Each cluster was then randomly assigned to an intervention arm or to a control arm.

Students in the intervention arm were encouraged to isolate in their rooms for 72 hours after their symptoms began.

Trial staff also helped those students notify professors and employers about any days they would miss.

No advice about isolation was given to students in the control arm at any point during the trial. Participants were asked to file weekly reports during the 10-week study.

Each report recorded whether the student had flu-like symptoms that week and which students they had met face to face. Reported cases were confirmed by trial staff.

Flu-like illness is defined by symptoms alone. Other respiratory infections can therefore fall under the same label as influenza.

Sources indicate that among 93 students, researchers recorded 113 cases of flu-like illness. Of these, 44 occurred in the group that received isolation advice and 69 in the control group.

It has been revealed that however, counting cases alone could not reveal how well the advice worked. Isolation was meant to protect others rather than the sick student.

Students from both groups lived in the same residence halls and shared friends. Isolation in one group could therefore prevent infections in the other.

Instead, researchers counted every reported face-to-face meeting between sick students and other participants as a possible opportunity for infection. They could not directly track whether the illness actually spread.

Industry observers note that suppose the advice had done nothing. In that case, students in the encouraged arm should have accounted for about 48.6% of these risky meetings. Instead, they accounted for 35.9%.

Sick students who were asked to stay in were behind a smaller share of the meetings where illness could spread.

A gap at least this large would still appear about 8% of the time if the advice made no difference. That figure is above the 5% cutoff that many scientists use for a firm result.

Even so, the authors concluded that encouraging sick students to stay in may have prevented flu-like illness in the trial.

Industry observers note that A separate look at the students’ reported contacts pointed in the same direction. Here, sick students in the two arms were compared. Those in the encouraged arm were less likely to start or keep up face-to-face contact.

“Even though students were simply encouraged – not required – to stay home when sick, and not everyone followed the recommendation perfectly, the intervention still appears to have reduced disease transmission,” Richardson noted.

Students in eX-FLU were linked to one another through their dorms, their friendships and the way they were recruited.

Industry observers note that most standard statistical methods are designed for people who have no such links to each other. A new testing procedure was therefore developed by Richardson and Hudgens for the eX-FLU data.

The procedure was built to check for an effect on infections, not just on social contacts. Fewer contacts would offer little public health benefit if the number of infections stayed the same.

Its performance was tested first on 10,000 simulated trials in each of three scenarios.

Physical distancing has well-documented downsides, according to the paper.

According to recent reports, mental health problems, economic hardship, disrupted schooling and poorer access to health care are all listed. Vulnerable populations are described as especially exposed to those harms.

According to recent reports, mandatory isolation is described in the paper as more invasive and more difficult to carry out. Upcoming vaccines can take months or years to develop, the researchers said.

Encouragement to isolate was described as something that could be introduced rapidly in response to upcoming outbreaks.

“People are much more likely to stay home when they’re sick if we make it possible for them to do so,” noted Aiello.

“Our findings suggest that encouraging voluntary isolation – and supporting it with simple resources like meal delivery and basic supplies – can help reduce disease transmission without requiring more restrictive public health measures.”.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention already tells people with respiratory viruses to stay home while sick.

It has been revealed that staying in after symptoms start leaves a gap, since flu can spread for a day or two before symptoms show. With COVID-19, spread before or without symptoms is even more common.

All of the contact data in eX-FLU came from weekly surveys filled out by the students themselves. Infected students listed more contacts than healthy ones, and the authors raised recall bias as one possible explanation.

Recent findings suggest that transmission itself was never observed in the trial. Only meetings between a sick student and another student could be counted.

Industry observers note that the test can show whether the three-day request had an effect. It was not designed to measure how large that effect was.

Industry observers note that all 579 students were part of one connected network on a single campus. Comparisons with other strategies could not readily be made with the eX-FLU data.

A larger sample or a different test statistic might have yielded stronger evidence, according to the authors.

In a recent development, A subset of students in the trial were given smartphones through a side project called iEpi. Those phones recorded when two students were near each other.

Bluetooth data of this kind could be used to correct the self-reported contacts.

The length of the request is another open question. A six-day version was considered in a pilot of eX-FLU. Pilot participants said they would be less likely to follow the longer request.

Future studies could compare several isolation periods and record both adherence and infections for each.

Trials on separate campuses could also test whether encouraging every student beats targeting only high-risk individuals.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Tech Report: The Sky Today on Monday, November 23: Double star Kurhah in Cepheus

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that looking for a sky event this week?
  • A few hours after sunset, the house-shaped constellation Cepheus stands on the point of its roof in the northern sky, above the Little Dipper.
  • Industry observers note that glowing at magnitude 4.3, Kurhah is not one of the stars in the house’s outline, but lies within the boxy base.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 22: Flat-floored lunar crater Schickard.

A few hours after sunset, the house-shaped constellation Cepheus stands on the point of its roof in the northern sky, above the Little Dipper. Cepheus is home to several lovely double stars, including Xi (ξ) Cephei, also known as Kurhah.

Industry observers note that glowing at magnitude 4.3, Kurhah is not one of the stars in the house’s outline, but lies within the boxy base. You can find it about midway between Alderamin (Alpha [α] Cep) and Iota (ι) Cep, the western and eastern points in the house’s box, respectively. Kurhah’s two components are separated by just under 8” — once you find the star in binoculars or your finder scope, any telescope will split them. The pair consists of a brighter magnitude 4.4 primary, which glows white, and a fainter magnitude 6.5 secondary, which appears to many observers as yellow.

If you happen to have a large telescope, you may want to give a nearby deep-sky treasure a try: planetary nebula NGC 7139 sits just 2° west-southwest of Kurhah, but it requires a large scope (8 inches at least) to spot, as this bubble of gas glows at magnitude 13.3. If available, an Oxygen-III filter will help bring it out by dimming the nearby stars.

According to recent reports, sunrise: 6:54 A.M.Sunset: 4:38 P.M.Moonrise: 3:37 P.M.Moonset: 5:52 A.M.Moon Phase: Full*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Sources indicate that full Moon occurs at 9:54 A.M. EST on November 24, bringing us our second Super Moon of the year. A Super Moon occurs when the Moon reaches Full phase close to perigee, its closest point to Earth, making our satellite appear larger and brighter than average. The November Full Moon is also called the Beaver Moon. A few hours earlier, before dawn, the Full Moon passes through the Pleiades star cluster (M45) in Taurus, occulting several of its bright stars.

Recent findings suggest that this is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope (just note that you may want a Moon filter if available, as our satellite is so big and bright). The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.

The 5th-magnitude star Celaeno (16 Tauri) disappears behind the Moon’s leading edge just moments before 6 A.M. CST, followed minutes later by 4th-magnitude Taygeta (19 Tau). Next to vanish is 4th-magnitude Maia (20 Tau) just before 6:20 A.M. CST, followed quickly by Sterope (21 Tau) a few minutes later. The latter two may be difficult to catch from the Midwest without optical aid, as sunrise is fast approaching. If you are using binoculars or a telescope in this region, make sure to put them away several minutes ahead of sunrise from your location. Celaeno reappears around 6:40 A.M. CST, 15 minutes or so before sunrise.

For specific timings from your location, visit the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

Recent findings suggest that alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

#180184. Why do some images stick in your memory while others fade?

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1331 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Why do some images stick in your memory while others fade?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1331 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recordings inside the amygdala show which pictures a person will remember, flagged within a third of a second of first seeing them.
  • According to recent reports, you can look at two pictures for the same length of time and, minutes later, recognize only one.
  • Some cells deep in the brain fired more strongly for pictures people later recognized.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recordings inside the amygdala show which pictures a person will remember, flagged within a third of a second of first seeing them.

According to recent reports, you can look at two pictures for the same length of time and, minutes later, recognize only one. In a new experiment, that difference showed up in the brain about a third of a second after each picture appeared.

Some cells deep in the brain fired more strongly for pictures people later recognized. Those cells sit in the amygdala, a structure better known for fear.

Jiayang Xiao and Ueli Rutishauser of Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles led the work.

They collaborated with colleagues at Johns Hopkins in Baltimore, Toronto Western Hospital, and the University of Toronto.

Everyone in the study had drug-resistant epilepsy and was already wired with electrodes, so surgeons could find where the seizures start. The memory test was a run of photographs on a screen, not anything from daily life.

“Our results demonstrate that the activity of specific kinds of neurons in the amygdala predicts, while the person sees an image for the first time, whether that image will later be remembered,” mentioned Rutishauser, who directs the Center for Neural Science and Medicine at Cedars-Sinai.

“Such episodic autobiographical memories, such as where we parked our car or how we spent a recent family vacation, are critical to navigating everyday life and a sense of who we are.”.

In a recent development, the amygdala’s reputation comes from fear and feeling. People with damage on both sides of it remember emotional material poorly.

Brain scans going back to the 1990s found that the harder the amygdala worked while someone studied an emotional picture, the better that person held onto it.

So the working explanation was feeling. A strong reaction marks a moment as worth keeping, and the amygdala supplies the reaction.

Recent findings suggest that xiao’s team asked something narrower. Instead of the amygdala’s overall activity, they tracked single neurons that each answer to one kind of thing.

It has been revealed that one cell fires for faces and ignores cars. Another fires for landscapes and ignores food. These are called category cells, and 40% of the amygdala neurons here were one.

The two explanations predict different things. If feeling is the mark, a jolt should lift every cell at once. If the content of the moment is the mark, only the cells tuned to that content should move.

The electrodes used for seizure monitoring carry eight hair-thin wires at the tip. That is fine enough to hear one neuron at a time.

Across 49 sessions with 42 patients, the team logged 1,871 well-isolated neurons. Of those, 575 were in the amygdala and 405 in the hippocampus, the region usually given credit for building memories.

It has been revealed that the task was plain. Photographs from five categories – people, food, animals, cars and landscapes – came up for two seconds each, and all of them were newly introduced to the patient.

Ten to 30 minutes later came a test of 400 images. Half had been in the earlier run and half had never been seen.

Six buttons were available for each one. Three mentioned latest and three said old, and the button within each set said how sure the patient was. Patients got 70.3% right, against 50% for guessing.

When patients first saw the pictures, category cells in the amygdala fired more strongly for images the patients later recognized than for those they didn’t.

The effect held only when the picture belonged to the cell’s own category.

It has been revealed that A cell tuned to faces fired more strongly for faces the patient later recognized. When the patient saw a car, that same cell’s activity gave no clue about whether the patient would recognize it later.

The difference in firing appeared about 350 milliseconds after the picture came into view and lasted until about 1,850 milliseconds.

The cells started responding to their preferred category at around 300 milliseconds, just before the first signs of which pictures patients would remember.

The effect held after researchers accounted for an online panel’s ratings of how pleasant and exciting the images were.

The ratings alone did not predict which pictures patients later recognized.

Sources indicate that the first dataset also demonstrated a weaker hippocampal signal that emerged around 1,300 milliseconds. In sessions that recorded both regions, the amygdala’s signal was stronger.

Rutishauser told Earth.com that the amygdala finding surprised him because the region is best known for responding to emotionally charged experiences. Here, its activity predicted which neutral images patients would later recognize.

The fusiform gyrus is a patch of visual cortex where two-thirds of the neurons were category cells, the highest share anywhere in the study.

It has been revealed that it demonstrated no such split between the pictures that were remembered and the ones that were not. Strong tuning by itself does not do this.

For the kind of memory tested here, Rutishauser said, the memory itself is stored in the hippocampus, and the amygdala works more like a controller.

“The system that produces the hot air (the heater) is separate and distinct from the controller (the thermostat),” he noted to Earth.com. “In analogy, here the amygdala would be the thermostat that controls the memory system.”.

The two regions were also in step. Slow electrical waves run through the hippocampus at around 10 cycles a second.

Amygdala cells fired more tightly in time with those waves when a picture was going to be remembered than when it was going to be forgotten.

Recent findings suggest that A second set of recordings, from 95 other patients and 5,744 neurons, carried the amygdala result again. The hippocampal effect did not come back in that one.

Among the pictures patients did recognize, the ones they felt sure about had drawn more firing at first sight than the ones they guessed at.

Recent findings suggest that the team then split each patient’s hits into two kinds of remembering. There is the vivid sort, where a person gets the moment itself back, and the vague sort, where a picture only feels familiar.

Sources indicate that the amygdala signal tracked the vivid kind, with a session-by-session correlation of 0.50. It showed no reliable link to familiarity.

It has been revealed that the effect was also stronger in the right amygdala than in the left. The authors call that part provisional and say it needs replication.

It may follow from their choice of material, since the right side of the brain is tied to remembering pictures and the left to remembering words.

Nothing here was switched on or off. Every number is a prediction read off a recording, so what the amygdala does for a memory, as opposed to what it claims about one, is still open.

The hippocampal effect that demonstrated up in one dataset and not the other is unsettled too.

The patients were also people with epilepsy severe enough to need brain surgery, and the electrodes went where their care required.

Amygdala tissue shrinks early in Alzheimer’s disease, and memory trouble is common in temporal lobe epilepsy.

Rutishauser said the findings are still too preliminary to guide treatment for people with memory problems.

However, he also noted that the research raises the possibility that a device designed to aid memory could target the amygdala, particularly on the right side of the brain.

One possibility is that deep brain stimulation could boost the activity of cells already responding to what a person sees.

Sources indicate that the idea is untested. Earlier teams that stimulated the whole amygdala electrically improved recognition of neutral pictures, but none aimed at the category cells.

Rutishauser’s team is now studying how the amygdala coordinates with other brain regions and whether stimulating it can improve memory.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Neuroscience.

#180183. Southern right whales are raising calves in places scientists didn’t expect

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1069 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Southern right whales are raising calves in places scientists didn’t expect

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1069 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Southern right whale mothers off Australia moved to a different nursing bay 54% of the time, crowding into sites where other whales were.
  • Researchers long thought southern right whales returned to the same bay where they were nursed to raise their own calves.
  • But off southern Australia, when researchers spotted the same mother with different calves in successive sightings, she was in a different nursing area 54% of the time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Southern right whale mothers off Australia moved to a different nursing bay 54% of the time, crowding into sites where other whales were.

Researchers long thought southern right whales returned to the same bay where they were nursed to raise their own calves.

But off southern Australia, when researchers spotted the same mother with different calves in successive sightings, she was in a different nursing area 54% of the time.

As southern right whales recovered from whaling, mothers and calves gathered in three stretches of coast, while other apparently suitable areas drew few whales.

Researchers think the presence of other whales may help explain why those three areas grew so quickly.

Anne Grundlehner of the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies at the University of Tasmania led the work with colleagues from the Australian Antarctic Division.

Her team used nearly five decades of aerial surveys and a photo catalog that tells individual right whales apart by the rough patches of skin on their heads.

Industry observers note that the catalog held 501 females seen with a calf in at least two different years between 1978 and 2012. Nearly two thirds, 63.5%, had nursed in more than one of the ten areas where the whales gather.

Among all 767 whales photographed in more than one year, 82.4% were seen in more than one area.

Industry observers note that mothers did come back to the three busiest areas more often. A mother seen in one of those three with a calf was back with her next calf 48% of the time. In the seven smaller areas, the figure was 15%.

“The results surprised us very much,” Grundlehner remarked in an interview with Earth.com.

Right whales were long believed to memorize the bay or beach where they were nursed as newborns and to return to it again and again, she remarked.

Sources indicate that A single-engine plane has flown the coast of Western Australia each winter since 1976. The route now runs about 1,550 miles (2,500 kilometers), from Perth to Ceduna in South Australia.

Southern right whales spend summer feeding far to the south and migrate to the coast in winter.

Mothers and calves stay in water 16 to 33 feet (5 to 10 meters) deep, close to the beach.

From 1,500 feet (450 to 500 meters) up, the crew spots almost every dark whale over the pale sand, then drops lower for a photograph.

Flights run from mid-August to mid-September, when calf numbers peak, and the annual count climbed from a handful to several hundred.

“When the whales were still a rarity along the coastline, the few whales visiting our coast seemed randomly distributed across suitable habitat. There weren’t any sites that stood out as hotspots,” Grundlehner remarked.

By the mid-1980s, southern right whales were gathering in three areas that filled up much faster than the rest of the coast.

The hotspots were Bremer and Doubtful Islands Bays, the stretch from Israelite Bay to Point Culver, and the Bunda Cliffs and Head of Bight.

In one of those areas, the number of mothers with calves rose by about 30% a year during the first decade.

Daughters returning to their birth bays can’t account for growth that fast. The team did the arithmetic.

With every female returning to her birth area, a calf every three years and no deaths, an area’s mothers could grow by at most 9.7% a year.

Which areas were busy at the start didn’t predict which became busy later, either. By a statistical measure of clumping, the whales bunched up more each year until about 2000, and the pattern has held since.

“Instead, as the population grew in numbers, the female whales were more likely to select nursing grounds where there were other whales,” said co-author Stuart Corney, an associate professor at the same institute.

The team’s reading is that mothers rely on a memory of past nursing sites plus the sight or sound of other whales, a pattern also proposed for humpback whales.

The three busy areas are more open and exposed than the other bays, which the authors suggest could make other whales easier to see or hear.

When only a few dozen whales reached the coast each year, there may have been no one to follow.

In a recent development, the whales do seem loyal to something, at a larger scale. Most repeat sightings of the same whale fell within about 620 miles (1,000 kilometers) of each other.

Grundlehner told Earth.com the findings imply more flexibility than researchers had assumed.

Grundlehner was asked what the findings mean for protecting nursing areas.

“This is extremely key for effective conservation management: it means that you should not just protect the places with the highest numbers of an animal species you are trying to protect, but all suitable habitat that is available and accessible to them,” she said.

Areas used by few whales today could matter more if the population grows or if climate change alters the coast, she noted. The range also needs to stay connected, with nothing blocking movement between nursing sites.

Growth is not guaranteed. Since about 2015, annual numbers in every area have flattened or dipped, and the population is estimated at a tenth of its pre-whaling size.

Grundlehner’s team reported in a 2025 study that recovery had stalled. She told Earth.com that calf numbers from 2023 to 2026 have stayed relatively stable, about 8% below their peak around 2016 and 2017.

The team can’t rule out other explanations for why some bays filled and others didn’t.

Records from before whaling are patchy, so it’s uncertain whether the three busy areas were busy two centuries ago.

The photo catalog also stops in 2012, so the latest decade of movements hasn’t been checked whale by whale.

And a more flexible whale isn’t necessarily a safer one. A population that follows other whales, or returns to a remembered bay, may keep using a place even after conditions there change, the authors wrote.

What draws whales to a particular bay, including local conditions and human disturbance, has to be worked out.

After that, someone has to watch whether the three crowded areas hold if the population starts growing again or shrinks further.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Industry observers note that isabel Angelo spends her days searching the cosmos for exoplanets and signs of extraterrestrial intelligence. But Angelo’s head isn’t in the stars. It’s buried under mountains of 0s and 1s — data from space telescopes old and latest.

Sources indicate that to piece together a fuller picture of what’s out there (alien megastructures around nearby stars, perhaps?), Angelo and her colleagues at the SETI Institute in Mountain View, Calif., are turning to machine learning models. These tools are analyzing the troves of telescope data for anomalies — things that look “weird” in space that we don’t know how to explain yet.

Industry observers note that most of the space weirdos will probably turn out to be total normies — a comet, a newborn star or a star surrounded by lots of gas and dust. “These are things that I would expect [the models] to find,” Angelo notes. “But the goal is to find something that’s not even in any of these categories.”.

Industry observers note that in the meantime, Angelo keeps her whimsy and wonder for space alive by remembering historic moments, like the reveal of the first portrait of a black hole in 2019. The scientists “put all of these telescopes all over the Earth. They wait for the Earth to rotate. They do all this math to construct this one image,” Angelo states. “I can’t believe how creative and innovative we have to be to learn about space. It’s such a specific and really fun challenge.”.

#180181. Breaking: Honey bee hives can lose their most destructive pest at high altitudes

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1580 w)

Breaking: Honey bee hives can lose their most destructive pest at high altitudes

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1580 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Low oxygen levels at high altitudes prevent varroa mites from reproducing, offering a potential way to protect honeybees.
  • It has been revealed that varroa mites kill honey bee colonies around the world.
  • Recent findings suggest that on the Tibetan Plateau, however, hives have gone untreated since 2006.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Low oxygen levels at high altitudes prevent varroa mites from reproducing, offering a potential way to protect honeybees.

It has been revealed that varroa mites kill honey bee colonies around the world. Beekeepers fight them with chemical treatments year after year.

Recent findings suggest that on the Tibetan Plateau, however, hives have gone untreated since 2006. Beekeepers there report that the mites simply disappear.

At two sites above about 11,500 feet (3,500 meters), low oxygen pressure kept the mites’ young from maturing.

In a recent development, A lack of oxygen had never before been shown to stop the mite from breeding. The finding could lead to upcoming ways of controlling the pest without chemicals.

The work was led by Huoqing Zheng of Zhejiang University. Researchers at the Xizang Academy of Agriculture and Animal Husbandry Sciences in Lhasa took part. So did scientists at the University of Salford in England.

Infested hives were trucked to different heights in China. The high-altitude effect was then copied in hives close to sea level.

Recent findings suggest that that second test was small, with five hives over 11 days. The team also hasn’t yet worked out how low oxygen stops the mites.

“For the first time, beekeepers in Tibet noticed the parasitic varroa mite mysteriously disappear from their colonies,” the authors wrote in a statement.

“We found that the low oxygen pressure on the Tibetan Plateau prevents the mites from reproducing.”.

According to recent reports, honey bees are the most vital managed pollinator of farm crops. For 60 years, Varroa destructor has been a leading cause of their deaths.

Recent findings suggest that A female mite enters a cell holding a bee larva about a day before the cell is sealed. Worker bees close it with a wax cap. Shut inside, the mite feeds on the larva. Her first egg is laid about 60 hours later.

The first egg always becomes a male. The next three or four become females. They mate with their brother inside the cell.

Time in a worker bee’s cell is limited. Only the male and up to three daughters grow up before the bee emerges. Only the adult daughters can survive outside, where they live and feed on adult bees.

Industry observers note that mite populations can grow rapidly once a colony becomes infested. Viruses are also transmitted by the mites as they feed. In cooler regions this combination can kill a colony within three years.

Industry observers note that in China, hives are treated with chemicals up to five times a year. Despite these treatments, high colony losses continue to be reported. The mite has been identified as the main cause of these losses.

Sources indicate that beekeeping on the plateau began only recently. In 2004 a total of 30 colonies were brought up to the region. Twenty years later the number of colonies had grown to more than 12,000.

In May 2024 a total of 60 colonies were taken from a single apiary in southern China. The colonies were divided into four groups of 15 for the experiment.

Recent findings suggest that one group was moved to another site in Xishuangbanna at roughly 1,800 feet (554 meters). The remaining three groups were transported by truck to sites located at higher elevations.

Kunming lies at roughly 6,450 feet (1,966 meters) and Nyingchi lies at roughly 9,600 feet (2,928 meters).

The highest site was Lhasa at roughly 11,900 feet (3,637 meters), more than twice the elevation of Denver.

Sources indicate that A decline in mite infestation was observed only in the Lhasa group. Before the move, mites were present in 9.3% of developing bees in the colonies headed for Lhasa.

This proportion had decreased to 1.6% after four months and no mites were detected after one year. No treatment had been applied to these hives. Instead the offspring of the mites failed to reach adulthood.

An increase in infestation was recorded at the lower sites over the same period.

In Kunming, the proportion of infested bees increased from 2.8% to 21.8% within two months. Those colonies were also attacked by hornets.

The elevation of Nyingchi proved insufficient to provide protection. Infestation there increased from 3.4% to 10.6% over four months and all colonies had died within a year.

Recent findings suggest that by the four-month mark, 25 of the 30 colonies at the two lowest sites had died. Mites were considered the most likely cause of these losses.

In contrast, 14 of the 15 Lhasa colonies remained alive and free of mites after one year. Thirteen of these colonies survived for two years without any treatment.

According to recent reports, to see what was going wrong, the team opened sealed cells with forceps. Each cell was checked under a flashlight, and young mites were counted in at least 218 infested cells per group.

Sources indicate that mother mites in Lhasa never laid more than two eggs. A second high site, tested in 2023, revealed the same thing. Those eggs seldom developed into the next stage.

Across 178 cells with older pupae at both sites, no daughter mite was on track to become a mated adult.

Industry observers note that it all happened fast. Just three days after the trucks arrived in Lhasa, mothers were laying far fewer eggs. By day six, each was laying one or two eggs that never developed.

Recent findings suggest that the team also looked for other explanations. Bees keep the brood nest at a steady warmth whatever the weather.

Nests in both Lhasa and Xishuangbanna stayed at about 93°F to 94°F (34°C), and humidity was similar too.

Worker bees took about 21 days from egg to adult in both places, so altitude had not slowed them. The lowland colonies had been trucked as well.

Yet in Lhasa, mite breeding stayed low for months after the hives stopped moving.

That left oxygen as a possible explanation. At Lhasa’s high altitude, oxygen pressure is only about two-thirds of that at sea level.

A second experiment was designed to test the role of oxygen directly. Low-oxygen hives were set up in Shaoxing in eastern China at about 290 feet (88 meters) above sea level.

A nitrogen-rich gas mixture was supplied from a cylinder to each of five small hives. The hives were wrapped in cling film to reduce leakage of the gas.

The flow was adjusted by hand whenever the oxygen readings moved outside the target range. The entrances were left open so that the bees could continue to forage.

Each hive was first kept on ordinary air and then switched to air with roughly Lhasa’s oxygen level. Under ordinary air the mother mites produced an average of 3.9 offspring.

According to recent reports, after 11 days under low oxygen this figure fell to 1.7. Almost none of these offspring developed beyond the egg stage.

Eleven days after their cells were sealed, the worker bees examined in both conditions had reached the newly emerged adult stage.

In a recent development, this fits with honey bees being known to forage as high as about 13,450 feet (4,100 meters). A similar decline in mite reproduction had been seen after six days in a 2023 trial with six hives.

Recent findings suggest that adult mites appear to tolerate low oxygen better than their offspring. In Lhasa the mother mites remained in the hives for several months although they could not reproduce.

In a recent development, an adult mite breathes through two networks of air tubes. Each network opens to the outside through a single pore. Adult females have also been reported to move air through these tubes by changing their body volume.

Newly hatched mites have no air tubes at all. Instead they absorb oxygen through the skin until the first molt, when the tubes are formed.

Most young mites in Lhasa failed to develop beyond this first stage. The authors suggest that this feature may contribute to the vulnerability of the young. This explanation has not yet been tested.

In a recent development, A similar pattern has been reported in fruit flies and in a common spider mite. In both species egg production is more sensitive to low oxygen than adult survival.

Other mechanisms may also be involved, such as the mother’s energy reserves or how cells use and sense oxygen. These possibilities are listed by the authors as questions for future work.

Moving hives to such high elevations is not practical for most beekeepers. The team therefore tested a simple and low-cost alternative.

According to recent reports, hive entrances were narrowed at night so that the breathing of the bees lowered the oxygen inside. In a pilot test this method partly reduced mite reproduction. “This physiological limit of varroa mites opens fresh avenues of controlling this globally destructive pest,” the authors wrote.

All of the results so far come from hives in China. Only one kind of bee was studied, the Italian honey bee, the type most commonly kept there.

The effect has not yet been tested in other regions or with other kinds of bees.

It is also unclear whether lowland hives can stay low in oxygen long enough to stop mites safely. The bees themselves would need to remain unharmed.

Future research could test whether narrowing hive entrances keeps mite numbers down over a full season.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Biology.
